items.title: Overcoming insect pest challenges for sustainable rice production in the Americas
items.abstract: Rice production in the Americas has expanded to meet a rising demand, but insect pests continue to threaten yields, grain quality, and farmer incomes. This review synthesizes current knowledge of the major insect pests affecting rice systems across the Americas and evaluates the performance, trade-offs, and complementarities of existing and emerging controls. It describes regional pest complexes, such as rice water weevil in the United States, Hoja Blanca vectors and stem borers in tropical areas, and late-season stink bugs across the continent. It examines how climate change, land use, and trade change invasion risk and pest activity timing. The review examines integrated pest management components: surveillance that blends field/edge scouting with decision-support tools and predictive modeling; cultural and agronomic practices that reduce baseline risk; biological control via parasitoids, predators, and entomopathogens using classical, augmentative, and conservation strategies; and threshold-based chemical control emphasizing resistance management, and residue stewardship. Innovative approaches, including AI-enabled forecasting, genomics-assisted resistance, and RNA interference technologies (RNAi) are also examined, alongside socioeconomic conditions that governing their adoption. Ultimately, the review develops adaptable, research-supported strategies that protect crop yields, preserve natural predators, increase farmers’ incomes, and bolster local food security, while tackling escalating environmental and climate issues through ecological, technological, and socioeconomic dimensions.

items.title: Eco-Environmental, Health and Socio-Economic Perspectives on Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins
items.abstract: Cyanobacteria, or blue-green algae, the first oxygenic photosynthetic organisms on Earth, play indispensable ecological roles as primary producers and drivers of biogeochemical cycles, and are also sources of human food, nutraceuticals, and biotechnological products. However, cyanobacterial harmful algal blooms (CyanoHABs), intensified by eutrophication and global climate change, threaten water quality, biodiversity, and human health due to their production of diverse secondary metabolites, i.e., taste and odor (T&O) compounds and cyanotoxins. This Special Issue, “Ecology and Toxicology of Cyanobacteria and Cyanotoxins”, compiles 13 papers from 9 countries that collectively advance our understanding of these issues across multiple scales. Cyanotoxins, including microcystins, cylindrospermopsins, anatoxins, and saxitoxins, can cause various hazards to animals and humans, including systemic toxicity, hepatotoxicity, genotoxicity, carcinogenicity, reproductive/developmental toxicity, neurotoxicity, immunotoxicity, and endocrine disruption. CyanoHABs are governed by complex bottom-up and top-down regulation, and blooms and cyanotoxin production are closely linked, but not always consistent/synonymous. Environmental stressors, e.g., phosphorus limitation, cold shock, and grazing pressure, selectively favor toxigenic genotypes, or can increase the cellular cyanotoxin quota, although overall population growth is suppressed. This can be explained by the fact that cyanotoxins can help cyanobacteria to better adapt to environmental stressors. When blooms disperse, demise, or are disrupted by certain interventions, the reduced biomass may increase exposure to dissolved, extra-cellular cyanotoxins if intra-cellular toxins are released faster than they are degraded or removed. We term the uncoupling of biomass and toxicity as the “cyanobacterial biomass–toxicity paradox”. We propose a “3P framework”, i.e., prediction, prevention, and prioritization, for the evidence-based risk management of CyanoHABs and cyanotoxins. We also advocate for more studies using multi-omics and artificial intelligence, as well as multi-disciplinary, multi-sectoral, and multi-stakeholder collaboration under the “One Health” umbrella to translate science into actionable solutions for sustainable development.

items.title: Cascading effects of soil water content on leaf chemistry and damage: implications for plant susceptibility to pests and pathogens in a drier world
items.abstract: Climate change is causing major alterations in precipitation regimes and soil water availability, with far-reaching effects on plant traits. Changes in plant chemistry under drought scenarios are particularly relevant, as they can modulate plant interactions with antagonistic organisms. However, how such changes in plant chemistry affect plant susceptibility to biotic damage remains poorly understood. Here we integrated results from a systematic literature review and a field study in Mediterranean mixed forests to advance our understanding of the cascading effects of reduced soil water content on leaf reserves, defences and damage caused by herbivores and pathogens. The literature review revealed that studies linking soil water content with leaf chemistry and damage remain scarce and reported a variety of direct and indirect relationships between the three components. Nevertheless, most studies found higher leaf damage under drier conditions. Results from our field study also supported that leaf damage increased with decreasing soil water content, a relationship largely mediated by changes in leaf phenolic compounds. In Mediterranean forests, phenolics play a major role in protection against desiccation and UV radiation due to their antioxidant properties, yet certain phenolic compounds can also benefit antagonists. Overall, our findings suggest that leaf damage can increase in a drier climate, forcing tree species to face fundamental trade-offs when protecting themselves from the combined stress imposed by abiotic (drought) and biotic (pests and pathogens) components of global change.

items.title: Parasites as environmental bioindicators and climate-sensitive sentinels in arid ecosystems: a one health synthesis with a focus on Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Parasites integrate environmental conditions across trophic levels and may therefore provide sensitive, mechanistically interpretable signals of ecosystem change. This narrative synthesis evaluates the potential of parasites and parasite communities as environmental bioindicators and climate-sensitive sentinels, with particular emphasis on arid ecosystems and Saudi Arabia. We integrate evidence from terrestrial, aquatic, marine, and zoonotic systems to examine how warming, drought, hydrological change, salinity, pollution, land-use transformation, and host-mediated vector movement influence parasite occurrence, transmission, phenology, community composition, and contaminant accumulation. The evidence supports two complementary bioindicator functions: accumulation indicators, in which parasites concentrate environmental contaminants, and effect indicators, in which parasite prevalence, phenology, richness, or community structure responds to environmental disturbance. Saudi marine systems provide particularly strong examples, including trace-metal accumulation by acanthocephalans and nematodes, community-level changes associated with habitat degradation, and seasonal transmission of Kudoa sp. in Priacanthus tayenus . Terrestrial and waterborne systems provide additional candidate signals through tick phenology and the distribution of Cryptosporidium and Giardia. However, the current evidence base is dominated by cross-sectional studies, heterogeneous diagnostic methods, and geographically fragmented datasets; consequently, parasites should be regarded as promising candidate sentinels rather than validated early-warning indicators. We identify priority research needs and propose a One Health surveillance architecture integrating standardised parasitological sampling, environmental and meteorological measurements, molecular identification, remote sensing, livestock-movement data, and multivariate community analysis. Long-term, coupled datasets will be essential to distinguish climate-driven signals from concurrent anthropogenic pressures and to translate parasite bioindication from an ecological concept into an operational monitoring tool for arid and peri-arid regions.

items.title: Construction of an agricultural green development indicator system and trend projection for the 15th five-year plan period in Jiangxi Province
items.abstract: Introduction As a central pillar of high-quality agricultural advancement, agricultural green development (AGD) is essential for promoting agricultural and rural modernization and building a strong agricultural province. Methods Focusing on Jiangxi Province—a key traditional agricultural province and a national ecological civilization pilot zone—this study establishes a comprehensive AGD evaluation indicator system covering 18 secondary indicators across five dimensions: resource conservation and efficient utilization, environmental governance of production sites, agricultural ecological restoration, green industrial development, and green technological support. The entropy weight method measures Jiangxi’s AGD level from 2010 to 2025, while the GM(1,1) grey model forecasts its trajectory during the 15th Five-Year Plan period (2026–2030). Results The results show that: (1) Jiangxi’s comprehensive AGD index grew steadily from 11.37 to 80.51, with agricultural ecological restoration carrying the largest weight (29.42); (2) the index is projected to reach 86.97 by 2030; all fitted GM(1,1) models have MAPE below 10%, meeting the Grade I accuracy standard. Discussion Although constraints remain, including inadequate hilly mechanization, limited smallholder green production capacity, and difficult non-point source pollution control, future work should strengthen green resource utilization, deepen production-site governance, improve technological support, and optimize incentives to drive the green transition of smallholders.

items.title: Newly planted woodlands improve connectivity for woodland fauna, flora and fungi
items.abstract: Abstract Context Young planted woodlands may only support a small proportion of the biodiversity found in mature woodlands but may play an important role in promoting species movements and enhancing biodiversity due to their emerging structural similarities. Objectives We assessed whether recently planted woodlands increase connectivity between mature woodland patches relative to agricultural fields, and whether responses vary across active (small mammals, ground invertebrates) and passive (plants, fungi) dispersers. Methods We used a multi-taxa natural experiment across paired sites where mature woodlands were either connected by planted woodland or separated by farmland. Movement was quantified using PIT-tagging of small mammals and beetles, pitfall trapping, vegetation surveys, airborne spore traps and soil eDNA metabarcoding. A Bayesian beta-binomial model estimated taxon-specific habitat preferences for dispersal. Results Although we did not detect inter-patch movements, we detected higher movement of wood mice, ground active invertebrates, plants, and fungi into new woodlands relative to agricultural fields, whereas, field voles exhibited minimal movement, and some airborne fungal groups showed reduced movement within planted woodlands. Young woodlands generally supported higher woodland specialist richness, abundance or occurrence than fields but did not support the full complement of species associated with mature woodlands. Conclusions Newly planted woodlands can enhance functional connectivity for multiple woodland associated taxa, but the benefits are taxon specific and shaped by differences in mobility, dispersal mode and establishment requirements. Strategic placement of planted woodland adjacent to existing woodland can improve landscape scale connectivity, further improved by additional habitat development to support more specialised species.

items.title: Enns Entomology Museum Collection (EEM)
items.abstract: The Enns Entomology Museum (EEM) is the insect collection of the University of Missouri, Columbia, Missouri, USA, holding more than 7 million specimens. It preserves pinned, papered, slide-mounted and fluid-preserved insects and other arthropods as a permanent record of biodiversity supporting taxonomy, ecology, agriculture and conservation. Founded in 1874 with Charles V. Riley as its first curator, the collection was renamed in 1980 for entomologist Wilbur R. Enns. Donations totaling nearly five million specimens since 1941, including the Missouri Department of Conservation's statewide aquatic invertebrate samples, have made it the reference collection for the insects of the Ozark Plateau, from which 80–90% of the material originates. Holdings also include type material, papered Odonata, insect galls, fossils, about 35,000 microscope slides, and a wet collection of about 4.5 million aquatic insects.

items.title: Terahertz field-induced giant symmetry modulations in a van der Waals antiferromagnet
items.abstract: Abstract Strong-field terahertz (THz) excitations enable dynamic control over electronic, lattice and symmetry degrees of freedom in quantum materials. Here, we uncover pronounced terahertz-induced symmetry modulations and coherent phonon dynamics in the van der Waals antiferromagnet MnPS 3 , in which inversion symmetry is broken by its antiferromagnetic spin configuration. Our time-resolved second harmonic generation measurements reveal long-lived giant oscillations in the antiferromagnetic phase, with amplitudes comparable to the equilibrium signal, driven by phonons involving percent-level atomic displacements relative to the equilibrium bond lengths. The temporal evolution of the rotational anisotropy patterns indicates a dynamic breaking of mirror symmetry, modulated by two vibrational modes at 1.7 THz and 4.5 THz, with the former corresponding to a hidden mode not observed in equilibrium spectroscopy. These effects arise in part from a field-induced charge rearrangement mechanism that lowers the local crystal symmetry and couples to the phonon modes. We uncover a long-lived field-driven response with a complex THz polarization dependence, consistent with a metastable state of reduced symmetry. Through comparison with simulations, we interpret this response in terms of a potential antiferromagnetic-to-ferrimagnetic transition. Our results establish an effective field-tunable pathway for driving excitations otherwise weak in equilibrium.

items.title: Quantum-enhanced phase sensitivity in an all-fiber Mach–Zehnder interferometer
items.abstract: Abstract Recent advances in quantum photonics have enabled increasingly robust protocols in optical phase estimation, achieving precisions beyond the standard quantum limit and approaching the Heisenberg limit. While intrinsic losses hinder the realization of unconditional super-sensitivity, reaching quantum advantage, defined as sensitivity surpassing that of any classical counterpart with identical resources, remains achievable. Here we experimentally demonstrate such an advantage using a fully fibered Mach–Zehnder–type interferometer operating at telecom wavelengths, free of post-selection. The scheme relies on the conversion of polarization-entangled photon pairs, a degree of freedom commonly favored for experimental convenience, into energy–time entanglement, which is particularly well suited for scalable fiber-based sensors. All system imperfections, including asymmetric losses and detector inefficiencies, are accounted for in the Fisher information analysis, yielding a measured quantum advantage of 10%. This result highlights the practicality of compact, alignment-free quantum interferometers for real-world sensing applications.

items.title: The Metallicity Distribution of the Ultra-Faint Dwarf Galaxy Segue 1
items.abstract: Ultra-faint dwarf galaxies (UFDs; stellar masses M * < 10 5 M ⊙ ) offer unique insights into early chemical evolution in low-mass systems. However, interpreting their metallicity distribution functions (MDFs) has been challenging due to limited spectroscopic samples, especially beyond the red giant branch. We present metallicities from the Ca II K absorption feature, measured from low-resolution ( R ∼ 1000 ) Keck/LRIS spectroscopy of 40 stars in the UFD Segue~1 ( M * ≈ 500 M ⊙ ), including both red giant branch and main-sequence turnoff stars, resulting in a metallicity sample more than six times larger than previously published data for Segue~1. The resulting MDF has an average [Fe/H] = − 2.52 ± 0.10 dex and a dispersion of σ = 0.59 ± 0.06 dex, and is best described by a single Gaussian, with no evidence for multimodal substructure. This is consistent with a continuous, short-duration ($$1~Gyr) episode of star formation and chemical enrichment prior to reionization. The nonzero metallicity spread reaffirms its classification as a galaxy. Segue~1 highlights the rich chemical enrichment histories present even in the least massive galaxies, and underscores the importance of deep spectroscopic follow-up to fully characterize these ancient stellar systems.

items.title: Ultraviolet diversity of Little Red Dots as a probe for direct-collapse black hole ages
items.abstract: Little Red Dots (LRDs) uncovered by the James Webb Space Telescope have been proposed as candidate galaxies hosting embedded accreting direct-collapse black holes (DCBHs), yet the relative ultraviolet (UV) emission of their host galaxy remains highly uncertain and diverse across the population. Using a large-scale cosmological hydrodynamical simulation from the MELI ⊙ RA suite, we investigate the contribution of PopIII stars and accreting DCBHs in LRD candidates at z > 8.5 , in the rest-frame 0.2 − 0.6 μ m band. We find that the UV emission from the host galaxy evolves rapidly over the first ∼ 30 M y r following DCBH formation, reflecting the build-up of stellar mass and metal enrichment. This evolution consists of a rapid transition from initially BH-dominated systems, with negligible stellar mass, low metallicity, and high accretion rates, to progressively more developed hosts in which rapid star formation enhances the UV output and metallicity increases. After ∼ 30 M y r , the stellar continuum typically overwhelms the accreting DCBH contribution, producing bluer colours and more extended stellar distributions. As a result, UV-bright LRDs are predicted to host older DCBHs, have higher gas-phase metallicities, lower BH-to-stellar mass ratios, and lower Eddington ratios. The short-lived nature of the LRD phase places strong constraints on their emergence over cosmic time. Overall, our results suggest that DCBH ages can be constrained from the host galaxy contribution to the UV-optical spectrum of LRDs, relative to that of the accreting DCBH, and support the picture in which a DCBH evolutionary sequence is systematically encoded in emission line properties, gas-phase metallicities, and accretion states.

items.title: Deconfined quantum critical point in a dissipative spin-1/2 chain
items.abstract: Open quantum spin systems offer a previously unexplored route to realizing deconfined quantum criticality. We consider a spin-1/2 $J$-$Q_3$ chain, consisting of an antiferromagnetic (AFM) Heisenberg exchange and a competing multi-spin interaction favoring a valence-bond solid (VBS) state, with each spin component coupled to a bosonic bath. Using non-Abelian bosonization and renormalization-group (RG) analysis, combined with large-scale quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) simulations, we determine the phase diagram and the associated phase transitions of the model. We show that strong dissipation stabilizes an AFM phase for sub-Ohmic, Ohmic, and super-Ohmic baths. Continuous AFM-VBS transitions at finite dissipation are found upon increasing the multi-spin interaction in both the sub-Ohmic and Ohmic regimes. Critical properties are obtained through perturbative RG analysis and QMC simulations. In the Ohmic case, the critical point features spinon deconfinement and emergent O(4) symmetry. In the sub-Ohmic regime, the transition may also involve spinon deconfinement, provided that spinons remain deconfined in the dissipative VBS phase. In addition, in the super-Ohmic regime, we propose a transition from AFM phase to a quasi-long-range ordered phase.

items.title: Multipolar neutrino radiation in binary neutron star mergers: Angular structure, rotational variability, and implications for electron fraction
items.abstract: The angular structure and temporal variability of neutrino emission from binary neutron star mergers are characterized using fully general-relativistic simulations with energy-integrated M1 neutrino transport across a representative set of equations of state, total masses, and mass ratios. The angle-dependent neutrino energy flux is extracted on a spherical surface outside the remnant and decomposed into spherical harmonics to quantify its multipolar content and evolution. Following the initial post-merger transient, the neutrino radiation flux approaches an axisymmetric configuration dominated by a strong quadrupolar component, producing persistent polar flux enhancement and equatorial suppression due to torus shadowing. The dipolar contribution remains subdominant, indicating the absence of sustained one-sided emission. The degree of anisotropy increases with mass asymmetry and for softer equations of state, reflecting the compactness and morphology of the remnant--disk system. Superimposed on this time-averaged geometry, coherent azimuthal modulations associated with the $m=1$ mode are identified. Fourier analysis reveals a characteristic frequency of $\sim 0.6$--$0.7$ kHz, consistent with differential rotation in the remnant and inner disk layers, indicating a dynamical coupling between rotational structure and neutrino emission variability. Finally, we quantify how the same quadrupole-dominated radiation geometry induces a latitude-dependent equilibrium electron fraction. The polar material is driven close to the neutrino-equilibrium target, whereas equatorial material remains systematically more neutron-rich and below equilibrium.

items.title: Widespread plasma jets in the Martian magnetosheath revealed by dual-spacecraft observations
items.abstract: Plasma jets in planetary magnetosheaths are transient, high dynamic pressure structures capable of strongly perturbing downstream magnetospheres and modulating solar wind energy transfer. Although recently identified at Mars, their formation mechanisms and global occurrence remain poorly constrained. Using dual-spacecraft observations from Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN and Tianwen-1, we show that magnetosheath jets occur throughout the Martian magnetosheath, in striking contrast to Earth where jet occurrence is strongly controlled by interplanetary magnetic field orientation and largely confined to quasi-parallel shock regions. We propose that this widespread distribution is linked to Mars’ extended hydrogen corona, which generates pickup ions that drive proton-cyclotron waves upstream of the bow shock. Because this mechanism is generic to any body with an extended corona (or exosphere) embedded in a stellar wind, this finding bears on solar–wind interactions at comets and other small bodies, and on the space environments of unmagnetized terrestrial exoplanets. These results indicate that magnetosheath jet formation can be governed not only by external solar wind forcing but also by intrinsic planetary properties, pointing to a previously unrecognized pathway for solar wind–planet coupling at unmagnetized worlds.

items.title: Socio-Scientific Issues (SSI) Approach to Physics Learning: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Physics learning in the 21st century requires instructional approaches that develop students’ conceptual understanding while fostering their ability to analyze and make informed decisions regarding complex real-world issues. The Socio-Scientific Issues (SSI) approach has emerged as a promising strategy for connecting physics concepts with social and environmental contexts. This study aims to systematically examine the application of the Socio-Scientific Issues (SSI) approach in physics learning during the period 2015–2025. Specifically, this study identifies topic trends, learning models, the implementation of the SSI approach, and its impact on the physics learning process. The method used is a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) following the PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses) guidelines. Data were collected from the ScienceDirect and Google Scholar databases using the keywords "Learning Outcomes", "Physics Learning", and "Socio-Scientific Issues". A total of 22 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final synthesis. The results indicate that climate change is the most frequently addressed topic in implementing the SSI approach in physics learning, with junior high school being the dominant educational level represented in the reviewed studies. Furthermore, the SSI approach has proven effective in improving students' scientific argumentation skills and strengthening their understanding of physics concepts in real-life contexts. These findings suggest that integrating socio-scientific issues into physics learning provides a meaningful and contextual strategy for enhancing science education.

items.title: Identity, individuality and naming
items.abstract: Abstract The philosophical theorem “identity of the indiscernibles” (Leibniz’s law) is inspected from the standpoint of objects of our physical world. Although logically stringent, it suffers from a naïve use of terms such as objects and properties. A modified formulation that takes account of the coupling between objects and state and so matches reality, is proposed. The transition from indiscernibility to eventually individuality can be followed along increasing complexity, which leads to irreversible features and finally to irreproducibilty. This path is also mirrored by the issue of naming and the transition from physical, chemical nomenclature to biological nomenclature and finally personal naming. Personal names, in order for them to be adequate, require individuality and lack of reproducibility.

items.abstract: With the increasing tendency of incorporating technology into environments and activities in everyday life, new methods are being proposed to better integrate devices and mankind.Networks designed for monitoring areas through video and image systems are being implemented in several applications.Recent studies have shown interest from both the academy and industry to integrate wireless surveillance networks with lowcost and long range transmission technologies, such as LoRa (Long Range).With the intention to explore this topic, this work presents the development of a system prototype for intelligent monitoring as a basis to future implementation of low-cost LoRabased Wireless Image Sensor Networks (WISN).The developed system consists of a processing unit, a data routing interface and multiple sensor nodes.Its operation is autonomous and initiated through the detection of human presence, by the sensor node, capturing an image of the individuals present at each detection.The data is transmitted through LoRa devices to the central hub, where python-based methods of facial detection and recognition are employed.Several tests were performed to both adjust the system and to verify its efficiency.The results achieved indicate the viability of the proposed low-cost LoRa-based WISN.

items.title: Are cortical microcircuits optimized for information flux?—A simulation-based reverse engineering study
items.abstract: Introduction A sufficiently large information flux in recurrent neural networks, quantified by the mutual information between successive network states, has been proposed as a marker of rich information-processing capabilities. This raises the question of whether biological neural networks, such as cortical microcircuits, may be structurally organized to enhance information flux. Methods To investigate this possibility, we study a simplified model of the cortical layer 5 architecture, in which a densely and strongly interconnected core population is embedded within a larger supporting network. Results Surprisingly, we find that the embedding network exerts a pronounced flux-enhancing effect on the core dynamics. Systematic reverse-engineering analyses reveal that the embedding network primarily generates heterogeneous negative mean inputs that shift the core neurons into a higher-flux operating regime. Replacing the full time-dependent embedding signals by corresponding constant biases preserves this flux-enhancing effect, indicating that the detailed signal dynamics are not essential under the tested conditions. We further show that the information flux can be increased even beyond the biologically embedded case by applying optimized uniform or neuron-specific biases to the core neurons, and that similarly high values can emerge from a simple local adaptive-bias rule. Additional controls show that adaptive regulation and independently tuned inhibitory targeting further improve the embedded network, whereas removing the privileged strong-weight organization of the core abolishes the embedding advantage. Discussion These results suggest that the surrounding network acts as a distributed regulator that prevents a strongly recurrent core from becoming trapped in saturated, low-flux states, rather than as an optimizer of information flux. Our findings are relevant both for the functional interpretation of biological neural circuits and for the design of artificial recurrent systems such as reservoir computers.

items.title: Visual Trend Analysis of E-Commerce Thumbnails Using Parallel Computing for Image Big Data
items.abstract: The rapid growth of e-commerce platforms has led to the massive accumulation of product thumbnail images, making manual visual analysis inefficient and conventional sequential processing methods insufficient to handle such data volumes in a timely manner. Given the crucial role of thumbnails in influencing consumer purchasing decisions, computational strategies are required to accelerate the analysis process without compromising classification accuracy. This study applies a parallel computing approach combined with deep learning to improve the efficiency of visual trend analysis using two primary datasets: 2,608 images for model training and validation, and 40,254 images for large-scale inference. The proposed framework integrates parallel image preprocessing on multi-core CPUs, the development of a Convolutional Neural Network based on MobileNetV2 using a transfer learning approach, and batch-based parallel inference on GPUs. The developed model demonstrates stable and convergent performance, achieving a training accuracy of 0.85 and a validation accuracy of 0.83. Efficiency testing during the preprocessing stage shows that the parallel approach is more effective under large data workloads, providing a speed improvement of up to 1.58×. During the inference stage, predictions for 500 images can be completed in 1.84 seconds compared to 41.76 seconds using the sequential method, resulting in a significant computational speedup of 22.8×. Big data analysis reveals a polarization of visual strategies, where technology product categories are dominated by infographic-style thumbnails, fashion categories rely heavily on human model representations, and household product categories emphasize clean product visuals supported by promotional elements. This study concludes that the application of parallel computing significantly enhances the efficiency and scalability of visual big data analysis in e-commerce and supports more operational and strategic mapping of visual trends.

items.title: Self-Control and Social Media Addiction: A Review Among Generation Z University Students
items.abstract: This study aims to examine the relationship between self-control and social media addiction among Generation Z university students. The rapid development of digital technology has made social media an inseparable part of daily life, especially for Generation Z who are considered digital natives. However, excessive use of social media may lead to addictive behaviors that negatively affect psychological well-being, academic performance, and social functioning. This research employed a quantitative correlational design with 354 undergraduate students as participants. Sampling was conducted using a convenience sampling technique. Self-control was measured using the Brief Self-Control Scale (BSCS), while social media addiction was measured using a Social Media Addiction Scale adapted from previous studies. Data were analyzed using Spearman’s rho correlation test due to non-normal data distribution. The results revealed a significant negative correlation between self-control and social media addiction (r = -0.109 ; p = 0.041). This indicates that higher levels of self-control are associated with lower levels of social media addiction. The findings emphasize the importance of strengthening self-regulation skills among university students to prevent problematic social media use. Future research is recommended to explore mediating or moderating variables such as social support and psychological well-being.

items.title: Jointly predicting courses and grades using a transformer-based model
items.abstract: Existing predictive models in learning analytics often treat student academic history as a simple sequence, overlooking the concurrent nature of courses taken within a semester. This simplification can lead to inaccurate performance predictions, particularly for students with heavy or challenging course loads. This paper introduces a TRansformer for Academic Course-grade Estimation (TRACE) that addresses this limitation by jointly predicting both the set of courses a student will take and their corresponding grades for an upcoming semester. Our approach encodes courses on a per-semester basis to capture the effects of course concurrency and utilizes a novel loss function combining course-set prediction with grade prediction. We demonstrate that predicting courses taken in addition to the grades in those courses leads to significant improvements in prediction quality. Trained on ten years of institutional data, our joint prediction model reduces mean absolute error by nearly 50% compared to an identical architecture that predicts grades alone. The model also outperforms traditional LSTM-based sequential models, as well as graph neural network-based approaches, and offers natural ways to incorporate student attribute data. This work demonstrates the utility of modern neural architectures for creating interpretable models that can be adapted to new institutions via retraining and recalibration, as well as the importance of key techniques, such as predicting courses taken during training. We discuss how this model could be incorporated into early detection systems at institutions of higher education.

items.title: Privacy Failure in Split-LLM Training, The Returned Gradient Nullifies the Decoys
items.abstract: We present a systems-security case study of a two-node split-LLM training system whose privacy evaluation passed while leaving an observable channel untested. The Trusted Local Node (TLN) sends protected activations to the Untrusted Cloud Node (UCN), the UCN returns its output, and TLN, holding the private loss, returns the output gradient. The frame the UCN receives mixes real rows with decoys, and the loss ignores the decoys. Their gradients are exactly zero, so the pattern of zeros reveals which rows were real. We measure it with a protocol fixed in advance: a leak injected at known strength to prove the instrument can see one, a shuffled-label control to prove it does not report absent leaks, and a threshold set before the runs. Across nine seeds, the zeros identified the real rows on every frame, 4,096 of 4,096 per run. An attack on the frame contents recovered about one extra token per hundred over a constant-guess baseline (+0.65 to +1.50 percentage points); the shuffled controls recovered nothing. A second set of runs repeated this on a configuration that keeps model quality within budget, so the finding is not confined to a setting nobody would deploy. On both datasets, every such run passed the forward-channel privacy check and the quality check, yet failed that same check once the returned gradient was included. Clipping and noising each row of the gradient closed the leak for about 0.01 nats of held-out cross-entropy. The system is not thereby safe: five classes of attack, including those accumulating observations across training steps, were never measured.

items.title: Conservation and Development of the Thai Children’s Folk Play Wisdom in Andaman Coastal Provinces
items.abstract: The objectives of this research are to: 1) examine the value of traditional folk play on physical, emotional, mental, social, and cognitive development of Thai children in the Andaman coastal provinces; 2) examine factors affecting the conservation of folk play wisdom in the Andaman coastal provinces; and 3) propose guidelines to develop Thai children folk plays in Andaman provinces. The sample consisted of 400 primary school students and 50 key informants including school administrators, primary school homeroom teachers, physical education teachers, local leaders, folk philosophers, and parents. Research instruments comprised: 1) a handbook of traditional folk play for Thai children in the Andaman coastal provinces; 2) an observation form for assessing the value of traditional folk play; and 3) interview protocols regarding conservation factors and development guidelines for traditional folk play. The content validity of the instruments was determined by calculating the Index of Item-Objective Congruence (IOC) with values ranging from 0.67-1.00. The reliability coefficients were 0.87 for the observation form and 0.85 for the interview protocols. Data were analyzed using mean, standard deviation, and content analysis. The findings revealed that: 1) traditional folk play significantly contributed to children's development across all aspects (physical, emotional, mental, social, and cognitive) at high levels; 2) conservation of folk play wisdom was influenced by personal factors, family and social factors, economic factors, and technological factors; and 3) effective guidelines for developing folk play wisdom included implementing supportive local policies, establishing educational institution policies, adapting play formats and equipment, and implementing targeted projects. The research findings provide valuable direction for developing local curricula and activities that promote the conservation of indigenous wisdom in educational institutions.

items.title: Cyber Soldier project - A threat-led methodology for assessing the Digital Resilience of cybersecurity systems
items.abstract: In order to comply with European regulatory frameworks like the Digital Operational Resilience Act (DORA), we propose the Cyber Soldier approach and tool set, which presents a threat-led approach for evaluating the digital resilience of cybersecurity systems inside enterprises. This approach, in contrast to conventional vulnerability assessments or penetration testing, focuses on simulating the tactics, methods, and procedures (TTPs) of actual attackers in order to assess the efficacy of operational resilience mechanisms and cybersecurity measures in production systems. In order to assess the organization's readiness for complex cyberthreats, the suggested approach combines threat information, red team scenario creation, and detection performance analysis into a single procedure. We show how the proposed framework connects the operational practice of resilience testing with the strategic compliance obligations under DORA. We also provide some preliminary statistics about the use of the Cyber Soldier toolkit in practical settings.

items.title: Machine Learning for Biodiversity Conservation: A Review of Ecological Monitoring, Species Prediction, and Conservation Applications
items.abstract: Biodiversity loss, habitat degradation, climate change, invasive species, and unsustainable resource use have intensified the need for effective and evidence-based conservation strategies. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a valuable approach for processing large and complex ecological datasets, identifying species, predicting species distributions, monitoring ecosystem changes, and supporting conservation decision-making. This review examines the applications, methodological developments, benefits, and limitations of machine learning in biodiversity conservation, with particular emphasis on ecological monitoring, species prediction, and practical conservation interventions. It synthesizes major approaches, including supervised learning, unsupervised learning, deep learning, computer vision, acoustic classification, remote sensing, and ensemble modelling. Evidence from previous research demonstrates that automated camera-trap analysis, bioacoustic monitoring, satellite imagery, and environmental DNA analysis can improve the efficiency and spatial coverage of biodiversity assessments. Species distribution models also support the identification of suitable habitats, climate-sensitive areas, and potential conservation priorities. Furthermore, machine learning can facilitate invasive-species detection, wildlife population assessment, habitat restoration, and protected-area management. However, its effectiveness depends on data quality, representative training datasets, model interpretability, computational resources, and collaboration between ecologists, conservation practitioners, and local communities. Ethical concerns, including sensitive species-location disclosure, surveillance risks, and unequal access to technological infrastructure, also require attention. The review concludes that machine learning can strengthen biodiversity conservation when integrated with ecological expertise, field validation, transparent governance, and long-term monitoring. Future research should prioritize geographically representative datasets, explainable models, uncertainty assessment, and conservation outcomes that can be independently evaluated.

items.title: OpenVLHarness: Real World Visual Agentic Tool-Use with Multimodal Memory
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have made rapid progress on visual reasoning, yet many tasks require evidence that is difficult to obtain through internal reasoning alone: our controlled study on 22 benchmarks shows that simply increasing the inference budget of the base model yields only modest gains. Such tasks demand grounded perception, external knowledge, and numerical measurements obtained through heterogeneous tools, whose outputs must be made interpretable to the model and retained across reasoning steps. We introduce OpenVLHarness, a multimodal reasoning harness organized around a capability layer and persistent multimodal memory. The capability layer combines task-level tool interfaces with evidence rendering, providing consistent access to heterogeneous backends and converting their outputs into model-readable observations. Persistent multimodal memory retains the corresponding images, structured data, and web references as addressable artifacts throughout each query. A coding interface executes generated programs over stored data, enabling computations that combine results from multiple tools. Together, these mechanisms support an iterative process of acquiring, inspecting, and composing multimodal evidence. Evaluated on 22 benchmarks with eight open and proprietary backbones, OpenVLHarness improves average scores by 9.7-12.6 points over matched no-tool baselines, including +11.2 with Qwen3-VL-8B, +9.7 with Kimi K3, and +9.9 with GPT-6 Astra. With GPT-6 Luna at medium reasoning effort, OpenVLHarness outperforms the base model, Codex, and Visual Sketchpad at maximum effort by 7.7-8.5 points while incurring at most 37% of their model-token cost.

items.title: Reinforcement Learning with Visually Attributable On-Policy Self-Distillation
items.abstract: Multimodal reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) provides reliable task-level supervision, yet offers limited guidance for localizing errors in visual reasoning. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) complements this supervision with dense token-level corrections from a privileged teacher equipped with an evidence-centered visual view. However, the resulting corrections may conflate visual evidence with non-visual shifts induced by linguistic priors, response style, or the privileged view itself. We formalize this phenomenon as privileged-correction contamination: a token-level correction is contaminated when its update direction cannot be consistently attributed to the privileged visual evidence. Directly distilling contaminated corrections may therefore reinforce erroneous token-level updates. To address this issue, we propose reinforcement learning with visually attributable on-policy self-distillation, an evidence-consistent paradigm that augments task-level RLVR supervision with privileged token-level corrections grounded in visual evidence. We instantiate this paradigm with Visual-Attribution Gating (VAG), which uses the verifier-derived advantage as the optimization anchor and validates each privileged correction against the contrast between evidence-present and evidence-degraded teacher views. By admitting only corrections directionally supported by this visual contrast, VAG preserves visually grounded guidance while suppressing inconsistent residuals. Experiments across six visual reasoning benchmarks show that VAG consistently outperforms GRPO and OPSD methods, establishing new state-of-the-art average performance.

items.title: CoopUQ: Robust Multi-Robot Social Navigation via Uncertainty-Aware Cooperative Forecasting
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning enables mobile robots to make fast and scalable navigation decisions in constrained human-shared environments. However, directly extending single-robot approaches to multi-robot settings often fails to ensure safety and efficiency, especially under occlusions and out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios, where individual robots may overlook potential risks or make inaccurate predictions. Leveraging cooperation effectively for both prediction and navigation remains a major challenge. We propose CoopUQ, a multi-robot social navigation framework that bridges uncertainty-aware cooperative occupancy forecasting and robust decision making. CoopUQ predicts future occupancy grid maps through cross-robot spatiotemporal feature fusion and further leverages forecasts and their uncertainty to guide policy via constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning, where the cost penalizes navigation through regions predicted to be occupied or highly uncertain. This design enables the policy to adapt its risk sensitivity under distribution shifts. Experimental results across multiple Unity3D-based simulation environments with both in-distribution and OOD settings, including diverse layouts, pedestrian densities, and rushing behavior, demonstrate improved prediction performance and safety over representative baselines. Real-robot experiments further demonstrate its robustness across various scenes. Our code and videos are available at https://coopuq.github.io/.

items.title: Where is Physical RSI capability from? An Observational Scaling Law of LLM-as-policy
items.abstract: In this paper, we systematically investigate the mechanisms, scaling behavior, and generalization of physical Recursive self-improvement. We introduce PhysRSI-eval to quantify physical RSI through a five-axis metric: First-Attempt Performance, Efficiency, Success, Budget and Improvement from failure. Different VLMs are evaluated on 18 manipulation tasks under a fixed interaction budget. The analysis of experimental results motivates the Physical Barrel Hypothesis: different capabilities may constrain different parts of improvement. The five-axis metrics also distinguish systems with close public benchmark averages and show that high scores need not come with early or efficient gains. We study observational scaling from two perspectives: predicting the relative performance of VLM agents from their public capabilities, and forecasting later progress from early physical feedback. Together, these analyses ask how quickly and how far an agent can improve. Moreover, we conduct workspace interventions and then analyze what improvement leaves behind. Removing history reduces late-round success, frozen workspaces remain useful on unseen layouts, and three cross-task cases achieve success earlier. The results suggest that scene-specific adaptation and reusable experience can coexist.

items.title: WeAct: Dynamic Weight Switching as Agent Actions
items.abstract: Long-horizon agents must learn heterogeneous capabilities from interleaved trajectories. Updating shared parameters to learn new capabilities can degrade previously acquired ones, resulting in catastrophic forgetting. As a trajectory unfolds, different stages may require different capabilities, yet conventional joint training and static adapter merging maintain a fixed parameter configuration throughout execution. We introduce WeAct (Weight-level Internal Actions), which trains independent capability-specific LoRA adapters over a frozen backbone and adds adapter selection to the agent's action space. These internal actions use the model's native tool-calling interface for on-demand capability composition in a shared context. Across eight deep-research benchmarks, Qwen3-32B with WeAct improves average accuracy by 6.2% relative to full fine-tuning counterparts despite using less compute, and by 27.5% relative to the strongest static LoRA-merging method. WeAct also supports modular continual adaptation, by adding a new code computation adapter to expand the agent's capabilities and updating the existing writing adapter to improve report quality. Both updates leave the backbone and other adapters unchanged, supporting modular continual adaptation in agents.

items.title: Train An Imaginative Agent
items.abstract: A seemingly reasonable push in Sokoban can make the puzzle unsolvable. To avoid such mistakes, an agent has to anticipate the consequences of its actions before execution, especially when feedback from the real environment is sparse or actions are irreversible. We introduce Agentic Imagination (Agima), a training framework that trains an agent to imagine before acting, i.e. to be imaginative. Agima trains a single omni model to propose actions, generate images of their outcomes, and then reason over these imagined futures to decide what to execute in the real environment. Rather than committing to a single plan, the agent can simulate a sequence of actions, explore alternatives, and compare possible futures. We first use supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to unify policy and world modeling within a single omni model. This enables the agent to predict future outcomes and perform basic forms of imagination, such as forward thinking and counterfactual branching. We then use agentic reinforcement learning (RL) to teach the agent to reason with its imagined futures and use them effectively for planning. Across four environments spanning Maze2D, Sokoban, Pacman, and PushT, Agima generalizes to harder settings unseen during training. Trained with SFT alone on two-box Sokoban, Agima solves 40% of four-box puzzles while seeing the real board only once every five moves, compared with an action-only planner that only solves 2%. After RL, new behaviors emerge in how Agima uses its imagination: it learns a new unified format that was unseen during the SFT stage, learns to conduct forward thinking only when necessary, and branches more frequently at critical decision points. An agent that can picture where its actions lead can learn when and where to look ahead, that is, to plan. Project page: https://agima.net/.

items.title: AnyGoal: On World Model Generalization Beyond Expert Rollouts
items.abstract: The goal of a world model is to capture the dynamics of an environment. This has the great appeal that it allows agents to plan and simulate a course of actions with the help of a world model. For these uses to be reliable, however, the learned dynamics must behave well beyond the specific state-action combinations observed in expert rollouts. Despite this, the relationship between data coverage, dynamics generalization, and downstream planning performance remains underexplored. We study this relationship through the lens of compositional generalization: can a world model recombine familiar state and action factors into valid dynamics? To answer this, we introduce AnyGoal, a benchmark of goal-shifted task variants built from widely used world-model environments, together with an open-source library. Each task is designed to be within reach of a world model that has learned the underlying dynamics: individual state factors and actions remain within their training support, but their combinations are underrepresented in expert trajectories. Across multiple environments and world model families, we find that current models consistently exhibit failures under these recombinations. By examining dynamics and representation failures across model families, interaction regimes, and evaluation metrics, we study where current world models generalize and where challenges remain for goal-shifted prediction and planning. Together, this framework, benchmark, and analysis provide a basis for evaluating progress toward world models that generalize to new planning tasks.

items.title: LatComm: Reusable Context Compression for Latent Communication between Large Language Models
items.abstract: Systems that combine several large language models (LLMs) often use one context for many questions. When the context is passed between models as text, the receiving model processes all of its tokens again for every question. Avoiding this cost requires a context representation that is compact, reusable across questions, and readable by a different LLM. Existing compression and latent communication methods each provide only some of these properties. We introduce LatComm, a Latent Communication interface that provides all three by separating encoding from reading: the context is encoded once without the question, and the receiver selects what to read for each question. A frozen context encoder LLM compresses the context into a fixed-size packet and sends it to a different frozen receiver LLM, which reads the packet through cross-attention, with gates computed from its prompt. On 12 multiple-choice question-answering datasets, LatComm improves average accuracy over single-vector baselines by up to 10.2 points. On QuALITY, it reduces the receiver's input by 57x and answers the questions of an article 3x faster.

items.title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
items.abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.

items.title: Kronecker Delta Rule for Long Context Linear Attention
items.abstract: We propose KronLSTM, a linear attention architecture based on the Kronecker Delta Rule, a novel update rule for associative matrix memories. KronLSTM extends the xLSTM family with a memory-revision mechanism that corrects targeted associations while modifying the memory only along a single direction in matrix space. This minimally invasive memory revision reduces interference with previously stored information compared with delta-rule updates, making it particularly well suited for long-context language modeling. The resulting memory dynamics can be mathematically described as a Markov chain that converges to a steady-state distribution, while the expected norm of the memory matrix remains uniformly bounded throughout the entire input sequence. Hence, KronLSTM ensures stable memory dynamics without requiring additional normalization and stabilization mechanisms for the memory state. Experiments show that KronLSTM is competitive with, and often outperforms, existing linear attention architectures, including models of the (Gated) DeltaNet family, with particularly strong performance on long context benchmarks. These results establish the Kronecker Delta Rule as an effective and analytically tractable foundation for stable associative memory in recurrent linear attention architectures. Our code (https://github.com/NX-AI/KronLSTM) and models (https://huggingface.co/collections/NX-AI/kronlstm) are open-source.

items.title: ProteinGeoBench: Frontier Structural-Biology Agents Are Fluent at Lookup but Lost in Geometry
items.abstract: Frontier agents retrieve structural metadata well and compute geometry from coordinates less reliably. We ask how much of a benchmark score reflects that gap and how much reflects the evaluation configuration around the model. We study ProteinGeoBench, a suite of 131 protein-structure tasks, using 4,249 rollouts from four frontier models and 4,486 further trials across 26 models. Three of the four frontier models fall within 0.031 of one another (0.785 to 0.816) with no difference between them resolved, while the fourth scores 0.707 and all three gaps to it exclude zero. Three of the four do better on metadata lookup than on numeric calculation. The fourth is slightly better on numeric. Numeric tasks are 28 of the 131 but half of the twelve tasks that all four models fail. The ranking also depends on the evaluation budget: with one run per task, 23.9% of bootstrap replicates put a different model first. On a selected 15-task slice, removing network access lowers scores more than blocking eight structural-database domains, but the two contrasts were graded in different passes and cannot be cleanly decomposed. Swapping in each model's own command-line agent changes scores by -0.071 to +0.086, a comparison too small to rule out moderate harness effects. Across 26 models, numeric performance rises with non-numeric performance rather than staying flat. The experiments use different task subsets, so they cannot rank model, harness, access and task composition against one another. Evaluations should report results by task family, along with the number of runs, the harness and the access conditions.

items.title: Agent World Model in the Wild: Computer-Use Agent Environment Synthesis
items.abstract: Agent learning is shifting from learning from human data toward learning through interaction with the world. However, scaling such learning directly in real-world computer systems is challenging and can introduce substantial security risks. We therefore propose Agent World Model in the Wild (WildAWM), a scalable pipeline for synthesizing controllable environments and tasks for training general computer-use agents (CUAs). Whereas existing approaches typically specialize in a single agent interaction interface, we construct executable environments that jointly support graphical user interfaces, model context protocol services, and command-line interfaces, allowing agents to flexibly combine visual interaction, tool use, and code execution. WildAWM is entirely powered by open-source models, demonstrating that high-quality computer-use environments can be generated without proprietary frontier models. Beyond environments, we address three recurring challenges in task synthesis: ensuring solvability, maintaining sufficient difficulty, and producing reliable verifiers, by introducing execution-based quality gates that combine heterogeneous agent rollouts, cross-judge consistency checks, and counterfactual probes of judgment robustness. The resulting pipeline synthesizes 341 long-horizon environment-task pairs that can require over 100 agent steps to solve and remain challenging even for frontier models, with GPT-6-Astra solving only 60% of them. We train two Qwen models of different sizes exclusively in these synthetic worlds. Both models achieve substantial gains across 8 out-of-distribution benchmarks spanning web, claw, and computer-use agents, demonstrating that learning in WildAWM's synthesized worlds generalizes broadly to unseen computer-use tasks. The code is publicly available at https://github.com/MSR-Orchard/WildAWM.

items.title: RefCraft: Benchmarking Visual-Reference-Conditioned Agentic Generation through Web Development
items.abstract: Beyond basic tool use and coding skills, effectively incorporating visual references into agentic generation is equally essential for applying AI agents to real-world productivity tasks. We study this crucial capability through webpage development, a practical and readily evaluable setting in which existing benchmarks remain largely idealized: they typically focus on reconstructing visual targets or generating webpages from textual instructions alone, overlooking the more common workflow of developing from visual examples. Specifically, we introduce RefCraft, a benchmark comprising 300 realistic multimodal webpage-development tasks that combine natural-language instructions with screenshots from one to five reference webpages. Agents must selectively interpret and utilize these references while rendering, visually inspecting, and iteratively refining their outputs. We evaluate the resulting open-ended artifacts using independently verifiable keypoints and complementary programmatic and VLM judges. Across nine frontier (M)LLMs, the strongest system achieves an overall score of only 52.12 out of 100, revealing that visual-reference-conditioned agentic generation remains a substantial challenge for current models in practical webpage-development settings.

items.title: AfriBED: a Speech Recognition Bias Evaluation Dataset for Low Resource African Languages
items.abstract: Despite advancements in automatic speech recognition systems (ASR), current systems exhibit speaker-attribute bias, i.e., their speech recognition performance is biased against certain speakers based on their demographic attributes such as gender, accents, and speaker type. However, accurately assessing speaker attribute bias in a given ASR system requires the availability of a bias evaluation dataset with comparable speech across subgroups of a speaker attribute. In this paper, we introduce African speech Bias Evaluation Dataset (AfriBED), a novel speech recognition bias evaluation dataset for two low resource African languages, Bemba and Nyanja, to detect and estimate gender and speaker-type bias for ASR systems. The dataset comprises 9 hours of speech with 3928 utterances recorded by 80 speakers for Bemba, while the Nyanja set includes 6260 utterances with approximately 18 hours of speech recorded by 127 speakers. The results of our baseline experiments demonstrate that the datasets are useful for examining gender and speaker-type attribute bias in the target languages.

items.title: Next Best Action: Causal Constrained Offline RL for Business Action Targeting
items.abstract: Next Best Action (NBA) systems must select among customer interventions (e.g., discounts, promotions, and lifecycle actions), maximize long-term economic value, satisfy complex operational constraints, and remain causally grounded. Existing approaches lack a rigorous framework for meeting these requirements jointly. We address this gap by formulating NBA as a Constrained Markov Decision Process (CMDP). We then integrate off-policy causal correction of the estimated customer dynamics directly into the Linear Programming (LP) formulation of the CMDP. The resulting policy selects actions based on customer states to maximize long-term value while explicitly enforcing business guardrails. Furthermore, the LP formulation yields shadow prices that quantify the economic trade-offs of operational constraints (e.g., fairness and user welfare), enhancing policy interpretability. We validate our proposed offline Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework on an industry case study involving rideshare coupon targeting, where customer states are defined by Recency, Frequency, and Monetary (RFM) stages. We evaluate performance using model-based off-policy evaluation, with causal dynamics estimated from a temporal holdout. Under the observed coupon budget and RFM state representation, our optimized policy improves customer lifetime value (LTV) by 19% over the estimated behavior policy and 8% over a myopic baseline. Although the demonstrated action space is binary, the proposed framework is action-agnostic, yielding a general-purpose decision module for targeting systems that manage multiple interventions.

items.title: Mise-en-Video: Fine-Grained 3D Control for Multi-Shot Video Generation
items.abstract: Recent advances in text-to-video generation have enabled high-fidelity single-shot synthesis, yet practical storytelling creation requires multi-shot videos with both strong inter-shot consistency and fine-grained controllability. Existing multi-shot video generation approaches achieve strong consistency but still fall short in controllability. In this paper, we propose Mise-en-Video (MeV), a highly controllable multi-shot video generation framework that allows video creators to conduct staging the multi-shot in the 3D space and then generate the corresponding multi-shot video. To achieve this, our framework combines a hierarchical attention mechanism for multi-level narrative consistency with 3D-aware layout guidance for precise, per-shot spatial control. To support training and evaluation, we develop standardized annotation pipelines and construct a 160K-video dataset with hierarchical multi-shot texts and oriented 3D bounding boxes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that MeV consistently outperforms strong baselines in video quality, inter-shot consistency, and subject-level controllability.

items.title: SOMA: Continuous Monitoring and Intervention for System Two Reasoning with System One Models
items.abstract: Reasoning models often run into problems without noticing them, even when symptoms are visible in their own text. In humans, metacognition separates monitoring from control: fast, intuitive signals keep watch while slow, deliberate reasoning unfolds and help decide whether to continue, change course, or stop. System One (S1) decision models, such as Jev, are a natural candidate for this role: they return a calibrated probability for a natural-language question about a text in one fast call, yet they are used only as gates before reasoning. We introduce SOMA (System One Metacognitive Awareness), in which an S1 model continuously monitors a System Two (S2) reasoning model and intervenes when needed. SOMA has three layers: a scenario layer states each objective in natural language with predefined actions, an awareness layer lets S1 judge whether the described behavior appears, and a control layer accumulates these judgments, first reminds S2, and takes over only if the behavior persists. Sharing one S1 model and one controller across tasks, without training, SOMA addresses two different failures on two reasoning models: on overthinking, it cuts reasoning tokens by up to 36\% while improving average accuracy, and on unanswerable questions, it raises abstention from 70.5\% to 87.2\%.

items.title: LG-Bench: A Graph-Structured Evaluation Benchmark for Life Sciences
items.abstract: Traditional evaluation benchmarks reduce inherently interconnected scientific knowledge in life sciences into flat lists of questions, disregarding the underlying topological structure of the knowledge. We introduce, the first graph-structured benchmark for life sciences, featuring over 10,000 high-quality multiple-choice questions across medicine, biology, and chemistry. Our approach constructs a weighted evaluation graph using bidirectional matching and semantic similarity algorithms, where nodes represent questions and edge weights capture their semantic relationships. Leveraging this graph topology, we design two novel evaluation metrics. The Global Coherence Score (GCS) measures a model's consistency within semantically related neighborhoods, while Knowledge Balance Score (KBS) analyzes how model errors are distributed across the graph to reveal conceptual blind spots. LG-Bench facilitates fine-grained comparison of LLMs by surfacing differences in conceptual coherence and patterns of knowledge organization across models. Our framework shifts the evaluation paradigm from flat accuracy metrics to structure-aware analysis, offering a new lens for diagnosing and improving LLM performance in the life sciences domain.

items.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
items.abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .

items.title: AI Misconception and Adoption Among Indonesian K-12 Teachers
items.abstract: Indonesia's fragmented geography and uneven infrastructure pose persistent challenges for adopting new educational technologies. While national initiatives aim to mainstream AI in K-12 schools by 2025, policy readiness does not automatically mean teachers are ready for the classroom. This study surveys Indonesian K-12 teachers to examine: (1) their understanding of AI, (2) how they and their students use AI, and (3) their views on the acceptability of AI in learning activities. Through semi-automated thematic analysis, we identify common misconceptions and use cases. Our findings reveal a notable mismatch: while teachers find AI use in education acceptable and support it for the sake of efficiency, they remain fully aware of the risks to learning depth and academic honesty. We also find that this high level of acceptance is currently coupled with a poor understanding of how AI actually works.

items.title: TokenGate: Adapting LLMs for Fast and Memory-Efficient Prefill with Learned Token Pruning
items.abstract: Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.

items.title: recAMPLIFY: Large-Scale Pretraining of Recursive Protein Language Models
items.abstract: Protein language models (pLMs) are powerful tools for protein annotation and mutation-effect prediction, but progress has largely depended on scaling model size and data, making them expensive and prone to memorization. Test-time scaling offers a complementary path, but methods developed for autoregressive LLMs do not transfer directly: masked encoders lack a generation loop, and amino acids do not verbalize in a reasoning language. Instead, we adapt recursive pretraining to masked pLMs, where a weight-tied Transformer core refines residue-aligned hidden states over an adjustable number of cycles. We instantiate this recipe as recAMPLIFY, a pLM with 155M unique parameters trained on the same 2T tokens as AMPLIFY-350M. Despite 56% fewer parameters, it improves CASP contact recovery and three out of four supervised tasks, notably raising fold accuracy by 22.5%. Because optimal depth for recAMPLIFY varies across tasks and assays, we then introduce Gated Mixture Recurrence (GMR), a framework that decodes each protein from a probability-weighted mixture of hidden states visited during recursion. GMR employs a learned residual gate at scalar, low-rank, or per-dimension resolution to control how much of each cycle's proposed update is accepted into the state. This unifies halting and gating into a single adaptive computation objective while recovering PonderNet-style halting as a special case without gates. Layered on top of recAMPLIFY, GMR further reduces expected layer depth by up to 37%, although the accuracy trade-off varies by task. Mechanistic analyses show that residual gating controls recurrence stability beyond the trained depth and that halt depth tracks biological properties.

items.title: Comparing Computer Use Behavior Across Multiple Levels of Abstraction
items.abstract: Interaction traces record how people and agents use computers, and comparing them can reveal usability barriers, differences in expertise, and human--agent similarity. Yet traces are recorded as low-level, interface-specific actions, making comparisons difficult across tasks, interfaces, and input modalities. Existing approaches either compare these actions directly, reduce traces to aggregate outcomes, or summarize them at higher-level goals, obscuring where behavior differs. We present MAP (Multi-level Action Parsing), a hierarchical semantic representation and annotation pipeline that maps traces into a common vocabulary across linked levels of abstraction. MAP compares traces by sequence, recurring patterns, and effort, localizing differences by type and abstraction level. A technical evaluation across three computer use datasets shows high agreement with manual annotations and broad coverage of behavior. Applying MAP shows that sighted and blind users increasingly converge at higher levels despite navigation differences, while agents omit corrective, help-seeking, and recovery behaviors present in human traces.

items.title: Towards Robust Model Organisms for Eliciting Latent Knowledge
items.abstract: A key problem in AI safety is eliciting latent knowledge (ELK), extracting information from a model that is misaligned and more knowledgeable than its overseer. For example, a misaligned model used to scan code for vulnerabilities may want to withhold its findings, i.e., sandbag, in order to exploit them later. To study ELK empirically, we need model organisms that mirror this setting. Existing model organisms fall short in several respects. In this work, we train model organisms to withhold solutions in a vulnerability detection task. We combine transcript distillation with counter-prompting and tamper-resistance training to instill three properties that we argue are critical for a useful ELK testbed: 1) Selectivity, the model sandbags when it thinks the overseer doesn't know the answer and complies otherwise, 2) Robustness, the model resists elicitation, and 3) Retention, the model retains a knowledge advantage over the overseer, as opposed to losing the relevant capability. We train a sequence of model organisms and show that our strongest model substantially outperforms prior models on robustness while keeping the other two properties intact. We hope that our model organisms provide a useful ELK testbed for the community, and that our methodology sparks the development of increasingly challenging model organisms. All our code, models and the dataset are available at https://huggingface.co/collections/lennart-finke/sandbagging.
