items.title: Governing medical tourism in Asia: comparative policy evidence and implications for China
items.abstract: Abstract Background Medical tourism connects patients with providers across borders, while responsibility for care remains divided among institutions and jurisdictions. We examined how selected Asian destinations allocate these responsibilities and what their arrangements reveal about emerging international medical services in China. Methods We conducted a purposive comparative analysis of public documents from Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Thailand, India and China. Five destination cases informed a focused examination of Shanghai and Boao Lecheng. The revised source register records institutional responsibilities, regulatory instruments, patient pathway stages, financial arrangements and evidential limits. Dated policies, programme descriptions and reported activity were analysed separately. Academic literature contextualized the comparison; heterogeneous patient and expenditure indicators were not pooled. Results The documents describe different allocations of authority. Japan links patient reception to accreditation and travel coordination; South Korea combines promotion with provider registration and liability insurance. Singapore places explicit limits on public hospitals’ recruitment of foreign patients. The Thai sources describe health authorities’ promotional roles, wellness assessment and a hospital–insurer payment process. India coordinates tourism, health, accreditation and visa functions through a national strategy and interministerial activity. These instruments provide different forms of information and accountability, but do not establish their effects on patient trust or safety. Shanghai already specifies insurance cooperation, complaints and statistical monitoring. Its published activity figures, like those for Boao Lecheng, do not isolate inbound medical tourists or demonstrate continuity after patients return home. Conclusions The comparison identifies where responsibilities are assigned and where implementation evidence remains incomplete. For China, priorities include distinguishing patient populations, evaluating existing safeguards and specifying responsibility at transitions between providers, insurers and jurisdictions. Additional national promotion alone would not resolve these questions.

items.title: Prevalence and Risk Factors of Child Sexual Abuse in Early Childhood Across Africa: A Protocol for a Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Child sexual abuse (CSA) in early childhood represents a significant public health issue and a critical concern regarding children's rights, with profound lifelong consequences. Despite the growing recognition of CSA as a severe form of child maltreatment, its prevalence and impact in Africa remain poorly understood, primarily due to underreporting and fragmented evidence. Existing studies have predominantly focused on broader populations of children and adolescents, thereby limiting our understanding of the prevalence and risk factors associated with CSA in early childhood. To address this knowledge gap, this systematic review and meta-analysis will examine the prevalence and risk factors of CSA among children aged 8 years and younger across Africa. Methods: The protocol adheres to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Protocols guidelines. We will conduct a systematic search of seven scientific databases (PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, African Journals Online, African Index Medicus, and Google Scholar) for studies published between January 1, 2016, and January 1, 2026. In addition, we will search for grey literature, including reports from UNICEF, the WHO Violence Against Children Surveys, and relevant government and institutional sources. Eligible studies will comprise observational studies (including cross-sectional studies cohort, and case control studies), randomized controlled trials (baseline data only), and mixed-methods studies that provide extractable quantitative data on the prevalence or risk factors of CSA among children aged 8 years and younger. Two independent reviewers will conduct screening, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment using tools from the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) critical appraisal tools, while the ROBINS-I framework will be applied to any non-randomized interventional designs where appropriate. A random-effects meta-analysis utilizing Freeman-Tukey double arcsine transformation will be performed for prevalence data. Heterogeneity will be assessed using I² and χ² statistics, and subgroup analyses and meta-regression will be conducted as feasible. Publication bias will be assessed through funnel plots and Egger's test. In instances where meta-analysis is not possible, a structured narrative synthesis will be performed. Discussion: This review will address a critical gap in early childhood research across Africa to highlight a frequently overlooked public health concern. Addressing this evidence gap is critical to strengthening early prevention and detection efforts, informing policy and resource allocation, and supporting the development of contextually appropriate child protection systems across the continent. Registration: PROSPERO (CRD420251085203)

items.title: Five-Year Longitudinal Changes and Determinants of Serum PFAS Exposure Profiles in a Community-Based Cohort from Southern China
items.abstract: Abstract Background Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent environmental contaminants widely detected in human populations. Although regulatory actions have restricted several legacy PFAS, longitudinal evidence on changes in human PFAS exposure and their determinants remains limited, particularly in rapidly urbanizing regions. This study aimed to characterize five-year changes in serum legacy PFAS concentrations and identify demographic and geographic determinants of longitudinal exposure among community residents in Guangzhou, southern China. Methods We conducted a prospective community-based cohort study of 958 residents from three communities representing distinct residential environments: an urban commercial area, an industrial/livestock/fishery area, and an ecological conservation area. Participants were examined at baseline (2018–2019) and follow-up (2023–2024). Serum legacy PFAS concentrations were measured using ultra-performance liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry. Temporal changes were assessed using paired analyses, and longitudinal determinants were evaluated using linear mixed-effects models with false discovery rate correction. Results Six legacy PFAS with detection frequencies approaching 100% were included in longitudinal analyses. Over five years, total PFOS, PFNA, PFDA, and total PFHxS concentrations decreased from 14.129 to 11.262, 0.998 to 0.871, 0.692 to 0.532, and 0.771 to 0.598 ng/mL, respectively, whereas PFOA increased from 5.534 to 9.789 ng/mL and PFHpA from 0.024 to 0.034 ng/mL. Older age was consistently associated with higher concentrations of all six PFAS. Residential location was also an important determinant, with higher PFAS concentrations observed among residents of the urban commercial and industrial/livestock/fishery communities than among those in the ecological conservation community. Conclusions Serum legacy PFAS exposure showed heterogeneous five-year trajectories in this community-based population in Guangzhou, with divergent temporal patterns across individual PFAS. The contrasting trends and persistent demographic and geographic differences highlight the complexity of human PFAS exposure following regulatory changes. Continued biomonitoring and identification of populations with elevated exposure are warranted to support targeted exposure reduction and public health surveillance.

items.title: Youth Firearm Victimization in Philadelphia: Trends and Disparities Among Middle and High School Aged Youth
items.abstract: Abstract Urban firearm violence remains a critical public health crisis, with adolescents, especially high-school-aged youth and young men of color, disproportionately affected compared with younger children. However, limited research distinguishes patterns of victimization between middle school–aged youth (11–13) and high school–aged youth (14–18), despite important developmental and contextual differences between these groups. This study examines annual, monthly, weekly, and hourly patterns among 16,229 shooting incidents in Philadelphia from 2015 to 2024, comparing demographic characteristics, temporal trends, and fatality outcomes across the two age categories. Chi-squared analysis revealed significant associations between race and sex, with Black males comprising the majority of victims, particularly among 14–18-year-olds (89.0%). Temporal trends showed pandemic-era surges peaking in 2021, followed by substantial declines by 2024. Age-stratified analysis demonstrated higher average fatality rates among 14–18-year-olds (14.9%) compared to 11–13-year-olds (10.2%), indicating greater severity among high-school-aged youth. By directly comparing these age groups, this study highlights distinct developmental vulnerability periods and informs targeted, school-aligned violence prevention strategies.

items.title: Employment-type inequalities in healthy working life expectancy in China: evidence from CHARLS, 2011–2018
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Healthy working life expectancy (HWLE) has become an important metric for evaluating the feasibility and equity of extended working lives. In China, ongoing retirement-age reform is occurring within a labour market characterized by significant differences in physical demands, social protection, and exit pathways across agricultural work, self-employment, and wage employment. This study estimated employment-type inequalities in HWLE among older Chinese adults. Methods: We analysed pooled person-wave data from the 2011, 2013, 2015, and 2018 waves of the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study. The analytic sample included 34,644 person-wave observations from 11,626 adults aged 50–100 years. Four joint health-work states were defined by functional health and current work status: healthy-working, healthy-not working, unhealthy-working, and unhealthy-not working. Employment type was classified as agricultural work, self-employment, or family-business work, and employee or other work using CHARLS work-module variables. Sex- and employment-type-specific age prevalence in each state was combined with sex-specific United Nations life-table person-years to estimate state-specific expectancies from age 50. An illustrative value analysis examined how retirement-age conclusions changed when unhealthy work was assigned a lower value. Results: Remaining life expectancy at age 50 was fixed at 27.11 years for men and 31.76 years for women. Among men, healthy-working life expectancy ranged from 17.12 years among employees or other workers to 18.91 years among agricultural workers, while unhealthy-working life expectancy was highest among agricultural workers (4.00 years). Among women, agricultural workers had the least favourable profile, with the lowest healthy-working life expectancy (16.06 years) and the highest unhealthy-working expectancy (7.65 years). Self-employed or family-business women had the highest healthy-working life expectancy (20.78 years) and the lowest unhealthy-working expectancy (3.22 years). Under the illustrative value specification, welfare-maximising ages differed by sex and employment type. Conclusions: Employment type significantly influences the distribution of later life between healthy work, unhealthy work, and non-work in China. Evaluating retirement-age reform solely on the basis of average longevity is insufficient. A public health approach should account for the unequal burden of unhealthy work, particularly among women in agricultural employment.

items.title: From Hippocrates to UTCI: Twenty-Five Centuries of Human Biometeorology
items.abstract: Abstract Human biometeorology, which describes how the atmosphere and the wider environment affect human health, well - being, and performance, was initially organized and presented as a 20th-century discipline, formalized by Tromp and Landsberg and later by physiological thermal indices such as the Physiologically Equivalent Temperature (PET) and the Universal Thermal Climate Index (UTCI). This paper takes a longer view. It traces a continuous, if uneven, tradition of linking atmospheric conditions to human health across more than two millennia: religious and mythological ideas, the weather knowledge of indigenous societies, biblical and ancient Near Eastern sources, the medical systems of Egypt, China and India, Presocratic natural philosophy, the Hippocratic Corpus, Aristotle and the Peripatetic school, and Hellenistic and Roman scholarship. It also argues that the thermal environment is not only something scholarship later described, but a force that helped shape culture itself - visible in the thermal picture of paradise and hell across unrelated traditions and in the open - air institutions of Greek public life. On the modern side, we place the decisive physical step earlier than usual: Konrad Büttner formulated the energy balance of the human body in the 1930s, three decades before Fanger and six before PET, and Wolf H. Weihe stated in 1976 the problem that still governs the field: especially the atmosphere acts through many factors, and their ranking depends on the question asked. Modern rational indices quantify a long-standing insight rather than inventing it: human health depends on several atmospheric factors acting together, not on air temperature alone.

items.title: First-line treatment of non-haemorrhagic early miscarriage in gynaecological emergencies in public hospitals on Reunion Island in 2022
items.abstract: Abstract Introduction: The prevalence of early spontaneous pregnancy loss (ESPL) is 12% for all pregnancies combined, and can be managed surgically or non-surgically. Non-surgical treatment is possible with in-town care. Health insurance reimbursement records revealed that the quotation for ESPL management in towns was very scarcely used in Reunion Island. Patients could benefit from more comprehensive care if they were seen in a local practice rather than in a hospital. However, the number of patients treated in hospital is unknown in Reunion Island. The primary outcome was to determine the first-line treatment preferred by patients with non-haemorrhagic ESPL in public hospitals in Reunion Island in 2022. Method: This cross-sectional descriptive study involved several hospital centres, with retrospective collection by review of gynaecological emergency department records from public hospitals in Reunion Island. Results: From January to December 2022, 947 patients were included in the four public hospitals of Reunion Island. Results varied slightly between centres. Non-surgical treatment as first-line therapy was chosen by 84 to 99% of women, depending on the centre; 42 to 69% received expectant management and 25 to 46% received pharmacological management (misoprostol). One to 16% of patients preferred immediate surgical management. The average timing of patient visits was mid-day. Conclusion: ESPL were largely treated by a non-surgical method as first-line treatment in public hospitals of Reunion Island in 2022. This encourages the creation of an out-of-hospital care network by the healthcare professionals concerned.

items.title: Patients’ Perceptions and Experiences of Medical Laboratory Service Quality in the Kumasi Metropolis, Ghana: A Convergent Parallel Mixed-Methods Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background : In recent years, laboratory services have become a significant feature of health care delivery in many developing countries. In Ghana, laboratory service provision has increased across private and public facilities. The study examined patients’ perceptions of quality and their experiences with medical laboratory services in the Kumasi metropolis, Ghana. Methods: The study employed a convergent parallel mixed-methods design. A survey of five hundred and thirty-nine (539) patients accessing medical laboratory services at Komfo Anokye Teaching Hospital (KATH), Ghana Health Service, Christian Health Association of Ghana (CHAG), Private Hospitals and Private Standalone Laboratories was conducted from 8th March to 26th November 2021. The Service Quality (SERVQUAL) model was used to measure patients' perceptions of laboratory service quality across the five dimensions of Reliability, Assurance, Tangibility, Empathy, and Responsiveness. In addition, fourteen (14) in-depth interviews were conducted with patients to explore perspectives on the provision of quality medical laboratory services. SERVQUAL was calculated as the difference between perception and expectation for each dimension; a negative score indicates dissatisfaction, while a positive score indicates satisfaction. Descriptive statistics and quantile regression analysis were conducted to examine patient-related factors that influence perceptions. Qualitative data were analyzed thematically, and relevant statements were quoted verbatim. Results : Quantitative findings: The study included 539 patients; 30.2% were male, and 69.8% were female. Patients’ expectations exceeded their perceptions of laboratory service quality, with an overall SERVQUAL score of -0.60. The largest gap (-0.66) was in the Responsiveness dimension, and the smallest (-0.57) was in the Assurance dimension. Facility type and sex were significantly associated with patients’ perceptions of laboratory service quality. Patients were more satisfied with laboratory service quality in private health facilities than in Government facilities (β = 0.26; 95% CI: 0.04-0.47; p = 0.02). Similarly, females were more satisfied with service quality than male participants (β = 0.23, 95% CI: 0.04, 0.41, p = 0.02). Qualitative findings: Patients expressed dissatisfaction with the timeliness of results, the unavailability of requested tests, and the lack of communication and feedback. Conclusion : Patients rated services favourably, but expectations consistently exceeded the service experience, with the largest gap in Responsiveness.

items.title: Dietary Non-adherence and Associated Factors among Adults with Type 2 Diabetes in Ethiopia: A Sequential Explanatory Mixed- Methods Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Diabetes mellitus (DM) is one of the leading causes of death globally and the most rapidly growing cause of health loss. Current evidence strongly suggests that lifestyle changes, along with weight reduction, seem to overcome the genetic risk of the disease in individuals with pre-diabetes or recent type 2 DM. Despite efforts, adherence to dietary recommendations remains limited in Ethiopia. Methods Sequential explanatory mixed methods were employed, with a quantitative cross-sectional study, followed by semi-structured interviews in public health facilities in Shaggar City. For the quantitative phase, 588 type 2 diabetic patients were selected using systematic random sampling. Quantitative data were summarized using descriptive statistics, and logistic regression was performed to identify factors associated with non-adherence to dietary recommendations. Qualitative data were analyzed using a thematic analysis approach. Results The magnitude of non-adherence to dietary recommendations was 68.90% (95% confidence interval [CI]: 64.9%, 72.8%). In multivariable logistic regression, household food insecurity (Adjusted Odds Ratio (AOR) = 4.04; 95% CI ( 2.07, 7.90), poor dietary knowledge (AOR = 2.14; 95% CI:(1.28–3.58), poor family support (AOR = 4.23; 95% CI: (2.44–7.31), normal body weight (AOR = 0.37, 95% CI (0.18–0.77), overweight (AOR = 0.41, 95% CI: (0.18–0.92) compared to obese, less than five years of follow-up (AOR = 2.56, 95% CI: (1.26–5.17), not receiving printed nutritional health education materials (AOR = 2.51; 95%CI: (1.31–4.81), and not accessing audio visual nutritional education (AOR = 1.98; 95%CI: (1.003–3.93) were significantly associated with non-adherence to dietary recommendations. Thematic analysis revealed that financial constraints, inflation, poor dietary knowledge, sedentary lifestyle, poor family support, and recent diagnosis of diabetes were barriers to adherence to dietary recommendations. Conclusions The magnitude of non-adherence to dietary recommendations was high, with multiple individual, household, and healthcare-related factors. Qualitative findings further highlighted economic constraints, sedentary lifestyle, and poor knowledge as key barriers, underscoring the need for multifaceted interventions to improve dietary adherence among diabetic patients.

items.title: Disparity in the Prevalence of Pit and Fissure Sealants Among 12-Year-Old Children in Puerto Rico: A Cross-Sectional Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Pit and fissure sealants (PFS) are an important tool in preventing and managing caries development on primary and permanent posterior teeth in children and adolescents. Among children living in Puerto Rico, particularly those of low socioeconomic status, this preventive measure has historically been underutilized. The completion of the Government Health Insurance (GHI) reform in 2000 marked a pivotal moment, expanding access to PFS across the entire island. In this study, we compared oral health data from 12-year-old school-attending children in Puerto Rico in 1997 and 2011 to evaluate changes in PFS prevalence and socioeconomic disparities, using school type as a proxy for socioeconomic status. Methods This cross-sectional study used two probabilistic samples (n = 1,587 in 2011 and n = 1,435 in 1997) of 12-year-olds enrolled in school, stratified by GHI region, school type, and sex. Calibrated examiners evaluated the presence of PFS on at least one permanent first molar. Logistic regression models compared PFS prevalence by school type in 1997 and 2011, adjusting for sex and region. A P -value ≤ 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results Sex distribution and school type were similar in 1997 (49% female; 18% private schools) and 2011 (53% female; 23% private schools). Between 1997 and 2011, PFS prevalence increased among all children (4.3% vs. 18.1%), as well as among children attending private (11.1% vs. 25.8%), public rural (3.4% vs. 16.3%), and public urban schools (2.5% vs. 16.9%). Participants attending public-rural and public-urban schools were less likely to have sealants, both in 1997 ( OR public−rural =0.19; 95% CI: 0.07–0.46; OR public−urban =0.17; 95% CI: 0.06–0.48) and in 2011 ( OR public−rural =0.57; 95% CI: 0.33–0.99; OR public−urban =0.60; 95% CI: 0.39–0.93), versus those from private schools. Conclusions PFS prevalence increased among 12-year-old school-attending children in Puerto Rico across all school types between 1997 and 2011, a period that coincided with island-wide GHI implementation. However, disparities between children attending public and private schools persisted. These findings suggest that expanded insurance coverage alone may be insufficient to eliminate disparities in preventive dental care and that socioeconomic background may influence PFS utilization.

items.title: Beyond a Decade of MENACTRIMS: Scientific Achievements, Publicly Documented Implementation Gaps, and a Roadmap to a Regional Learning Health System
items.abstract: Background: The Middle East North Africa Committee for Treatment and Research in Multiple Sclerosis (MENACTRIMS) has developed congresses, clinical guidance, registry research, training, certification, and advocacy partnerships. Evaluating this infrastructure requires distinctions between organizational activity, implementation, and attributable benefit. Objectives: To characterize documented achievements, compare the geographic distribution of major functions, identify public reporting gaps, and propose a measurable regional learning-health-system roadmap. Methods: A structured public-document audit and targeted literature synthesis covered activities from 2014 through 23 August 2026, with a documented update on 16 October 2026. Sources were classified by provenance and evidentiary purpose, without performance scoring. Geographic coverage used a fixed 19-jurisdiction Middle East and North Africa frame. Reported attendance terms and registry denominators were preserved. Results: Ten completed congresses were identified; seven with exact headline attendance had a median of 934 participants (interquartile range 761.5–1006.5). Seven congresses were hosted in the United Arab Emirates. Five major guideline outputs or revisions, multicountry registry studies, policy endorsements, and traceable grant- and fellowship-linked publications demonstrated sustained scientific activity. The public registry headline was 15,387, compared with 14,438 enumerable center records; variable displays represented 78.8%–93.9% of the headline, without establishing true field completeness. Iran, Egypt, and Kuwait contributed 75.4% of enumerable records. Council listings covered 15/19 jurisdictions, registry centers 8/19, and certified centers 2/19. Certification standards already specify three-year renewal and prefer registry participation; fellowship terms require reporting and career follow-up. Aggregated results of these processes were less readily ascertainable. Conclusions: MENACTRIMS has established substantial regional infrastructure. Differing geographic distributions identify questions about coordination and opportunity but do not establish organizational failure. A phased roadmap for 2027–2035 should build on existing systems through denominator reconciliation, publicly reported program outcomes, guideline-linked quality improvement, and meaningful patient and professional participation. Public-source limitations and the non-systematic synthesis preclude causal attribution of regional patient outcomes to MENACTRIMS.

items.title: Differences in Antibiotic Use Practices Among Children with Diarrhea in Urban and Rural Bangladesh
items.abstract: Background: Misuse and overuse of antibiotics in childhood diarrhea pose a high risk of antimicrobial resistance (AMR), which is a public health threat globally, and Bangladesh is no exception. This study aims to describe urban-rural differences and determine the factors associated with antibiotic use at home in children before seeking care for diar-rhea at the health care facilities. Methods: This cross-sectional study, over an 18-month period, included 5,894 children aged 1-59 months from two large health facilities: a rural secondary-level district hospital, located in Tangail, and an urban diarrhea specialized facility, icddr,b Dhaka hospital. Following clinical care, trained staff used a pre-validated structured questionnaire to collect data on child demographics, clinical symptoms, feeding practices, and treatment received prior to hospital visit. The primary outcome was antibiotic use at home before hospital presentation. Multivariable logistic regression models analyzed factors linked to home antibiotic use. Results: The preva-lence of antibiotic use at home before seeking care among diarrheal children was sig-nificantly higher in children visiting a rural facility as compared to that of the urban facility (90.0% vs. 68.4%). Pharmacies were the primary source of antibiotics for children in both rural and urban areas (64.1% vs. 61.2%). Multivariable analysis showed that in urban settings, children with diarrhea for 1-3 days were more than twice as likely (aOR:2.39, 95% CI:1.66.4), and those sick for 4 or more days were three times as likely (aOR:3.09, 95% CI: 2.21–4.43) to receive antibiotics at home compared to children who had less than one day of diarrhea. Children with no history of a prior hospital visit for diarrhea were also 1.86 times at higher risk of using antibiotics (aOR: 1.86, 95% CI:1.28–2.72). In a rural setting, children with diarrhea for 1–3 days had five times (aOR:5.11, 95% CI: 3.6–7.1), and those who had diarrhea for 4 days or more had two times higher odds (aOR: 1.97, 95% CI: 1.43–2.73) for antibiotic use. Moreover, children whose caregivers used ORS were 2.8 times more likely to use antibiotics at home (aOR:2.80, 95% CI: 1.06-7.35). Conclusions: This study demonstrates that antibiotic use at home before seeking care is alarmingly high among children with diarrhea in Bangladesh, particu-larly in rural settings, driven by informal pharmacy access and symp-tom-duration-driven decision-making in urban areas. This emphasizes the need to en-hance awareness in both sectors of the public and healthcare providers. Moreover, im-plementing and monitoring strict regulations for antibiotic sales over-the-counter in pharmacies is essential to impede escalating trends of AMR in Bangladesh.

items.title: Guaraci: A Reproducible Orchestrator for Direct Extraction of Brazilian Public-Health and Environmental Data
items.abstract: Brazilian public data relevant to health and the environment are dispersed across heterogeneous official systems - FTP servers (DATASUS), REST APIs (OpenDataSUS/DEMAS), and web portals (gov.br) - and published in legacy, often compressed formats (e.g., DBC/DBF) with schemas that change across years and topics, which makes integrated, reproducible reuse costly. Guaraci is an open-source (MIT), Docker-first orchestrator that acquires such data directly from the primary official sources, decodes legacy formats, harmonizes heterogeneous schemas, records full provenance, and delivers the result to a downstream data lake. It integrates 90+ sources spanning public health (DATASUS microdata such as hospital and mortality information system; OpenDataSUS arbovirus and immunization data; gov.br sanitation indicators) and the environment (NASA POWER climate series, FIRMS active-fire detections and GPM IMERG precipitation), behind a single asynchronous job engine exposed through a command-line interface and a REST API. Data are decoded to records with pyreaddbc/dbfread, harmonized by taking the union of all historical columns (null-padding missing fields) and exported to CSV, Parquet and SQLite with a machine-readable file capturing source, request filters and output paths. By abstracting unstable FTP servers, paginated APIs and legacy encodings behind one reproducible mechanism, Guaraci lowers the technical barrier to Brazilian public data and continuously supplies analysis-ready inputs for spatio-temporal epidemiological modelling, machine-learning applications and cross-source studies.

items.title: Claims-based frailty, dual eligibility, and potential unmet home-health needs in older breast cancer survivors.
items.abstract: Older breast cancer survivors often need home-based functional support, yet whether Medicare's restricted home health (HH) benefit leaves frailty-related need unmet at the population level is not quantified because measurement is lacking. Using linked Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results-Medicare-OASIS data, we studied 347 953 survivor-years during 2017-2020 from 134 410 women with invasive breast cancer 2-10 years post-diagnosis. We derived a claims-based predicted deficit-accumulation frailty index (DAFI), calibrated by penalized elastic-net to the observed OASIS Start-of-Care DAFI, the HH-need benchmark. Outcomes were any Medicare HH use and potential unmet need, defined as no HH use among high-need survivor-years (predicted DAFI ≥ 0.25). Logistic models estimated the marginal effects of DAFI on any Medicare HH use by frailty and dual eligibility, and disparities in potential unmet need. The claims-based DAFI was closely calibrated to observed OASIS DAFI (area under the curve = 0.715; slope = 1.111). Any HH use rose with frailty (+1.10 percentage points [pp] per +0.01 DAFI; 95% CI = 1.05 to 1.15), most steeply among never-dual survivors (+1.21 pp; 95% CI = 1.16 to 1.26) and less steeply among always-dual survivors (+0.41 pp; 95% CI = 0.30 to 0.53). Among high-need survivor years, 59.6% had no Medicare HH use. Long-term survivors had similar DAFI to 2-5-year survivors (0.216 vs 0.215) and lower HH use, but potential unmet need did not differ. A claims-based frailty proxy reveals potential frailty-related needs that Medicare HH does not reach. Expanding Medicare HH to better cover personal care and other home- and community-based services may help address frailty-related needs.

items.title: RESULT-Hip. The impact of restrictive compared with liberal transfusion strategy on cardiac injury and death in patients undergoing surgery for hip fracture : protocol for a multicentre, randomized controlled trial of two blood transfusion strategies.
items.abstract: Hip fracture is a global health issue. Complications are common, leading to reduced quality of life or death. These occur more frequently if anaemia is present. We hypothesize that correcting anaemia in the perioperative period may decrease major adverse cardiac events (MACE) and death after hip fracture. This multicentre prospective randomized trial compares transfusion strategies after hip fracture in patients aged ≥ 60 years. We initially planned to randomize 1,984 participants with anaemia, defined as haemoglobin ≤ 90 g l-1, to one of two transfusion strategies: liberal transfusion (aim haemoglobin 90 g l-1 to 110 g l-1), or restrictive transfusion (aim 75 g l-1 to 90 g l-1). The intervention lasts from randomization to hospital discharge or 30 days post randomization, whichever is soonest. The primary outcome measure was a composite of death or MACE adjudicated by blinded clinical experts. Secondary outcomes included all-cause mortality and quality of life, evaluated at 120 days. Cost-effectiveness and health economic evaluation will also be reported. This trial was funded by the National Institute for Health and Care Research, HTA award (National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) 130875) and registered at ISRCTN 28818784. Ethical approval was obtained to recruit patients in the UK. As recruitment fell short of the initial target, and following consultation with the funder, we refined our primary outcome to include myocardial injury after non-cardiac surgery (MINS), and reduced the required sample size to 842. Recruitment commenced on 10 June 2022. The first participant was recruited on 16 June 2022. We will engage clinicians and healthcare planners to implement the findings. We plan to recruit until 31 October 2026. Results will be disseminated to clinicians, policymakers, patients, and the public.

items.title: Association Between Neighbourhood-level Antibiotic Utilization and the Rate of Community-Associated C. difficile (CA-CDI) Infection: An Ecological Study.
items.abstract: Despite reductions in hospital-associated Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI) incidence in Canada and the United States, the incidence of community-associated CDI (CA-CDI) has remained high. We sought to investigate whether neighbourhood-level variation in antibiotic utilization is associated with CA-CDI. We conducted a neighbourhood-level ecological study across 1,520 neighbourhoods in Ontario, Canada. Residents aged ≥66 without hospitalization in the prior 30 days were eligible for inclusion from 2017 to 2023. Antibiotic utilization, CDI cases, and population were identified for each neighbourhood using comprehensive province-wide databases. CA-CDI rate was the outcome (incident cases of CA-CDI/10,000 person-years). Rate of antibiotic utilization (DOT per 1000 person-days) was the primary exposure. The rate-ratio (RR) of CA-CDI associated with increased antibiotic utilization was estimated using negative-binomial regression, adjusting for 8 demographic and health care covariates. We also evaluated risk based on low-, moderate-, and high-risk antibiotic strata based on published literature. We identified 19,757 CA-CDI cases. We observed substantial variation in antibiotic utilization across neighbourhoods (Median=21.1 DOT/1000 person-days; interquartile range [IQR], 16.7-25.6). After adjustments, we observed an association between overall antibiotic utilization (RR=1.13 per 10-point increase in DOT; 95% confidence interval [95%CI], 1.09-1.18). A gradient wherein higher risk antibiotic agents were more strongly associated with CA-CDI was apparent (Low-risk: RR=1.08; 95%CI, 1.01-1.15; Moderate-risk: RR=1.27; 95%CI, 1.15-1.39; High-risk: RR=1.73; 95%CI, 1.13-2.66). Neighbourhoods with higher antibiotic utilization, especially for moderate and high-risk antibiotics, have higher CA-CDI incidence. Reducing variability in neighbourhood antibiotic utilization could help reduce the burden of CDI.

items.title: Geographic Accessibility to Acute Stroke Care in Egypt: A Population-Level GIS Analysis With Hub-and-Spoke Network Optimization.
items.abstract: Egypt faces a disproportionate acute stroke burden, but geographic accessibility to intravenous thrombolysis (IVT) and mechanical thrombectomy (MT) has not been systematically quantified using modality-specific treatment windows. The objective of the current work is to measure population-level geographic accessibility to IVT and MT across Egypt's 27 governorates, characterize access inequality determinants, and model the clinical impact and cost-effectiveness of targeted hub-and-spoke network expansion. We verified 29 IVT-capable hospitals and 13 MT-ready centers through a 3-phase protocol. Onset-to-treatment time was computed for 120 settlements representing 89.3% of the national population (108.3 million). MT eligibility was based on noncontrast CT for ASPECTS scoring and CT angiography for large-vessel occlusion confirmation. Treatment windows were classified as optimal ( 270 min; MT >360 min). A maximum-coverage location problem model identified the optimal deployment for 3 new MT hubs and 4 IVT spokes. Cost-utility analysis expressed outcomes in quality-adjusted life years over 10 years using Egypt's GDP per capita of $3800. IVT optimal access was 71.8% nationally (77.0 million), while MT optimal access was only 56.2% (60.9 million), with 20.4% denied MT under the 6-hour threshold. Nine of 13 MT-ready centers (69.2%) concentrated in Cairo/Giza (19.2% of the population). Hub-and-spoke deployment improved MT optimal access from 56.2% to 75.8% nationally. Probabilistic sensitivity analysis demonstrated 73.2% and 91.4% probabilities of cost-effectiveness at 3× and 4× GDP thresholds, respectively. Egypt's MT access crisis reflects infrastructure maldistribution rather than patient ineligibility. A hub-and-spoke model using NCCT+CTA-based MT selection within the 6-hour window is clinically sound, operationally feasible, and probabilistically cost-effective.

items.title: The bacteriology of fallen leaves (Phylloplane) from council parks and green spaces in Northern Ireland: Clinical significance for at risk people living with cystic fibrosis (CF).
items.abstract: People living with cystic fibrosis (CF) may suffer from chronic respiratory infections due to acquired environmental organisms, ultimately leading in increased morbidity and mortality. Consequently, parents of children living with CF frequently ask their CF healthcare professional about sources and potential routes of transmission of environmental organisms to their child. This allows parents to make an informed decision regarding risk assessment/risk management of outdoor/ nature-based activities. Mitigations can then be put in place to help minimise or absolutely avoid exposure of the child to these sources, thereby helping to reduce/eliminate the potential for acquisition of a respiratory infection with such environmental organisms.Northern Ireland enjoys 96,470 hectares of green spaces along with just under 2,000 miles of off-road trials. To date, there has not been any scientific reports on the microbiology of fallen leaves, which children enjoy playing with during Autumn time. The aim of this study was therefore to examine the microbiology of fallen leaves from multiple public parks and green spaces in Northern Ireland, collected at Autumn time and to correlate these organisms with the microbiology from the Northern Ireland CF paediatric population, of shared bacterial genera and species, in order to ascertain the relative clinical importance of organisms identified from leaf litter to the CF paediatric population. Fallen leaves were collected from 22 public parks and greenspace sites in Northern Ireland during the Autumn 2023, which represented all 11 Council areas in Northern Ireland, with two sites per council area being sampled. Total viable counts (TVCs) were performed on each leaf litter and all organisms cultured were identified molecularly using 16S rRNA PCR and gene sequencing techniques. Direct antimicrobial susceptibility testing (DAST) of bacteria isolated from fallen leaves was determined for six antibiotics (four antibiotic classes), including the aminoglycosides, gentamicin; the fluoroquinolones, ciprofloxacin; the betalactams, ampicillin, piperacillin-tazobactam and meropenem, as well as the potentiated sulphonamides, cotrimoxazole (sulphamethoxazole & trimethoprim). Routine service microbiological records of respiratory specimens from 183 paediatric individuals with cystic fibrosis attending the Northern Ireland Paediatric Cystic Fibrosis Centre, Royal Belfast Hospital for Sick Children, Belfast Health and Social Care Trust, Belfast, were compared anonymously with organisms isolated from leaf litter. Comparisons were recorded at both genus and species levels. The mean TVC was log 7.35 ± 0.57/g leaves (standard deviation) and ± 0.12 (standard error of mean). The median TVC was log 7.23/g leaves. Patrician Villas Play Park, Strabane had the lowest count (log 6.49/g leaves) and Wallace Park, Lisburn had the highest count (log 9.38/g leaves). Fifteen bacterial genera and 17 species were identified in this study, comprising 11 Gram negative and 4 Gram positive genera, including Aeromonas sp., Arthrobacter koreensis, Arthrobacter sp., Bacillus sp., Buttiauxella agrestis, Buttiauxella sp., Carnobacterium divergens, Citrobacter sp., Citrobacter werkmanii, Enterobacter cloacae, Enterobacter sp., Lelliottia amnigena, Pectobacterium atrosepticum, Pectobacterium sp. Pseudomonas fluorescens, Pseudomonas fragi, Pseudomonas seleniipraecipitans, Pseudomonas spp., Pseudomonas veronii, Rahnella victoriana, Serratia fonticola, Serratia proteamaculans, Serratia spp., Sporosarcina contaminans, Stenotrophomonas rhizophila, Stenotrophomonas sp. and Yersinia kristensenii.Pseudomonas aeruginosa was not isolated from leaves collected from any site. Eight bacterial genera were shared between children living with CF and leaf litter and included: Aeromonas, Citrobacter, Enterobacter, Pseudomonas, Rahnella, Serratia, Stenotrophomonas and Yersinia. Only four species were shared between children living with CF and leaf litter, including: Enterobacter cloacae, Pseudomonas fluorescens, Pseudomonas fragi and Pseudomonas veronii. Bacterial organisms isolated from leaves from all sites were resistant to ampicillin (100%), but were fully sensitive to ciprofloxacin (100%), piperacillin-tazobactam (100%) and gentamicin (100%). Regarding meropenem and cotrimoxazole, resistance to these antibiotics was 45.5% and 4.5%, respectively. Fallen leaves isolated from public parks and green spaces in Northern Ireland were shown to harbour a diverse variety of bacteria, some of which have been isolated from respiratory specimens from children living with CF. None of these bacteria including the co-isolated species represented clinically significant respiratory pathogens of the CF lung and were regarded as transient colonisers of the CF lung. Pseudomonas aeruginosa was not identified in this study originating from fallen leaves. When deciding on the relative risk of children living with CF playing with leaves, parents of children living with CF need to make an informed decision, balancing the sensory exploration of nature through interaction with leaves, as well as physical, emotional and social benefits gained from nature play, with the relative risk of exposure to environmental organisms.

items.title: Perceptions of resident doctors on how digital clinical decision support influences decisions on use of resources.
items.abstract: There is a growing interest in the use of digital learning and clinical decision support (CDS) in medical education and clinical practice. However, until recently there has been little interest in the potential cost savings that could emerge from the use of digital CDS in clinical practice. This study attempted to fill this gap by asking frontline resident doctors by means of a questionnaire to what extent they value digital CDS resources as a way of saving costs. We developed a questionnaire to examine the perceptions of frontline resident doctors on CDS use. Topics explored included the use of CDS to save costs by avoiding unnecessary interventions; if and how CDS assisted with decision making, and barriers and enablers to achieving these outcomes. We emailed the questionnaire to frontline resident doctors. A total of 170 resident doctors were invited to participate in the study, with 105 completing the questionnaire (response rate 62%). Resident doctors are doctors who are in postgraduate training, but who have not yet achieved consultant status. A total of 42 respondents (40%) agreed or strongly agreed that CDS helped them avoid unnecessary referrals. Overall, 32 respondents (31%) agreed or strongly agreed that using the resource helped them reduce length of stay in hospital. A total of 44 respondents (42%) agreed or strongly agreed that using the resource helped them avoid unnecessary admissions. 76 respondents (72%) agreed or strongly agreed that CDS helped them avoid unnecessary investigations or treatments. The findings from this study show that some resident doctors can use CDS to reduce resource use. Resident doctors may find CDS a supportive tool to assist decision making and so to avoid some unnecessary tests and treatments.

items.title: Addressing the weight of the issue: gaps in obesity education among US osteopathic medical students.
items.abstract: Context Obesity is a significant public health concern, with the United States experiencing some of the highest obesity rates worldwide. Despite the widespread prevalence and negative impacts on patient health, obesity education in medical school curricula remains insufficient. This training deficit contributes to a lack of preparedness among medical students in the management of obesity, leading to healthcare provider bias and inadequate patient care. Objectives This study aims to identify potential gaps in obesity education within US osteopathic medical schools by assessing current osteopathic medical students' knowledge, confidence, and perceptions of medical school obesity education. Methods A quantitative cross-sectional survey was distributed to osteopathic medical students across all 42 US osteopathic medical schools through the Student Osteopathic Medical Association (SOMA) weekly emails, SOMA internal chapter emails, and SOMA social media accounts from October 2024 to December 2024. The inclusion criteria were that participants had to be currently enrolled first-, second-, third-, and fourth-year osteopathic medical students and provide informed consent. The responses were summarized utilizing descriptive analysis. Each survey question was analyzed independently, considering the varying number of responses received per question. Results A total of 208 students participated in the survey. Out of the 208 respondents, most students felt somewhat prepared (38.5 %) or unprepared/very unprepared (32.7 %) to manage obesity and provide nutrition education in the clinical setting. Due to the number of participants, the responses are considered in aggregate and not grouped by cohort year. In addition, there was nearly an even split among students regarding comfort in discussing obesity and weight management with patients, with 30.6 % stating that they are uncomfortable or very uncomfortable, 37.4 % reporting being somewhat comfortable, and 32.0 % feeling comfortable or very comfortable. Only 14.1 % of students reported having standardized patient encounters regarding obesity counseling, with most of these encounters (55.2 %) lasting less than 30 min. Regarding comfort discussing weight bias and stigma, 59.8 % of the students reported feeling somewhat comfortable, comfortable, or very comfortable discussing weight bias and stigma, while 40.2 % were slightly uncomfortable or not comfortable addressing the topic with patients. Given the limited sample size and response rate, these findings are exploratory and limited by a low response rate and potential response bias. Conclusions These findings suggest potential gaps in obesity education among the responding osteopathic medical students. While limited by sample size and possible response bias, the results highlight opportunities for strengthening obesity-related curricula, particularly in experiential learning and weight bias training.

items.title: Cancer Screening and Follow Up Among Individuals With Serious Mental Illness.
items.abstract: Purpose Cancer is the second leading cause of death in the United States. Individuals with serious mental illness (SMI) have higher cancer mortality, which may be due to lower screening rates and barriers to timely, effective care. The current study explored how individuals with SMI perceive cancer screening and follow up to identify barriers and facilitators to care. Method Using a qualitative interpretive description approach, we conducted individual interviews with 10 adults with SMI about their cancer screening experiences. Results The most frequently reported barriers were distrust of the health care system, psychiatric symptoms, fear, low prioritization, and shame. Facilitators included support systems, regular primary care, positive health care experiences, and personal agency. Conclusion Findings highlight the importance of providing supportive health care services and strengthening personal agency as key components of recovery and cancer screening and follow up in individuals with SMI.

items.title: Learners do not readily form abstract category representations across sensory modalities.
items.abstract: A long-standing debate in cognitive science centers around whether our internal representations of the external world are abstract and amodal or whether they are grounded by sensory modality. Perceptual category learning presents a unique test bed of this debate as categories exist within all sensory modalities, but there is mixed evidence about whether people form abstract representations that can be analogized across modalities. In the present study, we examine whether learners form such abstract representations of auditory and visual categories that share the same rule-based structure. Across three experiments, we examine whether learners spontaneously or explicitly form abstract representations across sensory modalities. Overall, we found no evidence of shared abstract representations even in the conditions that would theoretically most strongly encourage it-when information across modalities was conceptually aligned (rather than misaligned), when information across modalities was encountered within the same task (rather than separate tasks), and when participants were explicitly instructed to analogize across modalities (rather than doing so spontaneously). These results suggest that even when abstract representation across auditory and visual modalities is encouraged, the knowledge formed during perceptual category learning is modality-specific. These results highlight the importance of considering the role of modality in category learning and cognition more broadly. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: On bias in detecting bias: A signal detection analysis of attributions to gender discrimination.
items.abstract: Discrimination is the unjust treatment of people based on their group membership, and detecting discrimination is a necessary first step in countering it. Attributions to discrimination have often been conceptualized in terms of signal detection theory, with researchers speculating about the role of sensitivity (i.e., observers' ability to recognize discrimination) and response bias (i.e., their tendency to judge that discrimination is present) in observers' judgments. Here, we take a first step toward moving beyond conceptual applications to empirical signal detection theory analyses of attributions to discrimination across five studies examining judgments about gender discrimination in corporate pay raise decisions. We find that prototypes (Studies 1-3) and their alignment with the actual pattern of decisions (Studies 2-4) inform observers' response bias, reflecting differences in their attribution of unfair outcomes to discrimination (Study 5). In contrast, the extent of harm caused by discriminatory outcomes exerts a small effect on sensitivity and a large effect on response bias (Studies 1-3), which reflects observers' determination of a fair standard for decisions (Study 5). Theoretically, the present work contributes to the causal analysis of central factors shaping attributions to discrimination. Specifically, we shed light on whether effects of these factors are mediated by response bias or sensitivity, and assess their causal origin in either the application of a merit standard or attributional processing. items.title: Talking with language models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) produce text that invites us to treat our interactions with them as conversations, and to treat them as intelligent interlocutors who remember, act, and make commitments. We argue that this conversational presupposition is mistaken. We introduce the artifactual stance, which describes human–AI interaction in terms of their design and affordances, rather than potential intentional attitudes. On our account, LLMs produce candidate text that users interpret, evaluate, and sometimes adopt as their own speech. We argue that such exchanges are not conversations, since generating text does not itself constitute an utterance or the performance of a speech act. Rather the communicative and normative work of interpretation, commitment, and action remains with the user. Our framework explains both the sophistication and usefulness of LLMs, and the conversational appearances that can be traced back to properties of the interface and to artifact design. It also reframes puzzles about AI reference, the persistence of supposed interlocutors, and responsibility for AI-generated text. These questions are better approached through an account of how artifacts mediate human linguistic practices than through assumptions about AI speakerhood.

items.title: Examining cognitive correlates of motivated memory in older adults using standard and naturalistic paradigms
items.abstract: Background: Learning and retaining information is essential for daily function. Research within several sectors of psychology (e.g., educational, cognitive, behavioral neuroscience) suggests that motivation and the reward system interact with memory structures, thus potentially influencing memory performance. This has been termed motivated memory. Motivated memory has been studied in adults across the lifespan but has yet to be thoroughly explored using established and novel, naturalistic paradigms in older adults. Studying the effect of motivation on memory in older adults is particularly important because a decline in cognitive function (i.e., memory) over time can lead to decreased independence and quality of life and an increase of caregiver burden. Motivated memory mechanisms may offer unique opportunities for intervention for those with cognitive decline. As such, greater understanding regarding the extent to which motivation can impact cognition, especially for memory for naturalistic, ecologically valid information, is needed. The aim of the current study is to gain a more thorough understanding of how motivation impacts memory. Specifically, we aimed to address important gaps in the literature regarding 1) the cognitive correlates of the motivated memory effect (i.e., episodic memory, executive function), 2) the type of information and learning processes that are most influenced by motivation (i.e., item memory, semantic memory, associative memory; free recall, recognition), 3) the effect of motivation on memory, specifically in a population of older adults, and 4) using a paradigm that simulates naturalistic information. Methods: This study recruited 53 participants to complete two cognitive tasks: an established task called the Selectivity Task (ST) and a novel task called the Motivated Memory Task (MMT). Both tasks assessed recall of higher value information compared to lower value information (e.g., motivated memory). Participants also completed questionnaires assessing their current mood, cognitive function, and motivation. The ST utilized an arbitrary point value system, and the MMT was designed to present naturalistic, health-related information that is of higher value (dementia risk factors and prevention facts) and lower value (polio risk factors and prevention facts). Participants also completed a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment, from which we derived composite scores of cognitive domains to examine cognitive correlates of motivated memory. Regressions examined the cognitive correlates of motivated memory on the ST, using the selectivity index (ST-SI; Aim 1). A series of ANCOVAs were performed to evaluate the effect of motivation on recalling higher versus lower value items on the novel MMT (Aim 2). Results: Results suggest that the ST-SI was not associated with either episodic memory, executive function, or motivation score. Contrary to our hypotheses, on the MMT, participants recalled more semantic details about the prevention facts for polio overall, across all time points. However, consistent with hypotheses, participants recognized dementia risk factors with greater accuracy than polio risk factors on a test of delayed recognition. Conclusion: Motivation to learn health information may influence item recognition memory but not free recall and not semantic or associative memory, possibly providing support for the dual-process theory of memory and aging. These results suggest that healthcare providers should encourage patients to use cue-based recognition for their care rather than relying on free recall.

items.title: An exploratory study of relationships between the executive functions and spatiotemporal control in a complex motor task: the spatial tapping task
items.abstract: Executive functions (EFs) are cognitive processes enabling planning, control, and regulation of behavior. A variety of tasks have been developed to evaluate EFs, from complex reasoning to simpler inhibition tasks, reflecting the diversity of symptoms observed in patients with executive deficits. Recent research has emphasized their unity , proposing three core functions, working memory, inhibition, and switching, that share resources and combine to enable complex tasks. Yet, no single task captures both the unity and diversity of EFs, limiting the development of a unified framework and a balanced assessment. To address this gap, we designed the spatial tapping task, a timing paradigm combining finger tapping and circle drawing. Finger tapping requires working memory for explicit timing control, whereas circle drawing requires anticipatory control akin to switching to control movement trajectory, enabling implicit timing control. Participants produce taps along a circular trajectory with the tempo increasing progressively. A slow tempo favors discrete movements with long pauses between taps, whereas a fast tempo promotes continuous motion. Previous analyses supported a change in timing control mode with increasing tempo. Here, we explored the hypothesis that EFs are engaged accordingly: working memory in the slow/discrete phase, switching in the fast/continuous phase, and inhibition in the intermediate phase, where demands for continuous motion increase. In two studies combined into a single dataset, we compared scores with those from neuropsychological tests using correlations. We found that timing accuracy in the slow/discrete phase was associated with working memory, spatial accuracy in the fast/continuous phase with switching, and longer contact time in the intermediate phase with inhibition. We also explored whether performance was consistent with the EF deficits described in the literature, and the potential contribution of motor output, reporting scores obtained across populations with executive deficits (aging and dementia), combined executive and motor impairments (schizophrenia), and motor expertise (biscriptual writers), along with matched controls. Findings were consistent, although often more specific, and highlighted an important contribution of motor output. Altogether, our results provide initial evidence that the task can be used to investigate EFs, although cognitive, motor, and sensory contributions need to be disentangled to improve its specificity.

items.title: The construction of professionals' perception of emotional intelligence competence and the symbolic association of performance and project success in the UK construction industry
items.abstract: Research Gap - The UK construction industry faces challenges such as disputes, low productivity, and poor project delivery, partly due to the lack of soft skills, including communication, motivation, negotiation, ethics, and Emotional Intelligence (EI). The impact of EI remains unclear. This study argues that addressing industry issues requires both technical and soft skills, with EI being crucial. A gap exists in understanding EI awareness, perceptions, and use, especially its effect on performance and projects. Purpose - This thesis explores the link between EI competence and construction professionals' perceived performance, evaluating whether EI is vital for project success in the UK. Methodology - Using semi-structured interviews and reflexive thematic analysis via NVivo 14, the study maps EI to Goleman’s models to examine understanding and application of EI, recommending ways to foster an EI-aware workforce. Findings: Few participants received EI training; however, those who did showed improved engagement with stakeholders. Most lacked EI training, indicating unawareness. The holistic EI skills included stakeholder engagement, trust, communication, teambuilding, resilience, social awareness, relationship management, and humour, all of which are essential for conflict resolution, teamwork, and psychological safety. A lack of EI led to conflicts, delays, operational issues, and increased costs. Professionals see a broad industry need for EI awareness, recommending integration into competency frameworks by industry bodies such as RICS, CIOB, CIAT, ICE, and APM and academic curricula. Originality - The study highlights a critical lack of EI knowledge in the UK construction sector, advocating for EI to be part of mandatory training, standards, and education.

items.title: Post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation: Harnessing digital technologies and mirror therapy to improve stroke survivors' outcomes
items.abstract: Background: More than 70% of stroke survivors experience upper limb weakness. The rehabilitation process of upper limbs requires the effort of multidisciplinary health professionals and a package of interventions, of which digital technology and mirror therapy are being used, yet evidence on their implementation and effectiveness remains fragmented and inconsistent, especially in home settings. Therefore, this thesis addresses the extent of their use, the factors influencing their implementation, and their impact on the outcomes of stroke survivors with upper limb weakness. Methods: Five studies included: (1) a scoping review mapping research on home-based digital technologies for post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation (published); (2) an online survey assessing Allied Health Professionals' (AHPs) engagement with digital technologies in supporting stroke survivors with upper limb weakness in home settings; (3) a qualitative interview study exploring barriers and facilitators to AHPs' digital technology use in supporting stroke survivors with upper limb weakness in home settings, underpinned by the COM-B model; (4) a secondary analysis of randomised controlled trial data evaluating the impact of integrating mirror therapy (MT) into occupational therapy on health-related quality of life (HRQoL) in stroke survivors with upper limb weakness; and (5) a scoping review on the application of immersive virtual reality mirror therapy in post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation (IVRMT) (published). Results: The digital technologies used in home-based post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation were multimodal and system-based, comprising telerehabilitation, gamification, virtual reality, mobile technology, sensors, and robotics. AHPs' perceived engagement with these and other related digital technologies was limited and was influenced by their digital literacy, experience, belief, perceived effectiveness, and confidence, as well as simplicity of technology, and patient and organisational factors. Additionally, integrating MT into rehabilitation appeared to improve HRQoL, while IVRMT was applicable and effective in enhancing patient engagement and motor recovery. III Conclusions: Digital technologies augment post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation in home settings. Improving AHPs' digital uptake requires addressing identified barriers and implementing facilitators. Additionally, while traditional MT is still effective, its digital form (IVRMT) can maximise patient engagement and motor recovery. Implications: This thesis presents implications for AHP education and clinical practice, patient use and engagement with digital technologies, and the development and implementation of IVRMT in post-stroke upper limb rehabilitation. The findings reflect the need for targeted digital competency training, curriculum development, and ongoing professional development to support AHPs in effectively integrating digital technologies into home-based rehabilitation practice. At the patient level, the thesis emphasises the importance of personalised, user-centred approaches that consider cognitive ability, digital literacy, psychological readiness, social support, and home environment to maximise engagement and reduce digital exclusion. The findings also highlight the potential of mirror therapy, especially IVRMT, as an engaging and feasible adjunct to the existing stroke rehabilitation protocol, with implications for improving motivation and motor recovery.

items.title: When digital literacy meets negative bias: Understanding the adoption of online information and sentiment on X
items.abstract: Digital platforms increasingly mediate how citizens engage with public policy, shaping not only access to information but also the formation of collective interpretations and sentiments. In the context of Indonesia’s Free Nutritious Meal (Makan Bergizi Gratis: MBG) program, this study examines the relationship between individual digital literacy and online information adoption, while simultaneously mapping public sentiment and discourse dynamics on X. Employing a concurrent mixed-methods design, the study combines an online survey of 385 social media users drawing on the DigComp 2.2 framework and the Information Adoption Model with large-scale social media analysis of 87,589 MBG-related mentions on X collected between April and August 2025 using Drone Emprit. Regression analysis revealed that digital literacy significantly predicts information adoption regarding the MBG program (β = 0.581, R² = 0.549, p < 0.001), indicating that digital literacy explains 54.9% of the variance in information adoption and substantially enhances individuals’ capacity to evaluate and accept policy-related information. While digital literacy supports information adoption at the individual level, the overall online discourse surrounding MBG remained predominantly negative, suggesting a disconnect between individual informational competence and collective sentiment formation. Sentiment analysis further revealed that public discourse was predominantly negative (56%), compared with positive (43%) and neutral (1%) expressions, with significant surges observed in May and July 2025. Network analysis additionally revealed that negative sentiment is concentrated around accounts with high centrality and influence, thereby amplifying critical narratives through networked interactions. These findings highlight a structural tension between individual informational competence and collective sentiment formation in digital communication environments. This research contributes to the existing body of work on digital communication and public policy by illustrating that initiatives aimed at improving digital literacy should be complemented by network-aware communication strategies, such as influencer engagement and real-time discourse monitoring, to bolster public trust and legitimacy in extensive policy interventions.

items.title: Doray the Catbaloganon Explorer on Probability: Validation of a Mathematics Strategic Intervention Material (SIM)
items.abstract: Aim: This study aimed to develop and validate Doray the Catbaloganon Explorer on Probability, a culturally contextualized and gamified Strategic Intervention Material (SIM) for teaching probability to Grade 8 learners. Methodology:The study employed a descriptive-evaluative research design.Five experts and Grade 8 students evaluated the developed SIM in terms of content validity, clarity and readability, engagement and motivation, practicality and usefulness, design and visual appeal, and usability.Results: All 14 indicators obtained an Item-Level Content Validity Index (I-CVI) of 1.00, resulting in a Scale-Level Content Validity Index (S-CVI) of 1.00, indicating excellent content validity.The SIM received Very High/Excellent ratings across all evaluation dimensions, with mean scores ranging from 4.89 to 4.98 and standard deviations ranging from 0.02 to 0.08.Reliability received the highest rating among both experts (M = 4.97, SD = 0.03) and students (M = 4.98, SD = 0.02). Conclusion:The developed SIM demonstrated excellent content validity and very high ratings for instructional quality, usability, and acceptability.It may therefore be used as a supplementary instructional resource for teaching probability to Grade 8 learners.

items.title: Development of Communication Styles Scale (CSS) for University Students: Qualitative Item Generation and Content Validation
items.abstract: University life is one of the most challenging phases of a student's life because of the interplay of social and academic demands, resulting in anxiety and stress (Yan, 2025; Zhang et al., 2022; SAMFIRA, 2020). One of the challenges is maintaining good interpersonal relationships and communication is imperative to this (Horan et al., 2021, Griggio et al., 2019; Chandra, Mohammadnezhad, & Ward, 2018). However, as people vary both in verbal and non-verbal communication due to cultural differences (Mascarenhas et al., 2015); it is important to know more about this area to develop effective communication skills accordingly. The current study aimed to develop a scale to measure communication styles among university students. Following a rigorous literature review, which identified gaps in existing measures, two focus groups and three semi-structured interviews with clinical psychologists were conducted. After thematic analysis, a final pool of items was generated for expert review. For this, Content Validity Index was established by clinical psychologists through rating the relevance of the items to the construct (N=7) and 40 items were retained.

items.title: Monitoring AI-generated English research texts: lexical-semantic accuracy, source fidelity, and revision performance
items.abstract: Introduction Linguistically fluent AI-generated English texts can conceal lexical-semantic shifts, altered concept boundaries, source omissions, and unsupported causal formulations. This study compared English paragraphs generated under general and source-constrained conditions and examined how learners' global judgments and localized problem marking were associated with subsequent written revision. Methods Seventy-three agricultural and forestry students evaluated two English paragraphs generated from Chinese source materials under a fixed sequence of general and source-constrained prompts, then selected and revised one paragraph. The linked corpus comprised 146 AI-generated texts, 73 revised texts, 146 global judgment records, 657 expert rating records, 562 coded terminology units, and 511 participant-marked problems. Expert assessments covered lexical-semantic accuracy, source fidelity, and global discourse organization, while revision analyses examined global judgment discrepancy, localized problem marking, and individual-difference variables. Results Source-constrained texts received higher lexical-semantic accuracy scores (mean difference = 0.846, t = 10.634, p < 0.001, d z = 1.245) and source-fidelity scores (mean difference = 0.855, t = 8.819, p < 0.001, d z = 1.032), while global discourse organization differed little between conditions. Lexical-semantic accuracy was strongly associated with source fidelity ( b = 0.522, p < 0.001), whereas the 5,000-resample bootstrap interval for the product of the adjusted coefficients linking these measures to discourse organization spanned zero. After controlling for selected source-text quality, localized problem marking and domain knowledge were positively associated with revised quality, trust in AI-generated language output was negatively associated, and global judgment discrepancy showed no unique association. Discussion Source comparison and localized problem identification were more closely associated with successful written revision than agreement with expert global judgments. These findings highlight the importance of attending to linguistic form, semantic boundaries, and source information when evaluating and revising AI-generated English research texts.

items.title: Managing at the Margin: A Conceptual Framework of Nano-Enterprise Management, Collective Support, Survival and Real Graduation in Nigeria
items.abstract: Most Nigerian enterprises are very small, and since 2021, national policy has treated the smallest of them, those with turnover below ₦3 million and one or two workers, as a separate nano tier. Management research and support programmes often treat these ventures as miniature versions of larger firms, although their owners work under acute scarcity of capital, time and attention. This conceptual, theory-building paper integrates scarcity theory, evidence on management practices and business training in small firms, entrepreneurial bricolage and collective-action theory, and draws on the authors’ studies of cooperative membership and savings. Its specific contribution is a scarcity-based framework of nano-enterprise management that separates survival and income stability from real graduation to the micro tier, which is measured on turnover deflated to 2021 naira. Nine propositions, each with falsification criteria and boundary conditions, state that scarcity lowers the quality of management practices; those simple practices matter at least as much as conventional training for survival, and personal-initiative capability matters more for graduation; that bricolage protects survival but does not by itself produce growth; and that cooperative support helps where governance is sound and complements capability building. The paper concludes that short, simple support delivered through well-governed collectives is the most promising route to survival and graduation, although no proposition has yet been tested. It recommends that SMEDAN and development partners pilot and evaluate simple-rule and personal-initiative modules against conventional training and track graduation on deflated turnover.

items.title: Doing development differently: reframing academic development in the shadow of performance and scarcity
items.abstract: This study investigates how academic development (AD) is enacted in resource-constrained, performance-driven university contexts where formal structures are weak or absent. Drawing on qualitative data from a large private university in southwest China, the research introduces the concept of compressed institutional contexts to explain how academic work is reorganised under simultaneous demands for accountability, market responsiveness, and student outcomes. Rather than disappearing, AD is redistributed across overlapping roles and embedded within daily practices such as teaching, student support, and administrative coordination. The findings show that academic development persists in such contexts not through formalised centres or structured programmes, but as embedded and improvised practices woven into everyday academic work. Faculty development is increasingly shaped by institutional performance logics, including employability outcomes and evaluative targets, rather than by pedagogical ideals or reflective enhancement alone. Professional growth occurs primarily through multi-role enactment and real-time adaptation, as academics learn by integrating teaching, administration, and coordination responsibilities under conditions of institutional urgency. By reframing academic development as an organisationally situated and practice-based process, this paper contributes to a more inclusive understanding of AD that accounts for non-elite, market-facing, and resource-constrained institutions.
