items.title: The FU Ori Outburst of PR Ori B
items.abstract: Abstract We report the discovery of a nearby FU Ori–type outburst (FUor), PR Ori B, in the L1641 cluster of the Orion star-forming region. The high-amplitude variability was first identified in the NEOWISE (3–5 μ m) photometry of the unresolved PR Ori binary system. Long-term, resolved optical photometric monitoring demonstrates that PR Ori B is the driver of a Δ G = 5 mag outburst, while PR Ori A has remained constant over the past 20 yr. The near-IR spectrum of PR Ori B changes from a late K-type spectral type during quiescence to a viscously heated disk during outburst, including deep absorption in 12 CO and H 2 O bands. The optical spectrum also exhibits features that are commonly associated with FUors, including P Cygni profiles in Na i D lines and absorption in the Ca ii infrared triplet. The luminosity of the outburst ( L acc ∼ 30–40 L ⊙ ) is similar to that commonly observed in FUors. The comparison of Spitzer/Infrared Spectrograph and Very Large Telescope/VISIR spectroscopy shows some evidence of silicate crystallization during the outburst. PR Ori B is one of the closest and brightest FUors discovered over the past few years, only one magnitude fainter than the archetype of the class FU Ori. The proximity and brightness will allow for future high angular resolution observations to probe the physics of the inner disk and to evaluate changes in the disk due to the increased luminosity.

items.title: Exploring the dynamics of the Coma galaxy cluster by mapping its X-ray emission line profiles with XRISM
items.abstract: Abstract The intracluster medium (ICM) in merging galaxy clusters exhibits turbulence and bulk flows. Unraveling these components is crucial not only for elucidating the geometry of the cluster mergers, but also for understanding the physics of magnetic field amplification and relativistic particle acceleration. XRISM/Resolve data for two $3^{\prime }\times 3^{\prime }$ fields in the core of the Coma cluster reveals that the ICM in the central field moves with $\Delta cz = -430$ km s$^{-1}$ relative to the cluster galaxy average, while that in the southern field moves with $\Delta cz = -730$ km s$^{-1}$ (see XRISM Collaboration et al. 2025, ApJ, 985, L20; hereinafter “Paper I”). In this paper, we perform a more detailed analysis of these data sets to search for non-Gaussian features in the Fe K line complex profiles. In the spectra from the north-west quadrant of the central field, in addition to the main and redshifted ICM components ($\Delta cz = -6$ km s$^{-1}$) reported in Paper I, we find evidence of another, blueshifted, component, moving with $\Delta cz = -1274$ km s$^{-1}$. For a systematic search for other significant velocity components, we perform a bias-free $3$ eV step multi-component fit to the Resolve full-array spectra from the central and southern fields. This search uncovers another redshifted component in the southern field, moving with $\Delta cz \sim +1250$ km s$^{-1}$. We estimate the energy densities of the ICM turbulence and bulk motion to be similar to each other and several times greater than the energy density of the cluster’s $B\sim 5\, \mu$G magnetic field.

items.title: Can Auroral Heating Explain Brown Dwarf Thermal Inversions?
items.abstract: Abstract Recent modeling of the JWST spectra of the Y dwarf CWISEPJ193518.59-154620.3 and the T dwarf SIMPJ013656.5+093347.3 indicates the presence of a thermal inversion in their atmospheres, implying an additional source of heating. Auroral energy deposition has been proposed as a potential mechanism. In this work, we model auroral energy deposition processes and the resulting atmospheric response to assess whether physically motivated auroral electron beam energy spectra can reproduce the inferred thermal inversions. We simulate the effects of several auroral electron beam energy spectra consistent with observations of the Jovian population of auroral electrons and scale them to the total electron flux expected for brown dwarfs. We find that auroral energy deposition alone cannot reproduce both the magnitude and pressure level of the inferred inversion in either object. While inversions are produced in our models, they occur at pressures that are too low compared to those required by the observations. These results suggest that the actual population of auroral electrons includes a stronger high-energy component than considered here, that additional heating mechanisms contribute to the observed thermal inversions, and/or that heterogeneous heating of the atmosphere is important for determining the observed emission.

items.title: Systematic Effects of Hydrogen and Helium Atmosphere Mismatch on Radius Inference in PSR J0740+6620–like Synthetic NICER Data
items.abstract: Abstract Constraints on neutron star radii provide insight into the properties of the cold, dense matter in their interiors. Previous studies using synthetic Neutron Star Interior Composition Explorer (NICER) pulse waveform data have demonstrated that radius inferences derived therefrom are robust against several classes of modeling systematics. Here we explore the consequences of assuming the wrong atmospheric composition, using synthetic data based on the ∼2.1 M ⊙ pulsar PSR J0740+6620. We find that the assumption of a hydrogen atmosphere when the synthetic data assumed a helium atmosphere, or vice versa, produces little bias in the inferred radius at the spot-to-background ratio of the actual PSR J0740+6620 data. However, when we increase the spot-to-background ratio by a factor of ∼20 while keeping the total number of counts fixed at the observed ∼5.5 × 10 5 , we find that composition mismatch can produce significantly biased radius estimates while remaining hidden inside a fit with statistically acceptable residuals. Even in these cases, the Bayesian evidence consistently identifies the correct atmospheric model. Our findings reinforce the importance of using the Bayesian evidence for model comparison and goodness-of-fit tests.

items.title: Disk Truncation Triggers Relativistic Jet Launching of a Highly Accreting Supermassive Black Hole
items.abstract: Abstract Relativistic jets are among the most energetic phenomena in the Universe and influence galaxy evolution through energetic feedback, yet the physical connection between accretion flows and jet launching remains unresolved. Jet production is widely attributed to the Blandford–Znajek mechanism, which extracts black hole rotational energy via large-scale magnetic fields sustained by an accretion flow. Although this mechanism is observationally well supported for hot, geometrically thick accretion flows, highly accreting environments with strong jets present a paradox, as they are typically dominated by cold, geometrically thin disks incapable of sustaining large-scale magnetic fields. Here, we report coordinated X-ray microcalorimeter spectroscopy achieved by X-ray Imaging and Spectroscopy Mission (XRISM) and millimeter–radio interferometric observations by Global Millimeter Very Long Baseline Interferometry (VLBI) Array (GMVA), Very Long Baseline Array (VLBA), and East Asian VLBI Network (EAVN) of the broad-line radio galaxy 3C 120. High-resolution X-ray spectroscopy reveals a relativistically broadened Fe K α line, indicating that the cold, geometrically thin disk is truncated at ∼20 R g ( R g is the gravitational radius), with the inner region replaced by a hot, geometrically thick flow. Concurrently, radio imaging indicates that jet profile extrapolation toward the black hole horizon yields a radius comparable to or even narrower than the disk truncation radius. These results demonstrate that, even at high accretion rates, jet launching is linked to a hot inner flow, possibly via the Blandford–Znajek process, providing evidence for a universal disk–jet connection via geometric transition.

items.title: A Bayesian Inference Framework for Binary Lens Events Fully Incorporating Higher-order Effects
items.abstract: Abstract Higher-order effects, such as microlensing parallax and lens orbital motion, are essential for characterizing the physical properties of microlensing planetary systems, including their masses and distances. In practice, higher-order effects are often included in light-curve modeling only when their signals are strong, because their inclusion in weakly constrained cases tends to drive the inferred parameters toward regions of parameter space that are disfavored by standard Galactic models. This binary choice over physically continuous effects introduces an event-dependent selection function that complicates population-level interpretation and prevents strong and weak detections from being combined within a single uniform framework. In this work, we investigate the origin of instabilities associated with higher-order effects and show that such instabilities can arise from a mismatch between commonly adopted uninformative priors in the light-curve parameter space and the distributions predicted by Galactic models. Motivated by this, we develop a new Bayesian framework that enables higher-order effects to be incorporated in a stable and uniform manner. As part of this framework, we introduce the Galactic Prior Modeling Engine ( gapmoe ), a dedicated tool that enables efficient evaluation of the Galactic prior density and allows it to be incorporated directly into the light-curve inference. Using simulated events, we demonstrate that our framework robustly recovers the true physical parameters while fully accounting for microlensing parallax and lens orbital motion. This framework eliminates the need for ad hoc model selection and provides a scalable and statistically consistent pathway for analyzing the large samples expected from next-generation surveys such as the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

items.title: Accreting Neutron Stars in Low-Mass X-ray Binaries
items.abstract: Abstract Neutron star low-mass X-ray binaries (NS LMXBs) are systems in which a neutron star accretes matter from a Roche-lobe-filling companion via an accretion disc, releasing gravitational energy with an efficiency of order 10–20% of the rest-mass energy. Unlike black holes, neutron stars possess a solid surface and a magnetic field, making NS LMXBs uniquely rich laboratories for high-energy astrophysics and dense-matter physics. In this article we review the current understanding of accretion onto neutron stars in LMXBs, tracing matter from the outer disc radii to the stellar surface across five decades of observational discovery. We survey the principal classes of accreting neutron star systems — canonical atoll and Z-sources, ultracompact X-ray binaries, accreting millisecond pulsars, and transitional millisecond pulsars — and discuss how their spectral states, timing properties, and multiwavelength behaviour encode the physics of the inner accretion flow. We examine thermonuclear Type-I X-ray bursts as probes of nuclear burning and neutron star structure, and review the boundary and spreading layers where accreted matter decelerates onto the stellar surface. We discuss relativistic jets and ionised disc winds as regulators of the accretion–ejection cycle. Finally, we present X-ray polarimetric results from the Imaging X-ray Polarimetry Explorer ( IXPE ), which for the first time provide new, though model-dependent, constraints on the geometry of the emission regions — disc, corona, spreading layer, and jets — that spectroscopy alone cannot resolve, alongside complementary optical and infrared polarimetric observations.

items.title: Wine Quality Grading from Physicochemical Features: Comparing SVM and Random Forest with PCA/t-SNE Visualization
items.abstract: This study investigates multi-class prediction of wine quality scores (3–8) using physicochemical measurements from a Kaggle dataset. After removing the identifier field and standardizing features, we examine the data structure with correlation analysis and low-dimensional embeddings. PCA and t-SNE visualizations reveal substantial overlap among adjacent quality levels, implying gradual transitions rather than sharply separable classes. We then benchmark an RBF-kernel Support Vector Machine (SVM) and a Random Forest (RF) using an 80/20 stratified train/test split and 5-fold stratified cross-validation, tuning hyperparameters using Macro-F1 to account for class imbalance. Cross-validation slightly favors RF (Macro-F1 0.3271) over SVM (0.3078). On the held-out test set, RF achieves higher overall performance (Accuracy 0.7118, Macro-F1 0.3442, Weighted-F1 0.6897) than SVM (Accuracy 0.6332, Macro-F1 0.3072, Weighted-F1 0.6157). However, the relatively low Macro-F1 indicates uneven per-class performance, with limited effectiveness at rare quality levels, as reflected in confusion patterns that concentrate between neighboring grades (e.g., 5↔6 and 6↔7). RF feature importance highlights alcohol, sulphates, and volatile acidity as key predictors, offering interpretable evidence for the dominant decision cues.

items.title: High-Resolution Astronomical Imaging: Resolving Close Binaries and Stellar Surfaces via Optical Coherence
items.abstract: Due to the diffraction limit of conventional telescopes, the angular resolution of single-aperture instruments in the visible band is typically restricted to ~0.02 arcseconds, which hampers the effective resolution and imaging of close binary systems and stellar surface features. To overcome this limitation, optical interferometry has emerged as a powerful technique for high-resolution astronomical imaging, grounded in optical coherence theory and the van Cittert–Zernike theorem. By employing key technologies such as telescope arrays, baseline synthesis, closure phase calibration, and u−v plane sampling, milli-arcsecond angular resolution can be achieved, enabling precise determination of orbital parameters in close binaries, as well as accurate measurements of stellar masses and radii, while allowing direct imaging of stellar magnetic activity features such as starspots and faculae. Observational approaches are generally divided into model-fitting and image-reconstruction methods, each with distinct advantages and limitations. Nevertheless, ground-based interferometry remains constrained by atmospheric turbulence, sparse u−v plane coverage, limited sensitivity, and high computational complexity. Looking ahead, future developments are expected to focus on space-based interferometers, large-scale interferometric arrays, and artificial intelligence-assisted image reconstruction. These advancements not only enrich the fundamental database of stellar physics but also provide high-precision observational support for studies of stellar evolution, binary dynamics, and exoplanetary systems.

items.title: Thermospheric response to solar EUV variability probed with orbital-energy decay from NinjaSat CubeSat GNSS telemetry
items.abstract: Solar extreme ultraviolet (EUV) radiation heats and expands the thermosphere, modulating atmospheric density at altitudes in low Earth orbit and thereby increasing satellite drag and accelerating orbital decay. Previous studies have relied on empirical solar proxies, such as the F10.7 cm radio flux and Two-Line Element (TLE)-derived orbit solutions, which lack sufficient spectral resolution and temporal cadence to resolve wavelength-dependent thermospheric responses, and on orbital-decay metrics—most commonly the satellite altitude itself—that are not conserved quantities along the orbit and have rarely been validated against independent-density measurements. Here, we combine spectrally resolved EUV irradiance from the GOES-18 Extreme Ultraviolet and X-ray Irradiance Sensors at seven wavelengths (25.6–140.5 nm) with high-cadence GNSS position and velocity data from NinjaSat, an X-ray-astronomy 6U CubeSat orbiting at approximately 500–530 km altitude, over an 8-month period (April–November 2024). We derive the orbital-decay signal from the $$J_2$$ -corrected specific mechanical energy computed directly from the GNSS position and speed telemetry—a conserved quantity whose within-orbit scatter is about 50 times smaller than that of an altitude-based (point-mass energy) decay metric and which, unlike TLE/SGP4-based approaches, requires no propagated reference orbit. This energy-based decay rate correlates with independent thermospheric-density retrievals from the Swarm and GRACE-FO missions with Spearman coefficients of 0.85–0.92 (daily means), and its systematic-error budget (radiation pressure, unmodeled gravitational perturbations) remains below the statistical uncertainty of the daily decay rate. Cross-correlation analysis shows that the decay rate is strongly related to EUV and far-ultraviolet (FUV) irradiance (Spearman coefficients up to $$\sim$$ 0.8), with a positive lag of order 1–3 days. Using a block-bootstrap procedure that accounts for the strong autocorrelation of both series, we find that the 95% confidence intervals of the estimated lag overlap across all seven wavelengths, extending from the 6-h search floor to approximately 100 h, while the central lag estimates lie at roughly 30–70 h depending on wavelength and analysis choice; a wavelength-dependent separation of the response times is not statistically resolved with the present dataset and remains a plausible but unconfirmed hypothesis pending independent constraints from physics-based thermosphere models. These results demonstrate that standard GNSS telemetry from a CubeSat, combined with a conserved orbital-energy metric and independent-mission validation, can quantitatively characterize the thermospheric drag response to solar EUV forcing, offering a scalable observational approach for space-weather monitoring and satellite drag modeling.

items.title: Evaluating Magnetic Reconnection Through the Nanoflare Heating Model: Evidence from Modern Solar Observations
items.abstract: The solar corona reaches temperatures exceeding one million Kelvin, far higher than the approximately 5,800 K temperature of the photosphere, giving rise to the long-standing coronal heating problem. This paper reviews modern observational evidence related to the nanoflare heating model and discusses the extent to which it supports magnetic reconnection as a mechanism for coronal heating. A qualitative literature review was conducted using three representative studies that provide complementary perspectives: theoretical predictions of nanoflare heating, observational evidence from solar active regions, and the thermal evolution of individual coronal loops. The studies were compared in terms of observed heating signatures, consistency with theoretical predictions, and their main limitations. The reviewed evidence shows several behaviors consistent with impulsive nanoflare heating, including temperature-dependent emission sequences, heating and cooling patterns in coronal loops, and signatures associated with small-scale episodic energy release. These characteristics are observed across different spatial scales and generally agree with predictions of nanoflare-based models. However, the evidence remains indirect because individual nanoflares and their associated magnetic reconnection events cannot yet be directly resolved by current instruments. In addition, observational uncertainties and differences between modeled and observed loop behavior limit the strength of the conclusions. Overall, modern solar observations support nanoflares as an important potential contributor to coronal heating, but they do not establish magnetic reconnection through nanoflares as the sole primary heating mechanism. Further improvements in observational resolution and theoretical modeling are required to better determine the role of nanoflares in coronal heating.

items.title: Inspiring the Next Generation of Students through Active Participation in Radio Astronomy Research via International Partnerships
items.abstract: The growing demand for specialists in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) across Europe highlights the need for innovative educational approaches capable of attracting and preparing the next generation of researchers. In this context, radio astronomy represents a particularly effective multidisciplinary platform, combining physics, astronomy, electronics, telecommunications, software development, signal processing, and data science within a single scientific domain. The Erasmus+ project Radio Astronomy Collaboration between European Universities: Developing Scientific and Technological Skills Through Astronomy (RACOBEU) was established to leverage these characteristics and create an international framework for engaging secondary-school and university students in authentic scientific research. RACOBEU brings together the Public University of Navarre, Spain, Ventspils University of Applied Sciences, Latvia and Adam Mickiewicz University, Poland, together with associated secondary schools in all three countries. The project integrates research, education, and international mobility through a combination of student projects, practical workshops, remote observing activities, scientific conferences, and collaborative research placements. Students participate in activities ranging from solar and radio astronomy observations to satellite tracking, radio signal analysis, software-defined radio applications, and astronomical data processing. An important role within the project is played by the research infrastructure of the Ventspils International Radio Astronomy Centre (VIRAC), including the RT-32 and RT-16 radio telescopes and the LOFAR-Latvia station. These facilities provide students with direct access to professional astronomical instrumentation and datasets, enabling participation in studies of solar activity, space weather, radio-frequency interference, astronomical signal processing, spectropolarimetric observations, and radio source investigations. Additional educational opportunities are provided through the remotely accessible Jocelyn Bell Burnell radio telescope at UPNA, allowing students to perform real radio astronomy observations through a web-based interface. During the project, students and staff participated in international conferences held in Latvia, Poland, and Spain, completed multiple collaborative research projects, developed educational resources in four languages, established a new university-level radio astronomy course, and produced nine bachelor’s theses linked to radio astronomy and related STEM fields. Several of these activities resulted in peer-reviewed scientific publications and the development of new instrumentation and software tools for radio astronomy applications. The RACOBEU experience demonstrates that active participation in real scientific research, supported by international partnerships and access to modern astronomical infrastructure, significantly strengthens student engagement with STEM disciplines while fostering technical skills, scientific communication, and cross-border collaboration. The project provides a sustainable model for integrating research infrastructures into education and for developing future generations of scientists and engineers in Europe. Keywords: Radio astronomy; STEM education; Research-based learning; Astronomy education; Science outreach; Remote observations; Radio telescopes.

items.title: Fairness Vs. Personalization: Towards Equity in Epistemic Utility
items.abstract: Personalized recommender systems are rapidly expanding in applications across the web, encompassing social media, online shopping, search engine results, and more. Personalization provides significant value in navigating the vast array of items available, as it can help to disambiguate search terms and generally provide more accurate recommendations. However, alongside this growth, there has been increased recognition of the potential for algorithmic systems to exhibit and perpetuate biases. In particular, personalized recommender systems may risk unfairness in recommendations, leading to biases in access to information and epistemic utility. In this work, we differentiate between idealized and realized notions of personalization in the extreme to motivate our fairness definition: an equity-based approach to epistemic utility. Our approach bypasses many issues with comparative notions of fairness and instead aims to guarantee all users baseline access to information. We discuss key trade-offs and challenges for operationalizing our definition and provide policy recommendations towards achieving fairness in personalized systems.

items.title: Imaging-derived coronary fractional flow reserve: advances in physics-based, machine learning, and physics-informed methods
items.abstract: Purpose of Review: Imaging-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR) is rapidly evolving beyond conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD)-based pipelines toward machine learning (ML), deep learning (DL), and physics-informed approaches that enable fast, wire-free, and scalable functional assessment of coronary artery stenosis. This review synthesizes recent advances in computed tomography (CT)- and angiography-based FFR measurement, with particular emphasis on emerging physics-informed neural networks and neural operators (PINNs and PINOs), as well as key considerations for their clinical translation. Recent Findings: ML/DL approaches have markedly improved automation and computational speed, enabling prediction of pressure and FFR from anatomical descriptors or angiographic contrast dynamics. However, their real-world performance and generalizability can remain variable and sensitive to domain shift, due to multi-center heterogeneity, interpretability challenges, and differences in acquisition protocols and image quality. Physics-informed learning introduces conservation structure and boundary-condition consistency into model training, improving generalizability and reducing dependence on dense supervision while maintaining rapid inference. Recent evaluation trends increasingly highlight deployment-oriented metrics, including calibration, uncertainty quantification, and quality-control gatekeeping, as essential for safe clinical use. Summary: The field is converging toward imaging-derived FFR methods that are faster, more automated, and more reliable. While ML/DL offers substantial efficiency gains, physics-informed frameworks such as PINNs and PINOs may provide a more robust balance between speed and physical consistency. Prospective multi-center validation and standardized evaluation will be critical to support broad and safe clinical adoption.

items.title: AI-Generated Deepfake Financial Scams: A Missing Liability Regime for Consumer Protection Frameworks
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) outputs, such as deepfakes, can be useful for creating realistic simulations in education, news reporting, and the arts. However, the emergence of malicious deepfake scams has raised concerns about the quality and reliability of the information provided to social media users. This article argues that a liability regime for deepfakes is currently missing from consumer protection frameworks. Regulatory interventions do not explicitly target GenAI software developers and online social media platforms. However, the implementation of appropriate risk management safeguards is necessary to prevent unlawful deepfake activities. We contend that a shared liability regime for deepfakes among the multiple actors involved could offer adequate protection for victims of online financial fraud and would effectively target the deepfake supply chain. This shared liability regime would be complemented by the UK Financial Conduct Authority’s consumer duty rule, which acts as a preventive monitoring and enforcement mechanism to avoid foreseeable harm to consumers of AI applications.

items.title: Bridging Ethics and Institutions: Embedding Care in Gender-Focused Technology and STEM Reform
items.abstract: This paper argues that ethical technology design cannot be meaningfully addressed without transforming the institutional gender regimes that shape the science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) ecosystem. Drawing on care ethics and institutional gender theory, it develops an integrated framework for examining both the normative assumptions embedded in technology and the organizational conditions under which it is produced. Through a narrative review of gender-focused technology design and a cross-case synthesis of empirical studies on care ethics in practice, the paper shows how gender stereotypes, role congruity expectations, and ideal-worker norms constrain participation, leadership, and the ethical content of design itself. It critiques dominant ethical paradigms, particularly utilitarian and deontological approaches, for marginalizing the embodied, relational, and contextual dimensions of excluded groups' lived experience. In response, the paper advances care ethics as a generative framework that must be institutionally embedded if it is to challenge technocratic neutrality and support more inclusive design and policy practices. Rather than presenting care ethics as a self-contained solution, the paper positions it as a critical lens for rethinking both technological design and institutional reform, thereby contributing to more just, accountable, and socially responsive technological futures.

items.title: A randomised controlled feasibility trial of FREED-Mobile, a smartphone-friendly decision-making tool, designed to facilitate help-seeking in young people with eating disorders
items.abstract: Background Early intervention increases the likelihood of eating disorder recovery but many young people delay help-seeking. We developed a smartphone-friendly, online decision-making tool to address this gap (FREED-Mobile (FREED-M)). Aims To conduct a randomised controlled feasibility trial of the FREED-M decision-making tool with 16- to 25-year-olds with a suspected eating disorder and no previous treatment for this. Method Participants were randomly allocated to FREED-M or an active control in a parallel group, two-arm trial. Outcomes were measured at weeks 0 (baseline), 4 (post-intervention) and 12 (follow-up). The primary feasibility outcome was attrition at follow-up. Other outcomes included motivational, clinical and economic measures. Results We over-recruited with 204 randomised participants (including 20 fraudulent participants). Main analyses were conducted with 184 genuine responders (FREED-M: n = 91, control: n = 93). At baseline, participants’ mean age was 21.0 (s.d. 2.0) years, 89% identified as female and 64% as White. Mean body mass index was 23.1 kg/m 2 (6.3). N = 83 participants had an anorexia nervosa-like disorder, 101 had another eating disorder or high eating disorder risk. Attrition at week 12 was n = 112 (61%). Of the n = 42 FREED-M participants who provided acceptability ratings, 79% liked the intervention and 66% found it useful. Between-group effect sizes for motivation and readiness to change were small to medium at 4 weeks ( d = 0.27 and d = 0.15, respectively) favouring FREED-M, but differences were not sustained at follow-up ( d = −0.02 and d = −0.12, respectively). Discussions Although the attrition rate was high, recruitment exceeded expectations. Acceptability of FREED-M was high among participants who provided acceptability ratings. Motivation/readiness to change and help-seeking are candidates for primary outcomes in a future randomised controlled trial.

items.title: Enhancing synchronous patterned motion tracking and latency reduction through avatar prediction and visualization
items.abstract: Enabling online virtual reality (VR) users to move naturally and contextually within their environment presents transformative possibilities for enhancing human motion prediction accuracy and fostering a deeper sense of connection in shared remote settings. Latency in motion tracking remains a significant challenge, as it directly impacts the user’s sense of presence and engagement in VR environments. This study investigates the integration of real-time human pose tracking and motion prediction techniques to reconstruct context-aware, skeleton-based motion sequences from historical data.The findings highlight that improved motion tracking and prediction significantly enhance immersion and social connectivity in VR, particularly in interactive scenarios such as online dancing. By leveraging historical motion sequences and machine learning models, this research develops methods to accurately render human motion in avatar or mesh formats, enabling seamless synchronization of movements with dynamic contexts, including music beats in paired dance scenarios. The integration of predictive modelling and advanced learning techniques offers a robust framework for creating realistic and engaging virtual interactions. This research contributes to advancing immersive user experiences in networked VR applications by providing a novel approach to tracking, reconstructing, and predicting human motions. The outcomes emphasize the potential of enhancing user connection, enjoyment, and realism in virtual environments, paving the way for enriched interactive applications in areas such as virtual performances, remote collaboration, and social VR experiences.

items.title: A framework for digital twin integration into project delivery: Building on collaborative procurement principles in the built environment
items.abstract: Digital Twin (DT) technology has emerged as a potential enabler of systemic reform in the built environment industry, promising improved project delivery and long-term value creation. Yet, within a sector characterised by fragmented delivery models and adversarial procurement practices, DT integration remains limited and poorly defined. Policy direction remains underdeveloped, and governance support has diminished following the closure of initiatives such as the Centre for Digital Built Britain (CDBB), leaving a gap in national-level coordination at a critical moment for mainstream adoption. Despite rising industry interest and visibility among providers, and as the industry heads towards a more digitised, integrated future, there is a risk that DT may follow the path of earlier innovations: widely promoted but ultimately constrained by structural inertia and the absence of coherent implementation strategies. Fundamental questions persist around the distinction between DT and other digital tools, as well as how DT supports net-zero goals, and when and how it should be implemented. This study addresses these gaps by developing a novel Digital Twin–Collaborative Procurement (DT—CP) framework structured across the Royal Institute of British Architects (RIBA) Plan of Work. The framework responds to the unique demands of DT implementation, introducing a preparatory Stage 0+ focused on organisational alignment, data governance, and long-term lifecycle planning. It also proposes a new classification model for DT to reflect stage-specific functionalities and support integration across the project timeline. The resulting framework is retrospectively applied to the Edinburgh Home Demonstrator (EHD) Programme to evaluate its practical relevance within public sector housing delivery, and provide an illustrative application of its stage by stage implementation. The findings demonstrate the interdependence between CP principles and the successful deployment of DT, revealing that DT adoption requires not only technical provisions but also, and especially, cultural and procedural alignment. The research establishes that DT value varies across project stages, and it is most effectively realised when embedded from the pre-design phase through structured interorganisational alignment. It further positions DT as a strategic enabler of net-zero objectives, contingent on the effective capture and use of data. This research contributes a practice-oriented model for DT implementation, with implications for governance and policy development, and encourages longer-term thinking across project delivery. Ultimately, it aims to demystify DT and bridge the gap between academic discourse and delivery, motivating broader adoption of DT as a catalyst for systemic change.

items.title: Future in mind: Systematic review of compassion-based interventions in higher education and feasibility study of Compassionate Mind Training with pre-registration Mental Health Student Nurses
items.abstract: Nurse education faces challenges in meeting student nurse recruitment and retention targets and addressing increasing psychological wellbeing problems for higher education (HE) students, in the context of a national nursing workforce crisis, including burnout risk. Compassion-based interventions (CBIs) are emerging as effective techniques for preventing and addressing psychological problems. This thesis firstly describes a systematic review with narrative synthesis, which identified recruitment and retention strategies, and participant experience data collected in CBIs trialled in HE. The review found (n=33) studies, with a total sample size of (n=4,897) HE students, with most studies (n=23) relying on course credit and / or remuneration to recruit and retain participants. None of the included studies described research focused on pre-registration student nurse wellbeing. The thesis then recounts the design and implementation of a novel mixed methods, single group feasibility study of a specific CBI, Compassionate Mind Training (CMT), for first-year pre-registration Mental Health student nurses. The study’s design, conduct and analysis followed the Medical Research Council’s guidance for developing complex interventions. Study aims addressed feasibility and acceptability uncertainties regarding intervention and study processes, and predetermined benchmarks for considering next steps were established. The study was conducted online during the COVID-19 pandemic. Recruitment of (n=38) participants and retention of (n=35) was achieved. Participants’ group mean ratings for CMT’s enjoyableness, usefulness, clarity, and their intention to practice CMT techniques remained high during the study, with qualitative feedback also indicating intervention acceptability. Response rates for pre and post-test psychological wellbeing measures used demonstrated their feasibility, with group mean scores for those measures moving in positive directions pre to post-test. Study limitations include its quasi-experimental nature, the potential influence of the observer effect, and unintentionally high participant burden. Nonetheless, on balance, a further, randomised pilot trial, comparing CMT with mindfulness, is recommended. This research would incorporate student nurse and nurse educator involvement in the planning stages, including considering rewards for participation, and delivering the interventions in-person rather than online.

items.title: Does a Flux-Defined Markov Blanket Screen Self-Replicating Gray--Scott Spots? A Computational Test of a Blanket Condition from the Free Energy Principle
items.abstract: Friston's free energy principle holds that a system separated from its environment by a Markov blanket---a boundary whose states statistically screen its interior from its exterior---can be treated as performing approximate Bayesian inference, and that such blankets arise wherever coupling is short-range. We test this blanket condition in a concrete nonlinear pattern-forming system: self-replicating spots in a reaction-diffusion model that persist, compete, and reproduce. Directed boundary exchange and timescale separation hold up reasonably well, with qualifications. A flux-defined blanket does not screen interior from exterior. Flux removes only part of the linear dependence, and a nonlinear test shows that conditioning on flux \emph{increases} the dependence, consistent with conditioning on a collider, since flux is a joint function of concentrations on both sides of the boundary. The dependence is concentrated within about one organism radius of the boundary. A band of the surrounding field that thick screens the interior from the exterior beyond it, as any short-range field would, which is not evidence of inference.

items.title: Cross-disorder Learning of Imaging-derived Joint Mophometric Markers in Alzheimer's and Parkinson's Diseases
items.abstract: As two most prevalent neurodegenerative diseases (NDDs), Alzheimer's disease (AD) and Parkinson's disease (PD) shared commonalities both in symptomology and pathophysiology. However, to what extent and in what way these two distinct disorders overlap remain underexplored. In this study, we propose an explicit, interpretable and spatially adaptive transfer learning framework to elucidate the morphometric biomarkers linked to AD and PD. We applied such high-dimensional machine learning model to two most popular open-source neuroimaging datasets, i.e., Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI). On the one hand, our cross-disorder classifier revealed neuro-anatomical alteration patterns well aligning with previous neuroimaging research findings and underscoring patients' clinical presentations. On the other hand, the spatially adaptive trained classifier using shared prior achieved statistically superior diagnostic performance compared to respective individual models, which further highlights the cross-disorder framework's efficacy on modeling limited-size datasets across disease domains.

items.title: Representing short-term movement to reveal animal identity and learning progress
items.abstract: How learning progresses over time and varies across individuals is a longstanding question in cognitive and behavioral science. However, a major challenge is identifying observable behavioral measures that faithfully capture learning progression. Existing approaches commonly rely on predefined behavioral features or task-level performance, while fine-scale posture and movement in freely behaving animals remain less explored. In this paper, we ask: can short-term movement trajectories reveal learning progress and individual identity? We introduce a self-supervised representation learning framework built on a simple hypothesis: behavioral characteristics associated with identity and learning remain relatively stable over nearby time intervals. Using temporal proximity as supervision, our framework learns compact representations directly from movement trajectories without manually defining behavioral states or kinematic features. Using behavior data from freely behaving rats, we show that the learned representations not only improve prediction of identity and learning-related readouts over existing methods, but also provide a tool for investigating broader scientific questions about when and how these signals appear in behavior. Specifically, trajectories as short as one second contain informative learning and identity signals. Egocentric pose dynamics are more predictive of identity, whereas allocentric motion is more predictive of learning-related variation, and both signals are strongest at decision junctions in the alternation cohort. We further use a representation-conditioned diffusion model to inspect movement patterns associated with identity and learning progress. Our findings establish short-term movement as an informative behavioral "fingerprint" for studying learning and individual differences. Our code is available at https://github.com/pizhn/TRAIL.

items.title: Ontic state recovery through prediction
items.abstract: We encounter a system through its responses, yet its state concerns how the system is. Predicting further responses promises knowledge beyond what is immediately observed. What that knowledge tells us about the system's state depends on what we mean by a state in the first place. We give this notion a model-relative meaning: a state is the complete response profile over a specified query universe, and configurations agreeing on every query are regarded as the same state. From this perspective, a learned state is understood through the distinctions between these profiles that it retains. Prediction concerns selected observations; recovery concerns the profile as a whole. We examine their relationship through query ambiguity, state-space geometry, and the choice of prediction targets. Synthetic systems with known response laws and neural recordings provide complementary settings for this investigation. The aim is to clarify how prediction can become a way of knowing a system, and what it would mean for a learned state to preserve the state being studied.

items.title: District Size Matters: How Seats Per District Shapes Proportionality Under STV
items.abstract: We study the impact of utilizing multimember districts and Single Transferable Vote (STV) as the winner selection method on partisan proportionality. We start with detailed case studies of the upper legislative houses of Illinois, New Hampshire, and New Mexico, building ensembles of redistricting maps with mostly 2-member, mostly 3-member, and mostly 4-member districts for each state. These ensembles are constructed using two methods: building from precincts, and merging currently existing single-member districts. We also compare two ballot generation models for each experiment: a modified Bradley-Terry model and a Plackett-Luce model. We find that our ensembles of multimember districts paired with STV have results which are centered closer to partisan proportionality than when single member districts are used. However, the choice of district size affects partisan outcomes enough that this choice could be exploited by a partisan mapmaker to advantage a particular party. The findings are consistent across all combinations of district construction and ballot generation models within a single state. We then expand our study to 41 different states, obtaining consistently similar proportionality results and allowing us to empirically evaluate the two ballot generation models, as implemented in VoteKit, at a national scale.

items.title: DeGroot Dynamics on Multiplex Networks with Directed and Acyclic Interlayer Connectivities
items.abstract: In models of opinion dynamics, researchers typically examine how an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced by the opinions of their neighbors in a network. However, people's opinions on a topic are also influenced by their opinions and their neighbors' opinions on related topics. In an election, for example, the opinions of a voter on a variety of issues inform their opinions of electoral candidates. To consider the influence between people's opinions on multiple distinct topics, we study a multiplex extension of the traditional DeGroot consensus model. In our multiplex DeGroot model, different network layers represent distinct topics and directed interlayer edges (which are not allowed to form cycles) encode relationships between distinct topics. In our model, an individual's opinion on one topic is influenced both by the opinions of their neighbors on that topic and by their own opinions on related topics. We prove under mild conditions that our multiplex DeGroot model converges to a limit state. We also prove that strong connectedness in ``source layers'' (which represent fundamental beliefs) eventually yields a consensus opinion in each layer. In particular, we show that consensus on source layers can lead to consensus on other layers even when those layers otherwise would be polarized. By numerically simulating our multiplex DeGroot model on a two-layer network, we examine the effects on opinion dynamics of (1) different network structures and (2) different types of initial opinion data.

items.title: Analytical Chemistry at the Planetary Frontier
items.abstract: Planetary science depends on chemical measurements made under conditions very different from those in a terrestrial laboratory. This review treats the analytical methods of planetary science as one connected chain, from orbital remote sensing through in-situ measurements by landers and rovers and sample collection and curation, to the micro-analysis of returned material on Earth. Orbital methods, including visible and near-infrared reflectance, thermal emission and gamma-ray and neutron spectroscopy, are discussed first. In-situ techniques are then reviewed, including laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy (LIBS), micro-focus X-ray fluorescence (XRF), deep-ultraviolet Raman and fluorescence spectroscopy, evolved gas analysis with gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) and miniaturized mass spectrometry. Contamination control and curation practices are described, followed by laboratory techniques such as secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS and NanoSIMS), atom probe tomography (APT), thermal ionization mass spectrometry (TIMS), synchrotron micro-XRF and X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy. Accuracy, calibration and reference materials are discussed as the link between in-situ and laboratory data, and the role of chemometrics and data fusion is examined. Flight and laboratory instruments are compared in terms of spatial resolution, detection limit, sample consumption and throughput. Active neutron-gamma spectroscopy planned for the Dragonfly mission to Titan is also discussed. This comparison shows that in-situ and laboratory techniques are complementary. In-situ instruments provide context and select samples, while laboratory techniques provide isotopic, molecular and speciation data that cannot yet be obtained in situ.

items.title: Ammonia-Hydrogen Phase Equilibria in Planetary Envelopes from First-Principles-Based Machine-Learning Molecular Dynamics
items.abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen are major constituents of planets within and beyond the solar system, yet how they interact in planetary envelopes is poorly known. We perform large-scale two-phase coexistence simulations of the ammonia-hydrogen system from 500 to 4000 K and 0.1 to 100 GPa, driven by machine-learning interatomic potentials trained on density functional theory calculations. From these we map the compositions of coexisting hydrogen-rich and ammonia-rich phases, and the critical curve that separates conditions of complete miscibility from those of phase separation. The critical temperature increases with pressure, from 500 K at 0.1 GPa to 2000 K near 30 GPa, and we find no phase separation at 3000 and 4000 K up to 100 GPa. The slope of the critical curve decreases substantially between 0.3 and 30 GPa, and the curve nearly flattens above about 30 GPa and 2000 K, where molecules begin to give way to atomic species. The coexistence curves are asymmetric with an ammonia-rich critical composition. For the expected envelope compositions, the phase boundary lies close to, and intersects, published thermal profiles of Uranus and Neptune, implying ammonia may be raining out in these planets today. In contrast, in warm sub-Neptunes such as TOI-270 d, ammonia and hydrogen are likely miscible in all proportions. Together with previous studies, our results suggest that silicates, water and ammonia separate from hydrogen in sequence as planets cool, with implications for their compositional, thermal and structural evolution.

items.title: Beyond static torques: Self-consistent migration and dynamical trapping of low-mass planets in dusty disks
items.abstract: The rapid inward migration of low-mass planets remains a primary theoretical challenge in planet formation. While recent studies show that the solid component of protoplanetary disks can exert strong positive torques to counteract the negative gas torques, traditional static fixed-orbit models fail to capture the fully coupled dynamics of a migrating planet. In this work, we present 2D high-resolution, two-fluid hydrodynamical simulations using a comoving reference frame to track the self-consistent orbital evolution of embedded planets across a comprehensive six-dimensional parameter space. By allowing the planet to dynamically respond to disk-exerted torques, we identify a wide diversity of migration regimes, involving inward/outward migration and oscillatory radial confinement. We also find that massive cores can overcome dust-induced barriers, experiencing dust-mediated runaway outward or inward migration. Conversely, in dust-rich environments continuous gas-dust momentum exchange combined with planet torques dynamically regenerates co-orbital dust asymmetries, creating robust dynamical attractors where super-Earths undergo stable, oscillatory confinement, effectively halting inward drift without requiring pre-existing pressure bumps or disk substructures. This self-induced trapping mechanism could be relevant in the outer disk, beyond the water-ice line in environments with a enhanced local dust-to-gas ratio, where icy pebbles are moderately coupled to the gas. In low-metallicity or highly diffusive disks, planets generally adopt monotonic inward decay, apart from cases with outward migration. Ultimately, the diversity of these self-consistent trajectories demonstrates that static torque approximations are insufficient. Evaluating fully coupled kinematic feedback is essential for accurately predicting planetary survival and the final architecture of planetary systems.

items.title: Small Collisions, Big Impact: The Sensitivity of Atmospheric Temperatures to Collision-Induced Absorption
items.abstract: Collision-induced absorption (CIA) data are relevant to determining atmospheric temperatures and, in turn, the habitability of a diverse set of planetary atmospheres. However, these data remain sparse across broad wavelength and temperature ranges. Nevertheless, multiple, sometimes disagreeing, sources of experimental and theoretical data can be available for the same CIA pair. In this paper, we assess the impact of these varying sources on atmospheric temperatures and the limitations that the available data coverage can introduce. In order to inform future measurements and calculations, we test additional cases with extrapolated wavelength and temperature ranges. We first introduce a measure of the importance of CIA opacities depending on pressure and temperature by calculating the Rosseland mean with and without each CIA pair's contribution. Secondly, we employ each CIA source in a radiative transfer model of idealised atmospheres which maximise the effect of the CIA pair of interest. Our findings highlight the uncertainties related to the current data. Temperature differences between CIA data sources range from $\sim$10\,K when sources overlap in wavelength and temperature coverage to >100\,K when spectral gaps or temperature limits differ. Spectral windows or narrow temperature coverage can also hinder the model's convergence of the temperature profile. This work aims to provide guidance on the selection of CIA opacity datasets for atmospheric modelling and to identify the wavelength and temperature regimes in which further laboratory measurements and theoretical calculations are most urgently needed. We publish all our findings in detail in the form of an accessible website.

items.title: Planets surviving common envelope evolution should be rare, massive, and orbit very close to their host star
items.abstract: The discovery of exoplanets around white dwarfs uniquely informs our understanding of planetary survival through stellar evolution. Common Envelope (CE) evolution is one of the proposed mechanisms that could shape the orbital architecture of these planets around stellar remnants. In this work, we predict the occurrence rate and orbital separation/planet mass distributions for planets that could form around white dwarfs through CE evolution. We simulate populations of giant-planet systems, sampling initial conditions from observed mass and semi-major axis distributions for main sequence stars. We evolve the host star from main sequence to white dwarf to assess which planetary configurations could survive, and we predict the resulting post-CE planet population. Our results suggest that such planets should be rare, massive, and have very close orbital separations. We find that most of the surviving planets have masses of $>10\,M_{\rm{Jup}}$ and orbital separations $ 2a_{disrupt}$. The properties of CE survivors from our simulations contrast with the known closely-orbiting planet WD 1856+534 b, suggesting a different mechanism may be responsible for its formation.

items.title: The science case for an in-situ measurement platform in the Venus clouds
items.abstract: The next step for Venus exploration after the remote sensing missions of the early 2030s will be in-situ aerial platforms, the Venus equivalent of rovers for Mars. Sophisticated Venus balloon technology is already under development and presents an opportunity for the United Kingdom to act as a bilateral partner in missions exploring key questions about the volcanic and geological history of Venus, the potential habitability of the Venus clouds, and Venus as an analogue for exoplanets. White paper written for the UKSA Space Frontiers 2035 programme.

items.title: Constrained modularity maximization in complex networks via branch-and-price
items.abstract: Modularity maximization is widely used to identify community structure in complex networks. In many applications, however, community detection must also incorporate prior knowledge and domain-specific requirements beyond network topology. We study constrained modularity maximization with restrictions on the number of communities, must-link and cannot-link relations, and general resource constraints. While fast heuristics can provide high-quality solutions, they generally lack optimality guarantees, whereas exact mathematical-programming approaches can become computationally demanding as the network size and constraint complexity increase. We develop a unified optimization framework offering complementary heuristic and exact solution methods. These include a constrained Louvain heuristic for feasible solution generation, a column-generation heuristic with graph-partitioning-based pricing, and exact branch-and-price algorithms using mixed-integer linear programming and sparse mixed-integer quadratic programming formulations for the pricing subproblem. We develop a cutting-plane procedure providing independent upper bounds to assess solution quality when exact optimization cannot be completed. Experiments on 11 unconstrained networks with up to 1,005 nodes and 30 constrained instances with up to 379 nodes demonstrate the complementary roles of these methods. The column-generation heuristic rapidly improves the constrained Louvain solutions across the tested constraint classes, while branch-and-price using the sparse quadratic formulation solves 29 of the 30 constrained instances to optimality within a one-hour time limit. This formulation becomes particularly effective on larger, sparse, undirected networks by substantially reducing the size of the exact pricing model. Overall, the framework guides method selection to balance computational time, solution quality, and optimality guarantees.

items.title: A Geometric Principle for Path Selection in Directed Acyclic Graphs
items.abstract: There are many types of path between nodes of a Directed acyclic graph (DAG), including the shortest and longest paths. Here, we ask whether the choice of path used in any analysis reflects the geometry of the latent space in which the DAG is embedded. To do this we define L_p-cube spacetimes, a family of continuous ordered spaces in which a single parameter p determines whether the ordered distance satisfies the ordered triangle identity when p>1, or the reverse ordered triangle identity when 0 1, where the ordered triangle identity holds, the shortest paths provide the closest approximation to the continuum ordered geodesic while for 0<p<1 and p<0, where the reverse ordered triangle identity holds, this role is instead taken by the longest weighted path. We also test the robustness of this relationship in a geometric citation model in which the random geometric DAG is supplemented by a preferential-attachment-type mechanism allowing connections beyond the strict geometric cut-off. The same broad correspondence between latent geometry and ordered geodesic path type is recovered. Our results show that the preference for shortest or longest paths in a DAG is closely connected to the geometry assumed for its latent space, and suggest that path structure can provide information about latent geometry, even when that geometry is not directly observed.

items.title: Early neurocognitive outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation.
items.abstract: Objective Characterization of early neuropsychological outcomes following SEEG with radiofrequency thermocoagulation (RFTHC) is essential to guide patient expectations around return to work, study, and caregiving. The current study aimed to describe the early neurocognitive sequelae of SEEG. Methods Consecutive patients undergoing SEEG were prospectively recruited from two tertiary epilepsy centers in Melbourne, Australia. Patients were administered the Repeatable Battery for the Assessment of Neuropsychological Status (RBANS) via telehealth before and 3 weeks after SEEG (M = 19.69 days, SD = 4.41). Given the telehealth platform, the coding subtest was substituted for the Symbol Digit Modalities Test, and a modified score of global cognitive function was calculated. To evaluate group changes, paired sample t-tests were performed. Reliable change indices were computed to explore individual-level changes. Pearson's correlation coefficients evaluated relationships between change in global cognitive function and SEEG admission variables. SEEG patients were invited to complete a semi-structured interview canvassing the recovery following SEEG. Results Twenty-eight patients completed the neuropsychological examination (M = 37.89 years, SD = 9.72, range = 17-56 years, 54% female). All patients underwent RFTHC with a mean of 11.43 (SD = 6.87, range = 2-28) coagulation sites. At a whole group level, 3-weeks post SEEG there was no evidence for global nor domain-specific cognitive change. Reliable change indices with 90% confidence revealed only 4% (1/28) declined on at least two measures and 10% (3/28) showed psychometric improvement. Pearson's correlational coefficients showed no evidence for association between change in global cognitive function with SEEG factors including admission length, number of spontaneous or stimulated seizures, number of electrodes, or number of RFTHC sites. Subjective reports of language change tended to be accompanied by a decline on the RBANS language index that did not meet reliable change criteria. Most patients reported returning to work around 4 weeks post SEEG. Significance By 3 weeks, gross cognitive functioning tends to be in keeping with pre-SEEG performances for most patients. These findings have direct clinical implications for SEEG neuropsychological counseling. Plain language statement SEEG is increasingly used to guide epilepsy surgery. Despite this, little is known about the cognitive recovery in the weeks following the procedure. We found that for most patients, broad cognitive functioning 3 weeks after SEEG with coagulation was consistent with function before SEEG, with only a small minority showing significant changes. Some people who reported language difficulties also showed a decline on language testing, although this was often small. Of those patients working before SEEG, most returned to work by 4 weeks. These results provide important evidence to guide patient counseling, recovery planning, and management after SEEG.

items.title: Ipsilateral Versus Contralateral Femoral Access for Inferior Epigastric Artery Embolization: Impact of Patient Age on Procedural Efficiency.
items.abstract: Purpose Abdominal wall hematomas (AWHs) are relatively uncommon causes of acute abdominal pain but may represent potentially life-threatening vascular emergencies, particularly in elderly patients receiving anticoagulant therapy or in the setting of significant hemorrhage. Transcatheter arterial embolization of the inferior epigastric artery is the recommended first-line therapy. The contralateral femoral approach may be technically demanding in elderly patients with iliac tortuosity, calcifications, or diffuse atherosclerosis. This bicentric retrospective study compared ipsilateral versus contralateral femoral access for inferior epigastric artery embolization, evaluating procedural efficiency, radiation exposure, and clinical outcomes. Material and methods A bicentric retrospective study included 48 patients treated in emergency settings for epigastric artery bleeding between June 2022 and June 2025. Patients were divided into ipsilateral (n = 23) or contralateral (n = 25) femoral access groups, with further stratification by age ( Results Technical success was 100% in both groups, whereas clinical success was comparable between the contralateral and ipsilateral groups (96.00% vs. 95.65%, respectively). In patients ≥ 60 years, ipsilateral access significantly reduced procedure time (27.90 ± 6.40 vs. 33.30 ± 8.30 min, p = 0.046) and radiation dose (254.00 [IQR 219.00-272.00] vs. 283.50 [IQR 248.80-310.80] mGy, p = 0.023). No major complications or significant between-group differences in rebleeding or survival were observed. In exploratory multivariable analysis, ipsilateral access was associated with lower Air Kerma (β = -56.43 mGy; 95% CI, -91.91 to -20.95; p = 0.002), whereas the adjusted estimate for procedure duration was less precise and did not reach statistical significance. Conclusions Both femoral access routes are safe and effective. In patients aged ≥ 60 years, ipsilateral access was associated with shorter procedure duration and lower radiation exposure in unadjusted analyses. Exploratory adjusted analyses suggested an association between ipsilateral access and lower radiation exposure, whereas the adjusted association with procedure duration was not statistically significant. These findings require confirmation in larger prospective cohorts.

items.title: Symptom-related damage patterns in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis.
items.abstract: Objective This study was undertaken to elucidate the neuroanatomical and network substrates underlying diverse seizure symptoms in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy with hippocampal sclerosis (mTLE-HS) by applying multivariate support vector regression (SVR) to individualized structural symptom mapping and atrophy network mapping (ANM). Methods We retrospectively enrolled 216 patients with mTLE-HS and 460 healthy controls. Six non-mutually exclusive seizure symptoms were assessed. We performed left-right flipping of all images of right-sided mTLE-HS patients along the midline before processing the data. Individual atrophy gray matter maps were derived using normative modeling. Structural symptom mapping was performed using multivariate SVR lesion-symptom mapping. For each patient, indirect ANM maps were generated using a normative functional connectome and direct ANM maps using the patient's own resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging. Correspondence between the two ANM approaches was assessed using individual-level whole-brain spatial correlations of unthresholded maps and group-level Dice coefficients of thresholded maps. Results Individual structural atrophy patterns were spatially heterogeneous, whereas different seizure manifestations were associated with partially distinct structural patterns and more spatially convergent network-level associations. Focal to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures were associated with thalamic network involvement, gestural/limb automatisms with anterior cingulate-related networks, ictal vocalization symptoms with perisylvian language networks, dysmnesia with hippocampal-posteromedial networks, emotional phenomena with prefrontal-temporal networks, and autonomic phenomena with medial prefrontal and limbic networks. Furthermore, limited spatial correspondence was observed between the results of the direct and indirect atrophy network analyses, suggesting the indirect and direct ANM can be regarded as nonequivalent but potentially complementary approaches. Significance In mTLE-HS, heterogeneous seizure manifestations are associated with distinct patterns of atrophy and distributed functional network involvement. ANM provides a complementary framework for characterizing symptom-related network patterns, and differences between indirect/normative and direct/patient-specific connectome analyses may provide complementary information.

items.title: Automated Magnetic Resonance Volumetry to Measure Multiple System Atrophy Disease Progression in Clinical Trials.
items.abstract: Background Recent studies have reported longitudinal brain atrophy in multiple system atrophy (MSA) in relatively small patient cohorts. Objective To compare longitudinal regional brain volume and clinical changes as endpoint measures for MSA clinical trials. Methods MSA patients with 1-year longitudinal brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were selected from the placebo arm of the M-STAR Study (NCT03952806) and stratified into MSA-cerebellar (MSA-C) and MSA-parkinsonism (MSA-P) subtypes. A multisite healthy control (HC) cohort from international datasets was included for comparison. Baseline and longitudinal atrophy were assessed through automated MRI volumetry. Standardized longitudinal effect size values with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) and sample sizes required to detect treatment effect were estimated for 42 individual regional brain volumes, four combined volumetric indexes, nine clinical scales, and serum neurofilament light chain. Results The final study cohort included 129 MSA patients (76 MSA-C, 53 MSA-P) and 184 HC. The most atrophic structures at baseline were infratentorial regions in MSA-C and putamen in MSA-P. In both subtypes, infratentorial structures showed the largest longitudinal volume loss compared with HC. The annualized change of a cerebellum-pons-putamen volumetric index was the most powerful progression biomarker in MSA patients (effect size: -1.81 [95% CI: -2.14, -1.55]) and in both subtypes (MSA-C: -2.04 [95% CI: -2.58, -1.68], MSA-P: -1.55 [95% CI: -2.08, -1.22]), requiring the lowest sample size per arm (MSA, N = 55 to detect 30% treatment effect), and outperforming clinical measures (-59.6% patients required per arm). Conclusion These findings support longitudinal MRI-derived regional atrophy rates as sensitive imaging endpoints to assess treatment efficacy in MSA clinical trials. © 2026 The Author(s). items.title: Orbitofrontal-ventral striatal coupling: A model of the neurobehavioral architecture of craving in substance use disorders.
items.abstract: Neuroimaging has identified cue-elicited activity in ventral striatum and orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) as a reliable signature of craving, yet activation magnitude in either region is an inconsistent predictor of clinical outcome. This theoretical review develops a model on which the clinically consequential variable is not activation but effective coupling: the cue-evoked gain-the factor by which an input is amplified-with which OFC valuation signals modulate ventral striatal action-selection activity. I formalize this gain as valuation-policy coupling (λ), which governs the probability that a drug-related appraisal recruits approach and consumption policies; it is a latent construct indexed by effective OFC-accumbens connectivity, approach bias under load, and pharmacological challenge. Two moderators-meta-awareness and elaborative versus nonelaborative engagement-determine whether the urge is re-entered or exited, and jointly specify a neurocognitive space in which craving occupies a high-λ, high-meta-awareness, elaborative vertex. The framework predicts an awareness-amplification effect-noticing an urge intensifies it under high λ and weakens it under low λ-specifies when mindfulness-based relapse prevention should attenuate craving and when it should not, and yields a discriminative prediction: λ-reducing interventions should reduce cue-modulated OFC-ventral-striatum coupling while leaving regional activation comparatively preserved. λ is a parameter of craving rather than of relapse-which also requires cognitive-control parameters-and a candidate transdiagnostic mechanism. Claims are labeled by evidential status; the λ-meta-awareness interaction is the model's principal hypothesis, and failure conditions are stated explicitly.

items.title: Decision dynamics of negative bias in subclinical depression during ambiguous facial emotion perception.
items.abstract: Individuals with depressive tendencies may categorize ambiguous facial expressions toward negative rather than happy endpoints, but the associated decision-process components remained unclear. The study examined whether the categorization shift was associated with differences in perceptual criterion, discrimination sensitivity, response dynamics, or diffusion-model parameters. Fifty-nine participants, comprising a depressive tendency group and a comparison group, categorized morphed Sad-Happy and Angry-Happy expressions presented in a 750-ms face/mask sequence or a 1500-ms face/no-mask sequence. Psychometric functions, area-under-the-curve (AUC) analyses, quadratic mixed-effects models of response time, and a hierarchical drift-diffusion model were applied. Across conditions, the depressive tendency group showed lower points of subjective equality than the comparison group, indicating a relative shift in the categorization boundary toward the negative versus happy endpoint, without a corresponding group difference in discrimination sensitivity. AUC analyses similarly indicated higher negative-response probabilities in the depressive tendency group, particularly within the low-negativity portion of the continuum. Condition-specific patterns were observed, but direct tests did not support a larger Sad-Happy group difference in the 1500-ms than in the 750-ms presentation sequence. In the focal Sad-Happy 1500-ms face/no-mask sequence, the selected drift-diffusion model indicated a group-related drift-criterion shift toward the Sad boundary and modestly longer non-decision time in the depressive tendency group, whereas starting-point bias and boundary separation did not differ between groups. These findings are consistent with a relative categorization shift toward negative versus Happy facial-expression endpoints among participants with depressive tendencies. The diffusion-model results provided a model-dependent account of the focal choice-response-time pattern under the present presentation-sequence structure.

items.title: Spatiotemporal remodeling in habenula marks the onset of depression-related phenotypes.
items.abstract: Chronic stress has lasting adverse consequences that can lead, over time, to depression, yet the optimal timeframe for effective therapies remains unclear. The lateral habenula (LHb) has been implicated in stress-related behavioral repercussions, but the precise timing of its contribution is not understood. Here, using spatial transcriptomics, we generated a spatially resolved molecular atlas of the LHb of male mice, revealing a topographically organized and temporally defined remodeling of gene expression after chronic stress. Longitudinal in vivo two-photon calcium imaging of individual LHb neurons revealed progressively heightened excitatory responses to aversive stimuli. These neuronal adaptations mirrored both the progression of transcriptional changes and the emergence of depression-related behavioral phenotypes and were reversed by the antidepressant ketamine. Moreover, chemogenetically limiting LHb neuronal activity or administering ketamine at the onset of these changes exerted antidepressant effects. These findings link spatiotemporal signatures of LHb neuronal ensembles and genetic landscape with the onset of stress-induced depression-related states.

items.title: An amygdala-mediated simulation-to-decision cascade aligns interbrain dynamics to solve social dilemmas.
items.abstract: Mutual cooperation (MC) requires independent decision-makers to coordinate under uncertainty about each other's intentions. Using simultaneous intracranial electroencephalography from epilepsy-patient dyads playing a real-time iterated prisoner's dilemma, we identified neurocognitive mechanisms that enable interacting brains to align during mutual cooperation. Amygdala interbrain representational alignment (IBRA), similarity in fine-grained neural spectral patterns across partners, emerged selectively during MC and predicted trial-by-trial outcomes. Early θ-suppression-characterized IBRA reflected rapid, history-sensitive alignment, whereas later IBRA, characterized by low-frequency suppression and γ increases, supported coordinated commitment and action. Furthermore, mutual cooperation relied on an amygdala-mediated, simulation-to-decision cascade, operationalized here as a model-based prospective estimate of partner cooperation that guided self-choice. Amygdala low-frequency suppression tracked this prospective estimate of partner cooperation and θ-γ coupling linked this partner estimate to self-decision processes. Conditional cooperators strategically relied on partner tracking, whereas unconditional cooperators leveraged dispositional tolerance of uncertainty to transition into anticipatory neural alignment. These findings reveal the neural interdependency underpinning MC, redefining cooperation not as isolated decision-making but as a dynamic, interbrain, cognitive alignment.

items.title: Multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM): a reconfigurable platform for high-resolution light-sheet fluorescence microscopy.
items.abstract: Light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) enables gentle, rapid and efficient volumetric imaging of biological specimens. Despite its potential, LSFM has fragmented into multiple variants, each narrowly optimized for specific samples or imaging regimes, limiting its broad applicability. Here we introduce the multi-immersion oblique plane microscope (miOPM), an adaptable LSFM platform for high-resolution imaging ranging from subcellular dynamics to whole organisms and cleared tissues. miOPM supports seamless interchangeability of oil, water and air objectives and maintains diffraction-limited performance across a refractive index range of 1.33 to 1.51. It is compatible with standard sample mounting, current clearing protocols and high-throughput 3D imaging. We leverage miOPM to image diverse biological specimens at multiple spatial scales. By expanding the adaptability and ease of use of LSFM, miOPM is poised to democratize advanced 3D imaging.
