items.title: Trait judgements of faces using a task without word labels.
items.abstract: People attribute psychological traits to faces. Previous research has typically elicited these judgements using specific words provided in advance by the experimenter (for example, ratings on competence or trustworthiness), raising questions about completeness (these tasks use a limited set of words) and generalizability (for example, across languages). Here we asked over 3,000 participants to spatially arrange unfamiliar faces based on perceived trait similarity, without providing any word labels. Using predominantly White faces, experiment 1 yielded five dimensions that we interpreted as approachability, gender-specific warmth, competence, morality and youthfulness. Using White, Black and Asian faces, experiment 2 also produced five dimensions, which showed prominent effects of stereotypes associated with race. Comparisons with four other studies that used word labels argue that approachability or warmth emerges as a universal evaluative factor that integrates multiple trait facets (such as trustworthiness, warmth and competence) into a single holistic dimension and that race and gender stereotypes emerge depending on the set of face stimuli used.

items.title: Predicting trail-making test performance using 7-Tesla structural cerebral MRI.
items.abstract: Psychopharmaceutical therapy has seen a lack of improvement in efficacy, highlighting the need for a more individualized treatment approach that optimally leverages pharmaceutical effects. To achieve this, it is necessary to identify factors that can predict psychological attributes and treatment outcomes. We hypothesize that brain morphology may serve as a predictor of performance in psychological tests. A 7-Tesla-MRI system was used to measure 74 transdiagnostic patients and 41 healthy controls. Values for grey matter volume (GMV), cortical thickness and gyrification based on the Schaefer 100 Atlas for parcellation were determined. Using this morphological data, performance in a Trail-Making Test (TMT) - A and B was predicted with the help of a deep learning model. A SHAP analysis was conducted to identify the key variables important for the model. The accuracy in predicting TMT performance was very good at 0.795. The most decisive feature influencing predictions was gyrification. Areas indicating inter-group differences were focused in the frontal cortex, as well as in temporal and parietal regions. Morphological characteristics can predict test performance with high accuracy. These results support the implementation of a transdiagnostic approach in clinical practice to better address the underlying pathophysiology. Symptom prediction based on neuroimaging data appears to be an achievable goal.

items.title: Brain-derived tau in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid after surgery: a prospective cohort substudy.
items.abstract: Background Postoperative increases in plasma total tau (t-tau) protein have raised concerns that surgery can cause CNS injury. Brain-derived tau (BD-tau) is a novel biomarker that quantifies CNS-derived tau. We assessed BD-tau concentrations in plasma and CSF after surgery to investigate neuronal injury and mechanisms driving increases in plasma t-tau. Methods This was a substudy of a previous prospective cohort study enrolling adult patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty. We measured plasma and CSF BD-tau and t-tau before neuraxial anaesthesia (baseline) and at 4, 8, 24, 32, and 48 h after surgery and assessed cognitive performance at baseline and 3 months. Biomarker concentrations are reported as median (IQR) percentage change from baseline. Results Plasma BD-tau peaked at 4 h with a 254% increase (137-382%, P Conclusions Early postoperative increases in plasma t-tau are consistent with a CNS origin but not concomitant neuronal injury. Instead, the early plasma BD-tau increase and the inverse association between CSF and plasma BD-tau could indicate a redistribution of tau from the CNS to plasma.

items.title: Wide dynamic range of contrast-encoding in neural responses in macaque V1.
items.abstract: The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in the early visual system has been investigated at both single-neuron and population levels in animals using oriented stimuli such as gratings and Gabor patches. However, contrast-encoding of unoriented stimuli such as Gaussians has been less explored, even though such stimuli can evoke a large population response. In studies that employ Gaussians, contrast response functions (CRFs) of neurons and neural populations in primary visual cortex are typically characterized across a limited range of Weber contrasts up to 100%, which may not adequately reflect the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Indeed, our preliminary analysis shows that locations with center-surround contrasts far exceeding the level comparable to a Gaussian stimulus of 100% Weber contrast are ubiquitous in natural scenes. Thus, our current understanding of contrast encoding remains incomplete in the context of natural environments. Here, we measured spiking activities of individual neurons using electrophysiology and population responses using widefield calcium imaging in V1 of fixating male macaques ( Macaca mulatta ) while Gaussian stimuli were presented over a wide range of Weber contrasts, up to 900%. Both the average spiking response and the average population response continued to increase robustly above 100% Weber contrast. Only a small minority of neurons saturated below 100% Weber contrast. These results demonstrate that the dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 is broader than previously assumed and aligns more closely with the statistics of contrast in natural scenes. Significance Statement The dynamic range of contrast-encoding in V1 has typically been characterized using only a limited range of contrasts, often excluding the high contrasts commonly found in natural scenes. We measured contrast response functions of individual neurons and neural populations in V1 across a much wider range of contrasts. We found that the responses of the majority of neurons, as well as the overall population, increased robustly up to extremely high contrasts. These findings suggest that the dynamic range of contrast encoding in V1 extends well beyond the commonly tested range.

items.title: Fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic constraints of movement patterns.
items.abstract: In real-world motor tasks, body movements unfold in a high-dimensional space, whereas task errors are defined in a lower-dimensional space. How such low-dimensional errors propagate across redundant motor degrees of freedom to generate rapid corrective responses remains poorly understood. To address this question, we developed a redundant bimanual task in which human participants (males and females) manipulated a virtual stick with both hands to move its tip to a visual target. By shifting the tip position (task-relevant perturbation) or rotating the stick with the tip position fixed (task-irrelevant perturbation), we separated task-space errors from redundant-dimension errors. Participants rapidly corrected both types of perturbations using highly stereotyped movement patterns. Corrections to task-relevant errors consistently involved coordinated changes across redundant dimensions, and even perturbations that did not affect task success elicited systematic corrective responses. Together, these results demonstrate that fast corrective responses in redundant motor control are shaped by intrinsic coordination constraints that govern how visual errors propagate through the motor system. Significance Statement The motor system can correct a movement error within 200 ms of its occurrence. However, the compensatory movement pattern is not uniquely determined because of the many degrees of freedom in the body. How does the motor system rapidly select and execute an appropriate corrective pattern? Our bimanual stick-tip reaching task, in which participants controlled a cursor located at the tip of a virtual stick, allowed us to dissociate tip-displacing errors from stick-rotation errors. Tip displacements triggered fast corrections, but surprisingly, rotation-only perturbations also evoked rapid responses and biased the tip along its usual coordination between tip motion and stick tilt. Our findings show that fast corrections are constrained by intrinsic coordination patterns, limiting the ability to ignore goal-irrelevant perturbations.

items.title: Insulin regulates activity-dependent mitochondrial depolarization and calcium dynamics in dentate granule cells.
items.abstract: Systemic insulin resistance is associated with reduced hippocampal energy metabolism and cognitive impairment both in humans and animal models. However, whether insulin rapidly regulates neuronal metabolic stability during activity remains unclear. Here, we examined insulin signaling and queried the corresponding mitochondrial responses in dentate granule cells (DGCs) of adult female mice. This layer of excitatory neurons within the hippocampus plays an essential role in learning and memory. Insulin robustly increased Akt phosphorylation in dentate gyrus tissue when insulin degradation was inhibited, and this response was attenuated by genetic deletion of the insulin receptor in DGCs, consistent with cell-autonomous signaling. We found that insulin did not alter mitochondrial membrane potential at rest, but significantly limited activity-evoked mitochondrial depolarization induced by neuronal stimulation. However, this change had no measurable impact on cytosolic ATP availability and was instead associated with Ca 2+ dynamics. Removing Ca 2+ ions from the extracellular solution, or disrupting mitochondrial Ca 2+ uptake, prevented insulin modulation of the mitochondrial membrane potential. Furthermore, insulin limited cytosolic Ca 2+ accumulation through an insulin receptor-dependent mechanism that persisted despite Akt inhibition. Insulin also accelerated the clearance of mitochondrial Ca 2+ transients in active neurons, which occurred without changes in either neuronal excitability or pyruvate dehydrogenase phosphorylation. Together, these findings identify endogenous insulin degradation as a key regulator of hippocampal insulin signaling, and reveal a previously unrecognized interaction between insulin and Ca 2+ signaling in stimulated DGCs. This work also establishes a direct link between central insulin signaling and the maintenance of mitochondrial electrochemical homeostasis in the adult brain. Significance Statement Insulin signaling is known to influence synaptic plasticity, yet its direct effects on neuronal metabolism remain poorly defined. Here, we show that endogenous insulin degradation limits insulin signaling in adult hippocampal tissue. This finding suggests that inhibitors of the insulin degrading enzyme may hold the potential to improve the efficacy of insulin-based interventions aimed at improving learning and memory. Acute insulin signaling does not modify neuronal excitability, or cytosolic ATP availability. Instead, it stabilizes mitochondrial membrane potential and reduces calcium accumulation in active dentate granule cells. By identifying an insulin-dependent mechanism that regulates the electrochemical homeostasis of mitochondria in active neurons, this work provides insight into how brain insulin resistance may contribute to cognitive dysfunction in aging and neurometabolic disorders.

items.title: Prefrontal ensembles represent freezing of conspecifics.
items.abstract: Social buffering is a process in which the presence of other members of the same species (conspecifics) decreases stress reactions during threat exposure. In parallel, prior reports showed that groups of individuals display synchronous actions in non-threatening situations. However, it is unknown if individuals also synchronize actions when facing threats. Prior studies showed social buffering of freezing in pairs of subjects. We now expand these findings and show social buffering of freezing during exposure to a predator and a shock grid in mice of both sexes in a larger group of four conspecifics. Furthermore, mice also displayed synchronized freezing. The presence of freezing synchrony suggests the existence of a neural representation of conspecific freezing. We reasoned that this encoding might be in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC), as this region has been implicated in social behaviors and freezing. Strikingly, mPFC neural activity represented the average level of freezing across conspecifics. MPFC ensembles displayed differential encoding of self and conspecific freezing, and during predator exposure the mPFC encoded the number of conspecifics freezing and conspecific freezing bout duration. These data show, for the first time, neural representation of conspecific freezing, and suggest that the mPFC may coordinate behavioral responses to threat across conspecifics. Significance Statement Social animals display attenuated threat-elicited responses when encountering threats as a group. However, it is unknown how freezing signals from conspecifics are encoded by the brain when facing threats, as prior work has been limited to studies of pairs, or assays without social interactions. We identify a neural population in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) that represents conspecific freezing during grouped threat exposure, and these cells dynamically represent the duration of other animals' freezing bouts. Strikingly, the activity of these ensembles also represents the number of conspecifics freezing. These findings uncover a previously unknown function of the mPFC to encode conspecific freezing.

items.title: Specific regulation of transsynaptic nanoalignment and postsynaptic assembly by a novel NCAM family synaptic adhesion molecule.
items.abstract: Synapse formation underlies the organization of neurons into functional circuits and requires precise alignment and coordinated maturation of pre- and postsynaptic compartments. Many synaptogenic adhesion molecules have been identified that drive target recognition and sustained adhesion between appropriate synaptic partners. Yet the degree to which individual molecules serve distinct functions in synapse formation and maturation remains poorly understood. In particular, how exquisite nanoalignment of pre- and postsynaptic specializations flows from micron-scale adhesive interactions between synaptic partners remains a key unanswered question. Here we shed new light on this question by establishing a specialized set of synaptic functions for Epithelial limiter of Fasciclin II function (Elff ), an NCAM family member with previously unknown roles in the nervous system. Our structural and functional studies at the glutamatergic Drosophila NMJ of both sexes indicate that Elff is required for postsynaptic function and maturation as well as transsynaptic alignment; however, it is not required for presynaptic function, bouton formation, or developmental expansion of the NMJ. NMJs in elff null mutants display reduced glutamate receptor clusters beginning at the embryonic stage when NMJ synapses first form. Using super-resolution STED microscopy, we demonstrate that these poorly defined postsynaptic specializations are frequently out of register with presynaptic release sites. Surprisingly, the striking defects in elff nulls occur in the context of both normal active zone number and developmental expansion of the NMJ. These findings suggest an unexpected degree of specialization among transsynaptic adhesion complexes and demonstrate that Elff-mediated signaling is critical for transsynaptic nanoarchitecture of glutamatergic synapses. Significance Statement This work reveals a surprisingly selective role for a novel NCAM family member called Elff in coordinating postsynaptic assembly and precise transsynaptic nanoalignment without altering NMJ formation, expansion or presynaptic active zone number. This separation of phenotypes is new and provides crucial insight into molecular specialization of adhesion complexes during synaptogenesis. Because NCAM family member dysfunction linked to multiple neurological disorders, most notably schizophrenia, illuminating the molecular mechanisms by which they orchestrate synaptic organization and function is an important goal.

items.title: A pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts hippocampal synapse maturation and homeostasis.
items.abstract: AMPA receptors (AMPARs) mediate fast excitatory synaptic transmission and are critical for activity-dependent synapse maturation and circuit development. De novo missense mutations in AMPAR subunits are linked to neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs), yet how these variants disrupt neuronal function remains unclear. Here, we examine a recurrent pathogenic mutation in the GluA1 subunit (GRIA1 p.A636T) that alters AMPAR function and is associated with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and intellectual disability (ID). Using GluA1 A636T knock-in mice of either sex, we identify impairments in hippocampal-dependent learning and working memory. Quantitative proteomics combined with bulk RNA-seq revealed age-dependent molecular remodeling in mutant hippocampus. Synaptic protein alterations were present in juvenile and adult mice, whereas a pronounced upregulation of mitochondrial and glial-associated proteins emerged more strongly in adulthood. Transcriptomic analyses showed partial concordance and highlighted divergence between RNA and protein regulation. Consistent with these molecular changes, there were increases in markers of oxidative stress in juvenile and adult mutant animals, whereas altered mitochondria morphology emerged selectively in adult mutants. Electrophysiological recordings demonstrated reduced basal excitatory transmission, persistence of silent synapses in adulthood and exaggerated activity-dependent synaptic potentiation, which were associated with reduced spine size consistent with impaired synapse maturation. Together, these findings indicate that a pathogenic AMPAR mutation disrupts developmental synapse maturation with secondary metabolic adaptations emerging over time. Significance Statement Mutations in genes encoding AMPA-type glutamate receptors are increasingly linked to neurodevelopmental disorders, including autism and intellectual disability. However, how these mutations disrupt brain function and development remains poorly understood. Using a mouse model carrying a recurrent disease-associated mutation in the GluA1 AMPA receptor subunit, we show that the presence of this mutant subunit protein impairs the normal maturation of excitatory synapses in the hippocampus. Mutant mice retain immature "silent" synapses into adulthood, exhibit abnormal synaptic plasticity, reduced spine size, and deficits in learning and memory. Molecular analyses reveal age-dependent remodeling of synaptic and mitochondrial proteins, suggesting that metabolic changes arise secondary to disrupted synapse development. These findings clarify how pathogenic AMPA receptor variants alter brain function over time.

items.title: Representation of emotional expressions across the face and voice brain networks.
items.abstract: Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is fundamental to successful social interaction, yet how the brain represents emotional information across sensory systems remains unclear. Here, we systematically mapped the contribution of individually-defined face- and voice-selective cortical regions in 24 human participants of either sex to unimodal and crossmodal emotion expressions. Using multivariate pattern classification, we show that emotional expressions are robustly decodable from the dominant sensory modality across all individually defined face- and voice-selective areas, and that these representations cannot be accounted for by low- and mid-level stimulus properties alone. Strikingly, emotional information from the non-dominant modality-vocal expressions within face networks and facial expressions within voice networks-was also represented throughout the network, with the exception of the occipital face areas. Crossmodal decoding further revealed a shared neural code for facial and vocal emotions in the temporal voice areas, posterior superior temporal sulcus, and precentral gyrus, indicating that these regions contain emotion representations that generalize across sensory modalities. Furthermore, in most face- and voice-selective regions, audiovisual emotional expressions could be distinguished from representations elicited by the dominant unimodal modality, indicating that bimodal signals are not simply represented as their strongest sensory component. Together, these findings reveal that emotion representations are distributed broadly across face- and voice-selective regions and identify temporo-frontal regions as key sites supporting modality-independent emotion representations. Significance statement Recognizing emotions from faces and voices is essential for everyday social interaction, yet the brain mechanisms that integrate these signals remain poorly understood. Using functional MRI (fMRI) and advanced pattern analyses, we show that emotional expressions are represented widely across both face- and voice-selective brain regions-even when conveyed through a non-preferred sensory modality. Strikingly, specific temporo-frontal regions encode facial and vocal emotions using a partially shared, modality-independent neural code. We further demonstrate that seeing and hearing emotions together reshapes how emotional information is organized in the brain, revealing a graded transition from sensory-specific to multisensory representations. These findings challenge strictly segregated models of emotion processing and provide a more integrated account of how the brain supports social understanding.

items.title: Late Integration of Prior Expectations During Precision-Weighted Perceptual Decisions.
items.abstract: Adaptive perceptual decision-making relies on the ability to combine sensory evidence with prior expectations in a precision-weighted manner. Although Bayesian inference provides a clear normative account of how such integration should occur, the neural mechanisms through which the brain represents and combines priors and likelihoods remain poorly understood. Across two preregistered experiments, we investigated how the precision of learned priors and sensory likelihoods influence visual motion judgements and associated neural activity patterns during a random-dot motion estimation task. Neurotypical adult participants (N=80, 58 female) reported directions of visual motion stimuli, with motion coherence varying randomly across trials. Prior expectations over the continuous motion direction space were manipulated block-wise by implicitly varying the probabilities with which different motion directions were presented. Consistent with precision-weighted inference, response accuracy improved as motion coherence increased with robust response biases toward the expected motion direction. Neural activity measured using electroencephalography (EEG) revealed reliable effects of prior expectation on the univariate central-parietal positivity (CPP), consistent with reduced accumulation of sensory evidence under informative priors. Multivariate analysis using inverted-encoding models revealed robust effects of prior precision on stimulus-specific neural representations, but only late, during response planning stages. Together, these findings suggest that priors learned over a continuous space do not modulate the encoding of sensory evidence and are instead integrated later in the decision-process. Significance Statement Perceptual decisions require combining noisy sensory input with prior expectations about what is likely to occur. It remains unclear how the brain integrates prior expectations with incoming sensory evidence. Using a visual motion task and concurrent brain imaging, we show that expectations do not alter early stimulus-encoding, but are instead integrated at later stages of decision formation and action planning. These findings add nuance to influential theories proposing that learned expectations directly affect stimulus representations and instead highlight their contribution to later decision-related processes. This work advances understanding of how the brain uses experience to optimise perceptual decisions under uncertainty.

items.title: From data to wisdom: A new era of scientific inquiry.
items.abstract: Rapid advances in high-throughput technologies and computational tools have ushered in a transformative era for scientific discovery. However, the acceleration of data generation has outpaced our conceptual frameworks for interpreting it. By examining current challenges in drug discovery, phenotypic screening, and model transferability, I argue that the future of scientific integrity depends on our ability to balance technical proficiency with the classical principles of hypothesis negation. Because the scientists who interpret data are themselves prone to bias and error, these safeguards must apply to human judgment as rigorously as to computational tools. I also confront a central tension: the mechanistic understanding I advocate may not scale to systems of cellular complexity. Finally, I propose a collaborative training approach that sustains both experimental excellence and theoretical depth. Each challenge maps onto the Data-Information-Knowledge-Wisdom (DIKW) hierarchy: failures at the D→I transition (underdetermined models), at I→K (undefined null hypotheses and black-box modeling), at K→W (non-transferable animal models and cross-domain blindness), or in the collapse of the entire chain when paradigm inertia forecloses the revision that wisdom demands.

items.title: Cortex-wide imaging in naturally behaving mice with 1-gram wireless mesoscopes.
items.abstract: Revealing how distributed cortical circuits coordinate behavior in freely moving animals remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience, constrained by limited fields of view, low throughput, and the tethering required by current miniaturized microscopes 1-4 . Here, we present Airscope, a wireless mesoscope delivering 4 μm lateral resolution across a 6 mm field of view at 12.5 Hz, weighing 1.0 gram. An aspheric-lens design achieves a 2.84× shorter total track length than previous miniaturized microscopes 1,2,5,6 while matching the neuron yield of benchtop one-photon mesoscopes; a tailored wireless link supports cable-free calcium imaging from >8,500 neurons per animal (25‑fold increase). Paired with a zero-shot behavior analyzer, Airscope enables cortical imaging across rich behavioral conditions, including room-scale enriched arenas, swimming assays, and multi-organ implantation, with concurrent recording from multiple animals. Using Airscope, we demonstrate versatile applications of untethered cortical imaging across diverse behavioral paradigms. We identify cortical activity patterns across multiple dorsal regions that correlate with behavioral signatures of social dominance, and show dorsal-cortical population activity prospectively decodes competition outcomes across paired animals. We observe reward-location-associated cortical activity patterns during maze exploration, and characterize Granger-causal influence from spinal cord to cortex during fear conditioning, enabled by simultaneous brain-spinal recordings. By uniting large-scale, cellular-resolution recording with unconstrained behavior, Airscope makes naturalistic, multi-animal cortical recording experimentally practical, and provides a broadly accessible technology for systems neuroscience.

items.title: Endpoint-specific interactions between aerobic exercise and benfotiamine in chronic noise-induced prefrontal cortical dysfunction in mice.
items.abstract: Chronic environmental noise can impair brain redox and inflammatory homeostasis, but the effects of combined non-pharmacological and metabolic interventions remain unclear. This study investigated whether aerobic exercise and benfotiamine, separately or combined, attenuate noise-induced behavioral dysfunction and prefrontal cortical injury-related changes. Male Swiss albino mice were assigned to Control, Noise, Noise + aerobic exercise, Noise + benfotiamine (200 mg/kg/day), Noise + aerobic exercise + benfotiamine, or Noise + N-acetylcysteine (500 mg/kg/day) groups (n = 9/group). Noise-exposed mice received broadband industrial noise at 90 dB sound pressure level for 4 h/day for 28 days. Behavioral despair-like phenotypes, cortical redox status, inflammatory gene expression, and histopathology were evaluated. Noise increased immobility in the forced swim and tail suspension tests, elevated reactive oxygen species, nitric oxide, malondialdehyde, protein carbonyls, and pro-inflammatory transcripts, and reduced glutathione and antioxidant capacity. Both interventions attenuated multiple abnormalities. Aerobic exercise produced prominent behavioral effects and increased interleukin-10 expression, whereas benfotiamine strongly reduced reactive oxygen species, lipid peroxidation, and interleukin-1β. Significant exercise × benfotiamine interactions occurred for both behavioral tests, reactive oxygen species, tumor necrosis factor-α, interleukin-1β, and interleukin-10, but not for several other endpoints. The combined intervention frequently produced the most favorable absolute values, although significant interactions were generally subadditive rather than synergistic. Aerobic exercise and benfotiamine therefore provide broad but endpoint-specific protection against chronic noise-associated prefrontal cortical dysfunction.

items.title: Association of early life adversity and peer victimisation with psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic risk in adolescents from the eBRAIN study: the role of sex and diet.
items.abstract: Background Adolescence is a sensitive developmental period during which psychosocial stress can become biologically embedded, increasing risk for psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic dysregulation. Early life adversity (ELA, such as maltreatment and household dysfunction) and peer victimisation frequently co‑occur, yet their cumulative association with adolescent psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic risk remains poorly understood. Diet may be a modifiable pathway linking stress to both psychopathology and inflammatory and metabolic processes, yet evidence integrating multiple adversities with both subjective and objective dietary measures is limited. This study aimed to investigate whether co-occurring ELA and peer victimisation were associated with adolescent psychopathology and inflammatory-metabolic markers, and to test whether diet mediated these associations. Methods In an ethically and socio-economic diverse community sample of adolescents (N = 230, age: 12.9 ± 0.9 years), we assessed: 1) exposure to ELA and peer victimisation via structured interviews; 2) Internalising and externalising symptoms, using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ); 3) Age‑adjusted body mass index (BMI) and plasma levels of C‑reactive protein (CRP), as indicators of metabolic and inflammatory risk; and 4) Diet, using self‑reported dietary intake from a Food Frequency Questionnaire (FFQ) and urinary metabolic signatures of diet from spot urine samples measured via ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography and triple-quadrupole mass spectrometry (UHPLC-Q-q-Q MS). Linear regression models examined the associations between multiple exposures to ELA and peer victimisation with psychopathology, CRP and age-adjusted BMI, and mediation models tested the role of diet. Results Participants exposed to both ELA and peer victimisation showed more internalising (B = 3.3, 95%CI: 2.0 to 4.6) and externalising symptoms (B = 3.9, 95%CI: 2.5 to 5.3), higher log 10 CRP (B = 0.4, 95%CI: 0.1 to 0.7) and age-adjusted BMI (B = 1.0, 95%CI: 0.3 to 1.6), and a higher likelihood of unhealthy dietary patterns (76% vs. 51%, pairwise p = 0.020), compared to those with no exposure. However, urinary metabolic signatures were not associated with adversity exposure. An unhealthy diet was associated with higher CRP (1.2 ± 3.8 vs. 0.4 ± 0.6 mg/L; p = 0.013), but not with psychopathology, and did not mediate associations between adversity and outcomes. Exploratory sex‑stratified analyses suggested that associations between multiple adversities and higher CRP and BMI were stronger in boys (log 10 CRP: B = 0.6, 95% CI: 0.2 to 1.1; age-adjusted BMI: B = 1.2, 95% CI: 0.2 to 2.2) than in girls (log 10 CRP: B = 0.2, 95% CI: -0.2 to 0.6; age-adjusted BMI: B = 0.6, 95% CI: -0.2 to 1.6), though the moderation effect for BMI did not reach statistical significance, but, again, diet did not mediate these differential associations. Conclusions Risk for both behavioural difficulties and elevated CRP and BMI was higher among adolescents exposed to multiple forms of adversity, especially boys. Although diet alone may not explain these associations, it remains a relevant target for reducing inflammation and metabolic risk. Future longitudinal research should explore how diet and other modifiable lifestyle behaviours can mitigate the long-term impacts of adolescent adversity.

items.title: Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer for multimodal EEG-fMRI learning in ADHD diagnosis.
items.abstract: Background Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is associated with distributed alterations in large-scale brain systems, making reliable diagnosis from neuroimaging data challenging. EEG-derived and fMRI-derived static functional-connectivity profiles summarize patterns of electrophysiological coupling and hemodynamic covariation, respectively, but their heterogeneous signal mechanisms make direct multimodal alignment difficult. New method We propose a Cross-Modal Masked Connectome Transformer (CM-MCT) for EEG-fMRI based ADHD diagnosis. Instead of imposing direct correspondence between individual connections, CM-MCT treats each Desikan-Killiany 68-region cortical atlas (DK-68) region of interest (ROI) as a connectivity-profile token and learns to recover masked ROI-level connectome information within and across modalities. The model contains modality-specific Transformer encoders, cross-modal masked connectome objectives, and a bidirectional cross-attention fusion module for diagnostic prediction. Cross-fitted mask perturbations are used to characterize ROI-level model dependence, with explicit assessment of associations with nodal strength and perturbation magnitude. Results Experiments using repeated five-by-five stratified evaluation of 210 paired HBN subjects demonstrate that the proposed method achieves 89.7% accuracy (95% confidence interval: 85.7%-93.3%) and 94.3% AUC (95% confidence interval: 91.5%-96.8%). Comparison with existing methods Compared with the evaluated methods under matched splits, preprocessing, validation, and model-selection rules, CM-MCT shows the highest mean performance, although the AUC difference from the strongest baseline does not reach statistical significance after multiplicity correction. Conclusions CM-MCT supports multimodal learning from the complementary network-level information provided by static EEG and fMRI connectivity profiles. Perturbation analysis yields modality-specific ROI sensitivity patterns that are modestly associated with the assessed factors. These heatmaps characterize model dependence without establishing causal involvement or identifying ADHD biomarkers.

items.title: Heterogeneity in Time-Outcome Associations After Endovascular Thrombectomy: A Binational Registry Study.
items.abstract: Background Although "time is brain" remains a core principle in acute stroke care, the association between treatment timing and functional outcomes after endovascular thrombectomy (EVT) varies across patients. Some individuals treated in extended time windows still achieve favorable outcomes, a phenomenon termed the "late window paradox." Differences in stroke pathophysiology across etiologies may contribute to heterogeneity in the time-outcome relationship after EVT. We investigated factors associated with heterogeneity in time-dependent EVT responsiveness, with particular attention to stroke etiology. Methods We analyzed data from two multicenter registries in Korea (CRCS-K) and Taiwan (TREAT-AIS) from January 2019 to April 2023. Patients with anterior circulation acute ischemic stroke due to cardioembolism (CE) or large artery atherosclerosis (LAA) were included. Multivariable regression and interaction analyses were performed to evaluate the association between onset-to-puncture (OTP) time and 90-day functional outcomes and to identify effect modifiers. Results Among 4,719 patients (mean age 72.0 years; 42.9% women; median NIHSS 15), longer OTP time was associated with lower odds of 90-day functional independence (adjusted OR per hour, 0.97; 95% CI, 0.96-0.98; p=0.001). The impact of OTP time varied by stroke characteristics. CE etiology, MCA occlusion, higher NIHSS, and male sex were associated with greater time sensitivity. In CE strokes, each hour of delay reduced the odds of functional independence by 4% (aOR, 0.96; 95% CI, 0.94-0.97; p _interaction =0.028). Conclusion The association between EVT timing and functional outcome varies according to stroke etiology and clinical characteristics, highlighting heterogeneity in time-outcome relationships among EVT-treated patients and providing observational insight into outcome variability in extended treatment windows.

items.title: Individualized Prediction of Patient-Defined Treatment Success to Support Patient-Centered Clinical Decision-Making.
items.abstract: Objective Clinical prediction models often target generic thresholds for treatment success, such as the Minimal Important Change. The Personal Meaningful Gain was introduced as a personalized threshold, capturing the improvement an individual seeks to achieve in a self-chosen domain to become satisfied with the treatment results. This study developed and internally validated a treatment-conditional prediction model estimating the probability of achieving the PMG within 3 months in patients with common hand and wrist conditions. Methods This study used real-world data from 25 specialized hand and wrist care clinics in the Netherlands. We included 6263 patients (training data: n=5010; test data: n=1253) treated for common hand and wrist conditions. The prediction target was the PMG achievement at 3 months post-treatment. Model performance was evaluated using discrimination (area under the curve [AUC]) and calibration. The final model was selected based on AUC, calibration, and the number of model features. Results We selected a gradient boosting machine algorithm with thirteen predictors. The model had an AUC of 0.73 (95% CI: 0.70 to 0.76, indicating acceptable-to-good discrimination) and excellent calibration in the test set. Following a user-centered design, we built a Shiny app visualizing the probability of reaching the PMG for different treatment options (i.e., hand therapy ± injection, injection, or surgery) (https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.31084375). Conclusions A treatment-conditional prediction model using a patient-defined threshold for treatment success can provide individualized estimates of the probability of achieving outcomes that matter to patients. This generalizable approach may enhance shared decision-making and expectation management in preference-sensitive care.

items.title: Circadian and Sleep-Wake Modulation of EEG Functional Connectivity Across Brain States and Its Associations With Cognition in Humans.
items.abstract: Sleep and circadian rhythms both influence human brain function, but their distinct contributions to large-scale network organization remain unclear. We quantified the effect of brain state (wake, NREM, REM), sleep-wake history, and circadian phase on functional connectivity using over 1,200 hours of artifact-free EEG recorded during a 10-day forced-desynchrony protocol. We derived principal components of functional connectivity and found that both sleep-wake history and circadian phase significantly modulated functional connectivity, with sleep-wake history exerting a broader influence. Complementary cosinor analyses further demonstrated circadian rhythmicity in several NREM and REM connectivity measures. Across sleep, global connectivity increased progressively during NREM sleep, particularly in the delta and sigma bands, but declined during REM sleep. During controlled resting wakefulness, increasing time awake was associated with higher global alpha-band connectivity, which was associated with poorer concurrent cognitive performance. Connectivity during NREM sleep was also associated with subsequent cognitive performance, with lower global theta and, to a lesser extent, higher sigma connectivity linked to better performance. REM connectivity was not associated with these cognitive measures. Together, these findings reveal opposing NREM and REM trajectories in large-scale EEG functional connectivity and show that these brain-state-specific network dynamics are shaped by both sleep-wake history and circadian phase and are associated with cognitive performance.

items.title: Validating gene-brain-behavior associations in autism: A replication study.
items.abstract: Background Autism is characterized by heterogeneity in clinical characteristics, neuroimaging and genetic profiles. To elucidate the multi-level heterogeneity, Buch et al. (2023) identified biologically meaningful subgroups in Autism Brain Imaging Data Exchange (ABIDE). However, ABIDE contains non-biological sources of variability due to retrospectively aligned site protocols. To separate biological from site-related variability and test the robustness of these subgroups, we assessed how well their findings replicate in a deeply phenotyped, prospectively collected autism dataset (EU-AIMS LEAP). Methods We included 270 autistic (7.5-30.3 years; 73% male) and 216 non-autistic participants (6.9-31 years; 63.4% male) from LEAP. Regularized canonical correlation analysis (RCCA) was conducted between functional connectivity and three clinical measures (verbal IQ [VIQ], and Autism Diagnostic Observation Schedule-2 [ADOS-2] social affect [SA] and restricted/repetitive behavior [RRB]). Next, subgroups identified by hierarchical clustering based on canonical variates were characterized by behavior, functional connectivity patterns and gene enrichment analyses. Results Three of four autistic subgroups showed behavioral profiles consistent with the original study. Three subgroups shared stronger thalamocortical connectivity, while all four displayed distinct connectivity involving default mode network (DMN), salience (SN), visual and somatomotor networks. These subgroup-specific connectivity patterns were further linked to autism-associated and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related gene sets. Across preprocessing pipelines, subgroup assignments were partially preserved. Subgroup2 (globally affected behaviors) and Subgroup4 (less social difficulty, but more restricted behavior) retained more consistent behavioral profiles and connectivity alterations, whereas Subgroup1 and Subgroup3 were more sensitive to the precise preprocessing steps. Conclusions These four subgroups showed partly consistent behavioral profiles, connectivity alterations and genetic patterns, extending our understanding of the multi-level heterogeneity of autism.

items.title: Reduced Somatomotor Cortical Thickness in Women With PTSD After Childhood Sexual Abuse: A Structural Correlate Distinct From Adult Sexual Dysfunction.
items.abstract: Background Childhood sexual abuse (CSA) is a major risk factor for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and adult sexual dysfunction in women. Although adverse childhood experiences have been linked to altered brain structure, cortical alterations specifically associated with CSA and PTSD in women remain poorly characterized, and their relationship to adult sexual functioning is unknown. Methods Women with CSA and current PTSD (n = 52), women with CSA without current PTSD (n = 32), and control women without CSA or PTSD (n = 48) underwent structural magnetic resonance imaging. Cortical thickness, surface area, and cortical volume were examined using whole brain vertex wise analyses. Sexual functioning was assessed in a subsample (n = 41). Results Women with CSA and current PTSD showed reduced cortical thickness within a left somatomotor cluster relative to controls (cluster wise p = .017). Anatomical characterization localized the cluster to motor and premotor regions involved in bodily self representation and sensorimotor integration. No group differences were observed in cortical surface area or volume. Women with CSA and PTSD also reported lower sexual functioning, particularly in arousal, lubrication, satisfaction and pain. Cortical thickness within the somatomotor cluster was unrelated to sexual functioning and did not mediate the association between CSA severity and sexual dysfunction. Conclusions These findings suggest that somatomotor cortical alterations represent neurobiological correlates of trauma related psychopathology following CSA in women. The absence of associations with adult sexual functioning suggests that structural alterations within the somatomotor cortex may be distinct from mechanisms contributing to sexual dysfunction.

items.title: EEG Resting-State Beta Band Dynamic Functional Connectivity Reveals State-Dependent Disruption of Language Network Lateralisation in First-Episode Schizophrenia.
items.abstract: Language disorganisation is a core feature of schizophrenia with significant functional consequences. However, its neurophysiological substrates remain poorly characterised, particularly in the early stages of the illness. This study investigated whether first-episode schizophrenia (FES) is associated with disruption in the organisation of language-network lateralisation, using both static and dynamic functional connectivity metrics in the EEG beta band. Thirty-one FES patients and 32 age-matched healthy volunteer subjects (HVS) underwent resting-state 64-channel EEG. Source-level connectivity was estimated using the weighted phase lag index with sliding windows, yielding 979 connectivity matrices per participant. Brain network states (BNS) were identified via k-means clustering. Static connectivity was obtained by time-averaging. Temporal features, graph-theoretical metrics, and language-network laterality indices were extracted for both whole-network and language-specific analyses. Group comparisons used permutation-based tests with family-wise error correction. Static connectivity yielded no significant group differences in any metric. Dynamic analysis identified six BNS. FES showed a significant increase in the variability of the temporal dynamics and graph-theory features of BNS5, a state characterised by parieto-occipital dominance. The core language network laterality index was significantly reduced in FES within BNS1, a state characterised by auditory-visual dominance. BNS1 occurrence correlated negatively with language disorganisation scores. Dynamic BNS-specific language network metrics correlated with verbal fluency performance exclusively in FES. These findings demonstrate that language dysfunction in early psychosis is expressed as state-dependent disruption of brain network stability and language lateralisation, detectable only through dynamic connectivity analysis.

items.title: Interaction with NEGR1 affects mGlu<sub>5</sub> cell signalling and the neuroprotection induced by the positive allosteric modulator VU0409551.
items.abstract: Background and purpose The metabotropic glutamate receptor mGlu 5 plays an important role in neuronal survival and synaptic plasticity. We and others have shown that mGlu 5 positive allosteric modulators (PAMs) are biased agonists, triggering the activation of neuroprotective pathways and promoting neuronal survival. As mGlu 5 biased pharmacology arises from drug-induced interactions with different protein partners, in this study, we analysed the mGlu 5 interactome to identify novel binding partners capable of modulating receptor cell signalling. Experimental approach To identify new mGlu 5 partners, we employed mass spectrometry, followed by co-immunoprecipitation experiments, which confirmed the interaction between mGlu 5 and the neuronal growth regulator 1 (NEGR1), a cell adhesion molecule. We next evaluated how NEGR1 affects mGlu 5 cell signalling and cellular distribution using lentivirus transduction on primary neuronal cultures to knockdown NEGR1 expression. We also assessed whether NEGR1 plays a role in the neuroprotective effects of the mGlu5 PAM, VU0409551, by evaluating apoptotic cell death and neurite degeneration. Key results The interaction between NEGR1 and mGlu 5 is important for mGlu 5 synaptic localization and for its coupling with Homer, thereby modulating cell signalling pathways activated by mGlu 5 receptors. For instance, NEGR1 knockdown led to decreased mGlu 5 -dependent activation of ERK1/2 and reduced expression of ARC/ARG3.1 and BDNF. Importantly, NEGR1 knockdown affected mGlu 5 pharmacology, as the neuroprotective effect of VU0409551 was not observed in neurons expressing low levels of NEGR1. Conclusions and implications These results indicate that NEGR1 is essential for mGlu 5 -biased activation of neuroprotective cell signalling pathways and for the neuroprotective effects triggered by VU0409551.

items.title: An acetylcholine-inhibited sleep-active hippocampal interneuron orchestrates memory consolidation.
items.abstract: Memory reactivation during hippocampal ripples is critical for sleep-dependent memory consolidation. However, the molecular-to-circuit mechanism enabling sleep-predominant ripple generation remains unresolved. Here, we discovered that a sparse population of GABAergic interneurons in the mouse hippocampus specializes in gating ripple generation and memory consolidation. While all known genetically labeled hippocampal interneurons were highly active during wakefulness and rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep, genetic targeting of M2 acetylcholine receptor (Chrm2)-expressing neurons isolated a specific population preferentially active during non-REM (NREM) sleep and quiet wakefulness. These acetylcholine-inhibited interneurons inhibited the entire hippocampus in an infra-slow rhythm (∼0.015 Hz). Suppressing their activity in dorsal CA3 or ventral hippocampus impaired spatial and social memory, respectively. Furthermore, Chrm2+ neurons were closely associated with ripples; their activity bidirectionally modulated ripple occurrence via widespread inhibition. Thus, Chrm2+ interneurons are critical in linking neuromodulatory state to memory consolidation, offering genetically targeted access to sleep-active memory circuits implicated in cognitive disorders.

items.title: Hunger recruits a parallel circuit encoding alcohol reward.
items.abstract: Internal states like hunger, pain, thirst, and arousal can bias behavior by affecting sensory and memory processing. Internal states are critical to understand in the context of alcohol addiction because they influence cravings, reinstatement, and relapse. Norepinephrine plays a key role in both hunger and alcohol-induced arousal and preference, but the circuit-level mechanisms through which it modulates the influence of hunger on alcohol preference are not well understood. We sought to address this using intersectional genetic tools for manipulating neurons expressing octopamine, the invertebrate analog of vertebrate norepinephrine. We identified a single octopamine neuron required for ethanol seeking only when Drosophila are food deprived. Hunger increased baseline activity in this neuron, thus making it more responsive to an odor cue previously paired with ethanol. A combination of genetic and connectome analyses revealed that the synaptic partners of this octopaminergic neuron form a functional module that acts on Drosophila memory circuitry. Thus, we show that hunger recruits a parallel circuit that drives learned ethanol preference, providing a neuronal framework through which internal state influences the expression of memory for ethanol-associated cues. items.title: Clinical utility and transparency in randomized trials of biportal endoscopic lumbar discectomy: a systematic review.
items.abstract: Introduction Unilateral biportal endoscopic discectomy has grown rapidly as a minimally invasive treatment for lumbar disc herniation, supported by an expanding body of randomized controlled trials. However, randomization alone does not guarantee a trial is clinically useful, and no prior study has evaluated whether these trials are designed and reported in a way that supports confident clinical decision-making. The Van't Hooft framework assesses this dimension directly, scoring clinical utility and transparency separately from conventional risk-of-bias tools, addressing a gap left by prior appraisals focused on effect estimates alone. Methods A systematic review of PubMed, Cochrane Library, and Scopus identified randomized controlled trials evaluating unilateral biportal endoscopic discectomy for lumbar disc herniation. Two reviewers independently screened studies and scored each included trial using the Van't Hooft framework, yielding clinical utility (maximum 14), transparency (maximum 12), and total usefulness (maximum 26) scores. Item-level frequencies and temporal trends by publication year were summarized descriptively and with univariable linear regression. Results Four trials (324 patients) met inclusion criteria. Mean clinical utility was 9.5±1.0, mean transparency was 8.5±1.3, and mean total usefulness was 18.0±0.8. Value-for-money reporting and assessor blinding were absent in all four trials. Clinical utility rose nonsignificantly over time (β = 0.519/year, P = 0.222), while transparency declined nonsignificantly (β = -0.815/year, P = 0.053). Conclusion Randomized trials of biportal endoscopic discectomy address clinically relevant, patient-centered questions but report transparency inconsistently. Future trials should prioritize preregistration, data sharing, and cost evaluation to strengthen the evidence base guiding this increasingly common procedure.

items.title: mechanoLight: A genetically encoded fluorescent biosensor for visualizing 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction in live cells.
items.abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) are pivotal sensors of the mechanical environment, yet how they sense and transduce physical stimuli into biochemical signals within live cells remains largely elusive. Here we introduce mechanoLight, a genetically encoded red fluorescent biosensor designed to report the mechanical activation of the 5-hydroxytryptamine 2A receptor (5-HT2AR). By incorporating a circularly permuted mApple (cp-mApple) into the third intracellular loop of 5-HT2AR with the optimized linker (m-linker), mechanoLight selectively detects conformational changes of 5-HT2AR in response to fluid shear stress while exhibiting minimal sensitivity to 5-HT. In sharp contrast, psychLight2, the previously developed green 5-HT2AR biosensor, primarily detects ligand-induced 5-HT2AR activation, suggesting that mechanoLight and psychLight2 capture distinct conformational modes of 5-HT2AR activation. Integrated analysis of linker-swapping experiments, structural modeling, and molecular dynamics simulations revealed that the flexibility of the m-linker underlies the mechanosensitivity of mechanoLight. We further extend this strategy to other mechanosensitive GPCRs, enabling visualization of their mechanoreactivity in live cells. The mechanoLight signal reflects the mechanosensitivity of 5-HT2AR, as shear stress-induced 5-HT2AR activation triggers Gα q -dependent signaling pathways, including phospholipase C (PLC) activation, intracellular Ca 2+ mobilization, and ERK phosphorylation. Mutational analysis further identifies N-terminal glycosylation and helix 8 as structural determinants of 5-HT2AR mechanotransduction. Together, our findings establish 5-HT2AR as a mechanotransducer and introduce mechanoLight as a powerful tool for deciphering the molecular principles of GPCR mechanotransduction in live cells.

items.title: REM Atonia Index Cutoffs for REM Sleep Without Atonia: A Systematic Review with Meta-analysis of Adult Diagnostic Performance.
items.abstract: Study objectives To synthesize evidence on REM Atonia Index (RAI) thresholds and reference values, quantify adult diagnostic performance for REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD), and distinguish diagnostic cutoffs from physiological reference limits and pediatric values. Methods: We conducted a focused systematic review of studies using automated RAI, rescreening studies from a previous review and updating PubMed/MEDLINE through July 27, 2026. Adult diagnostic accuracy was synthesized with a bivariate binomial-normal random-effects model. Continuous RAI differences were pooled as raw mean differences. Normative adult and pediatric evidence was synthesized separately because these represented different estimands. The review was retrospectively registered in OSF Registries on August 20, 2026 (https://osf.io/v3kqa). Results Thirty unique studies were included. Eight adult studies contributed to the diagnostic-accuracy meta-analysis; thresholds ranged from 0.80 to 0.90. Pooled sensitivity was 0.850 (95% CI, 0.766-0.908) and specificity 0.895 (95% CI, 0.814-0.944). Eight studies contributed continuous data; RAI was lower in RBD by a pooled mean difference of -0.263 (95% CI, -0.335 to -0.190). Only two methodologically non-equivalent adult studies provided physiological reference limits, 0.85 and 0.91, precluding pooling. Pediatric evidence supported age-conditioned interpretation. Conclusions Adult chin-EMG RAI shows good overall discrimination of established RBD, but current evidence does not support a universal numerical boundary for REM sleep without atonia. Evidence defining physiological reference limits is substantially less developed than diagnostic evidence, and normal RAI varies with age. RAI should therefore be reported continuously, with thresholds interpreted according to their intended diagnostic or physiological purpose.

items.title: Oxidative signaling thresholds shape vulnerability in the central and peripheral nervous systems.
items.abstract: Neurodegeneration is frequently associated with oxidative stress, yet the mechanisms that convert reactive oxygen species (ROS) into irreversible degenerative signals remain incompletely understood. Neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems often differ in their responses to injury, but these differences cannot be reduced to a simple contrast between weak and strong antioxidant capacity. This Essay proposes that neuronal vulnerability is shaped by multilayered signaling thresholds comprising ROS production, antioxidant and thiol buffering, redox-sensitive signal detection, molecular gating, and commitment to degeneration, survival, or repair. This framework may help explain selective neuronal vulnerability in neurodegenerative diseases and identify intervention points downstream of global ROS suppression.

items.title: Image-guided focused ultrasound for non-invasive modulation of superficial and deep tissues.
items.abstract: Focused ultrasound (FUS) enables non-invasive, spatially precise modulation of biological tissues. This protocol describes assembly, calibration, and implementation of a diagnostic ultrasound-guided FUS (dUS-FUS) platform for real-time targeting of superficial and deep tissues in small-animal models. We demonstrate reversible sciatic nerve modulation in a rat acute pain model and assess sensory and motor functions using behavioral tests. The platform provides a reproducible workflow for image-guided tissue modulation and can be adapted to diverse preclinical applications. For complete details on the use and execution of this protocol, please refer to Sangwan et al. 1 , 2 .

items.title: SI-ATRP of spiropyran methacrylate from gold surfaces: optimisation for light responsive devices.
items.abstract: Copolymer brushes of spiropyran methacrylate and methyl methacrylate were grown from gold surfaces by oxygen-tolerant Cu(0)-plate surface-initiated ATRP, giving uniform coatings with photoresponsive polarity switching, as shown by contact angle measurements. This approach overcomes the limitations of drop and spin casting and offers a route to light-responsive gold-based medical devices, such as nanovalves for gated release.

items.title: Mentoring Undergraduates in Aging and Disparities Research: Hopkins USTAR.
items.abstract: The Johns Hopkins Undergraduate Summer Training and Research Program (Hopkins USTAR) was a 2-year program funded by the National Institute on Aging R25 Advancing Diversity in Aging Research through Undergraduate Education. Hopkins USTAR was designed to provide undergraduate students primarily from underrepresented backgrounds in biomedical and behavioral science with interdisciplinary research training in aging and health disparities research. From 2023 to 2025, a total of 15 undergraduate students participated in faculty-mentored research projects, professional development, research education, and national research conferences. Program evaluation methods included pre- and post-program surveys and interviews. Results suggest that the Hopkins USTAR program significantly increased aspects of participants' research self-efficacy and strengthened perceived science identity. Despite the early termination of Hopkins USTAR, the program's short-term outcomes indicate modest success in fostering positive feelings about science and preparing participants for graduate school. Continued follow-up to assess long-term program outcomes will be important to measure impact.

items.title: Context-dependent effects of social isolation and behavioural recovery in two populations of Lymnaea stagnalis.
items.abstract: Social context is a key modulator of behaviour and cognition across taxa, yet the effects of social isolation (SI) and subsequent recovery remain poorly characterised in invertebrate systems. Here, we developed a longitudinal behavioural procedure to examine how SI and social reintroduction (SR) influence feeding, exploration, and operant conditioning behavioural assays in the pond snail Lymnaea stagnalis. To capture biologically relevant variation, we compared two populations with differing environmental backgrounds: a long-established laboratory strain (W) and a "wild" population (TC1). Isolation was associated with reproducible changes across multiple behavioural domains, including reduced feeding and impaired memory performance in an operant conditioning assay. These effects emerged more rapidly in laboratory-inbred snails, whereas the "wild" ones required a longer isolation period to exhibit comparable behavioural alterations, indicating differences in response dynamics between populations with distinct environmental backgrounds. Following SR, behavioural recovery was modulated by social context. In W snails, social reintroduction with familiar conspecifics was associated with substantial recovery, whereas social reintroduction with unfamiliar conspecifics produced more limited improvement. In contrast, TC1 snails showed a delayed onset of behavioural disruption and less complete recovery after social reintroduction within the tested Timeframe, irrespective of conspecific familiarity. Together, these findings demonstrate that responses to social isolation in L. stagnalis are strongly influenced by population background and the social environment during recovery. By integrating laboratory-reared and "wild" populations within a multi-behavioural approach, this study establishes a tractable framework for future investigations linking social context to the neural and molecular mechanisms underlying behaviour and learning.

items.title: Functional connectivity and treatment response in obesity and eating disorders: Current evidence and empirical data.
items.abstract: Alterations in large-scale brain networks have been reported in obesity (OB) and eating disorders (ED), but their relevance to treatment outcomes remains unclear. We reviewed evidence on neurobiological predictors of treatment outcome in ED and OB and present preliminary empirical analyses exploring baseline rsFC differences between individuals with anorexia nervosa (AN), obesity with comorbid ED (OB + ED), and obesity without ED (OB - ED) and healthy controls (HC), and examining whether these connectivity differences are associated with treatment outcome in the clinical groups. A total of 98 women (AN = 27, OB + ED = 25, OB - ED = 21, HC = 25) underwent resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). rsFC networks were subsequently identified using probabilistic independent component analysis (ICA), and their associations with treatment outcomes were examined within each clinical group. Both OB groups showed reduced rsFC relative to HC within a thalamic-basal ganglia network, specifically in a cluster located in the left inferior occipital cortex encompassing extrastriate visual regions. Baseline connectivity in this occipital cluster showed a positive, although non-significant, association with treatment outcome in the OB - ED group, whereas no significant associations were observed in AN or OB + ED. Given the non-significant nature of this exploratory association, the observed relationship should be considered hypothesis-generating and requires confirmation in adequately powered samples. Further work is needed to clarify the role of sensory-integrative networks in treatment response across extreme weight conditions.

items.title: The bystander effect: lesion spatial extent as a foundational artifact in Lesion Network Mapping
items.abstract: Lesion network mapping (LNM) has provided a compelling framework in clinical neuroscience, linking focal brain damage at heterogeneous anatomical locations to shared functional networks across behavioural syndromes. Recently, the methodological specificity of LNM has come under discussion following observations that derived network maps tend to converge onto the normative connectome's generic degree distribution. While current efforts largely treat this convergence as a statistical inference challenge addressable via post-hoc spatial null models or individual-level analyses, we identify a foundational upstream measurement artifact operating within individual patients: the lesion "bystander effect". Because pathological lesions follow biological constraints rather than functional brain parcellations, a typical lesion encapsulates both a symptom-driving critical node and surrounding asymptomatic bystander tissue. By averaging connectivity profiles across the entire lesion mask, LNM mechanically dilutes focal clinical signals. Across empirical clinical cohorts, individual-level machine learning classifiers, synthetic within-cohort lesion unions, and whole-brain spherical simulations, we demonstrate that increasing lesion extent deterministically drives network maps toward the connectome degree vector following a mathematical power law. Fulfilling the clinical promise of LNM will therefore require computational strategies that isolate the causal functional core from surrounding bystander tissue prior to network projection.

items.title: BOWIe: Wireless Headstage for Optical Stimulation in Closed-Loop Optogenetics Experiments in Freely-moving Rodents
items.abstract: Optogenetics is an invaluable technique in neuroscience to study brain circuits, but conventional optogenetic systems use tethered approaches to deliver light to the brain which can hinder natural behavior. Optoelectronic advances led to the development of wireless optical stimulators for optogenetics experiments, but most reported devices have low widespread use due to complex builds and reduced versatility, which has also limited their integration in closed-loop systems. Here, we developed BOWIe, a battery-powered, low-weight, wireless headstage for photostimulation in optogenetics experiments with rodents, especially designed for simple integration in multiple behavioral setups, including those requiring closed-loop operation. BOWIe is based on a Bluetooth-Low Energy system-on-a-chip that allows simultaneous control and communication capabilities with a reduced number of components, and can be paired with an Arduino-based transmitter for simple integration in any behavioral paradigm using analogue or digital triggers. Two modes of optical stimulation are possible, either with ferrule-coupled optical fibers or μLED neural probes, which permit adapting the headstage according to material availability or experimental demands. A user-friendly app was also developed to simplify headstage pairing, definition of stimulation parameters, and protocol design. BOWIe was validated in two behavioral paradigms, including in a closed-loop experiment using computer vision, Bonsai RX, and Deeplabcut Live to track behavioral parameters online and remotely trigger photostimulation upon detected events. BOWIe's modular design and flexible integration with behavioral setups make it a practical tool for in vivo experiments with optogenetics.

items.title: What Does a Donor Need to Know? Content Analysis of Informed Consent Documents Used for Brain Organoid Research.
items.abstract: Donors of cells used to create induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) and brain organoids may not understand what brain organoids are, how they will be used, or the long-term implications of the research. Informed consent documents (ICDs) often contain highly technical language and are written at reading grade levels higher than those attained by the target population. Our goal was to evaluate informed consent documents used for brain organoid research. We compared 20 currently active, IRB-approved consent documents to published templates/guidelines for iPSC research consent. Analyzed ICDs adhered to guidelines in explaining risks and benefits, de-identification, commercial potential, storage, and results sharing. However, descriptions of current and future use were lacking in detail, and the average reading level of ICDs far exceeded that of the general population. Our findings suggest additional transparency in ICDs would assist participants in making an informed choice about participation in iPSC and brain organoid research.

items.title: Autonomic dysfunction in patients with Huntington's disease: Evidence from standardized cardiovascular reflex testing.
items.abstract: BackgroundAutonomic dysfunction has been reported in Huntington's disease (HD), but its extent and mechanisms remain unclear. This study aimed to evaluate autonomic function using standardized cardiovascular autonomic reflex tests (CRTs) in a cohort of genetically confirmed HD patients.MethodsIn this single-center, cross-sectional study, we assessed 16 patients with manifest HD using head-up tilt test (HUTT), Valsalva maneuver (VM), deep breathing test, cold face test, and handgrip test, all performed under continuous blood pressure (BP) and heart rate (HR) monitoring. Age- and sex-matched healthy controls (HC) were included for comparison.ResultsBased on medical history, 56% of HD patients reported symptoms of orthostatic intolerance while standing. During HUTT, they showed a significant reduction in ΔBP. BP overshoot during VM was also significantly reduced. HR responses and BP changes did not differ significantly between groups across all other maneuvers. When stratified by disease stage, parasympathetic indices were lower in later-stage patients.ConclusionsHD patients exhibited subclinical adrenergic abnormalities on CRTs, with initially preserved cardiovagal control, a pattern compatible with central autonomic involvement and possible progressive impairment of both sympathetic and parasympathetic systems over time.

items.title: Factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis.
items.abstract: Objective To identify demographic and clinical factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival using three well-characterized cohorts of patients with Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS). Methods ALS patients from the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta ALS Register (PARALS) diagnosed between 1995-2019 interval who underwent tracheostomy were included. A multivariable Cox proportional hazards model was used to identify factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival. Significant findings were tested in two independent cohorts, the Emilia-Romagna Region ALS Register (ERRALS) and an incident ALS cohort from South Sardinia. Results A total of 449 patients from PARALS underwent tracheostomy during the study period, with a median post-tracheostomy survival of 16.3 months (IQR 4.0-45.0). Younger age at tracheostomy was associated with longer survival (HR 1.03 per one-year increase, 95%CI1.01-1.05, p = 0.001), as being married/cohabiting (HR 0.78, 95%CI0.61-0.98, p = 0.033), a longer diagnosis-to-tracheostomy interval (HR 0.84 per one-year increase, 95%CI0.79-0.90, p p = 0.012). These associations were replicated in the independent cohorts, when data were available. Additionally, discharge to nursing homes was associated with poorer survival in the Sardinian cohort (HR 4.23, 95%CI2.49-7.19; p p = 0.019). Discussion We identified multiple factors associated with post-tracheostomy survival in ALS patients, encompassing clinical and demographic characteristics at tracheostomy as well as local factors influencing peri- and post-operative care. These findings may support decision-making and clinician-patient communication in the advanced stages of ALS.

items.title: Gender Differences in the Development of Growth and Fixed Mindsets Among Chinese Adolescents: A Cross-Lagged Panel Network Analysis.
items.abstract: Introduction Students' mindsets about the malleability of their abilities shape their academic performance, social adaptation, and psychological well-being, making it important to track how these beliefs change during adolescence. Although mindsets undergo substantial change in this period, most studies have used latent variable models that ignore the dynamic interactions among mindset items. Examining how specific items change over time can thus reveal how mindsets develop and whether this process differs between boys and girls. Methods This study examined the temporal links among the 10 growth mindset items and the 10 fixed mindset items, identifying the central beliefs within each network, in 15,386 students (40% girls; Mage = 16.73 years) from 31 secondary vocational schools in China, followed annually over 3 years. Mixed-design ANOVA and cross-lagged panel network (CLPN) analysis were used to compare mindset development between genders. Results Boys consistently reported higher aggregate scores on both growth and fixed mindsets than girls, though these differences were small. The CLPN analysis showed gender-specific trajectories: girls showed earlier and more pronounced changes in the growth mindset network, whereas boys showed slower integration of growth-related beliefs. By contrast, the fixed mindset networks developed similarly across genders. Item-level cross-lagged associations were small, and network comparisons were descriptive. Conclusions Conceptualizing mindsets as interconnected networks, this study identifies gender-specific developmental patterns in mindset organization among Chinese vocational students, showing how mindset items co-develop over time and suggesting candidate targets for gender-sensitive interventions in the future.

items.title: Psychoplastogens to Reduce Persistent Cognitive Symptoms for Traumatic Brain Injury as a Chronic Condition.
items.abstract: There are currently no available effective pharmacological therapies for treating chronic cognitive deficits after traumatic brain injury (TBI). Psychoplastogens, including atypical psychedelics, classical serotonergic psychedelics, and neuroplastogens, are a class of small molecule drugs that can enhance neuroplasticity by inducing rapid and sustained effects on neuronal architecture and function, with the potential to have broad therapeutic effects. Ketamine, psilocybin, and dimethyltryptamine (DMT) have demonstrated therapeutic efficacy for treating multiple psychiatric conditions, and their ability to enhance neuroplasticity is hypothesized to be the primary mechanism. However, the administration of psychoplastogens for the treatment of cognitive impairments in TBI and other neurodegenerative diseases is nascent. In this review, we discuss the following: (1) relevant TBI pathologies and how neuroplasticity is impaired following TBI, (2) psychoplastogens and their use in neural repair models, and (3) the potential of psychoplastogens as treatments for TBI to alleviate various pathologies and improve cognitive behavioral outcomes. The underlying pathologies observed after TBI, including impaired neuroplasticity, synaptic dysfunction, neuronal atrophy, altered neurotransmission, and cellular dysfunction, are shared with several psychiatric disorders. Based on the multiple pathophysiological targets, there is a critical unmet need to investigate psychoplastogens as therapeutic interventions during the chronic phase of TBI for cognitive outcomes and underlying impact on neuroplasticity.

items.title: Spatiotemporal Analysis of Molecular Continuity in Pathogenesis of Squamous Cell Carcinoma: From Normal Epithelium to Precancerous Lesions and Carcinoma.
items.abstract: Squamous cell carcinomas (SCCs) develop from the stratified epithelia of the esophagus, head and neck, lung, and skin, providing a tractable model to investigate how altered epithelial fields progress toward invasive cancer. Across SCC subtypes, evolution often begins before overt malignancy, with age- and exposure-associated mutant clones expanding within histologically normal epithelia. As lesions advance, early driver selection becomes coupled to copy number alterations, chromosomal instability, and epigenetic remodeling, whereas later stages are shaped by branching diversification, cellular plasticity, and regionally constrained selection. Despite tissue-specific differences, several recurrent principles emerge, including clonal expansion within mutated normal fields, transition bottlenecks marked by genome-scale instability, and the spatial organization of subclonal architecture and invasive-front states. In this review, we synthesize recent progress in the temporal ordering and spatial patterning of SCC evolution and discuss how genetic alterations, epigenetic remodeling, and tissue ecology jointly drive disease progression. We further highlight the implications for early interception, biomarker development, immune evasion, and evolution-informed prevention and therapy.
