items.title: Constructing melanopic light exposure profiles from sparse daily-route measurements.
items.abstract: Daily light exposure is temporally structured, yet calibrated spectral measurements are usually available only at selected locations and times. Turning such a sparse library into a schedule-resolved profile requires an assignment rule: a decision about which measurements may represent each unmeasured part of the day. We examined how much that decision matters. Sixty-three eye-level spectral irradiance measurements, collected across home, commute, office and lunch settings on three June days in Ottawa, were mapped onto a schedule of 22 half-hour slots. For each of six assignment rules we generated 100,000 profiles and computed melanopic dose and time above thresholds of 250, 1,000 and 10,000 melanopic lx. Indoor-only and outdoor-only assignments gave contrasting bounds, with median doses of 16,536 and 119,995 lx ⋅ h. Among the four rules that combined indoor and outdoor measurements, median dose varied only from 44,257 to 48,337 lx ⋅ h, whereas the central 95% of the generated dose distributions spanned ranges differing by nearly a factor of two. Central estimates were set largely by the composition of the eligible measurement pools rather than by the structure a rule preserved; the rule mainly determined spread. Targeted substitutions, in which only commute and lunch conditions were changed, raised median dose by 28,600 lx ⋅ h, with outdoor lunch contributing more cumulative dose and outdoor commuting more time above 10,000 lx. The framework supports sensitivity and scenario analysis rather than reconstruction of continuous personal exposure, and shows why the assignment step must be reported explicitly for a constructed profile to be interpretable.

items.title: Species-specific PM retention by urban tree bark is associated with functional traits under controlled exposure.
items.abstract: Urban tree bark plays a critical yet underappreciated role in mitigating atmospheric particulate matter (PM) pollution, particularly during leaf-off periods when foliage is absent. However, the relative contribution of bark versus other plant organs and the functional traits governing interspecific variation in bark PM retention remain poorly understood. In this study, we implemented a trait-based modeling framework utilizing modified open-top chambers to minimize external meteorological disturbances and reduce environmental variability. Results showed that: (1) at the unit-area scale, bark retained significantly more PM than leaves or branches across 11 of the 12 core calibration species (p -2 ), whereas Juniperus formosana exhibited the lowest (112.1 ± 13.6 μg cm -2 ); (2) upscaling to the whole-plant scale revealed that aggregated bark PM 2.5-10 retention was 1.40 times that of leaves, while PM 2.5 retention between bark and foliage was comparable, indicating a distinct size-selective filtration advantage of bark; (3) Spearman correlation analysis and mathematical modeling indicated that interspecific bark PM variation was associated with specific micro-topographic traits (p < 0.05), with lenticel density, surface roughness, and groove prominence showing consistent positive associations with bark PM retention, and the resulting predictive models showed acceptable consistency with the limited independent validation data; and (4) an exploratory application to twenty-six dominant urban greening species in Hangzhou suggested a 4.83-fold interspecific variation in potential bark PM retention under controlled exposure. These findings suggest that neglecting bark retention may lead to underestimation of tree air purification capacity, providing a basis for incorporating bark-specific parameters into dynamic vegetation models.

items.title: Water Type Modulates Particle State and Toxicity of Polyethylene Terephthalate Nanoplastics.
items.abstract: Nanoplastic toxicity is typically assessed using pristine particles under simplified laboratory conditions, despite growing evidence that environmental transformations can substantially alter particle behaviour and biological effects. Here, we investigated how water type influences the particle state and toxicity of polyethylene terephthalate nanoplastics (PET-NPs) in the freshwater zooplankton Daphnia magna. In a chronic life-history assay, exposure to 0.5 mg L -1 PET-NPs caused no detectable effects on survival, growth or reproduction, whereas exposure to 10 mg L -1 resulted in complete mortality. We then incubated PET-NPs for four days in reverse osmosis water, ASTM artificial freshwater or natural freshwater to examine short-term particle transformations prior to exposure. Toxicity remained high following incubation in reverse osmosis water (80% mortality) and ASTM water (60% mortality), with ASTM-transformed particles additionally reducing growth and reproduction. In contrast, PET-NPs transformed in natural freshwater caused no detectable lethal or sub-lethal effects under the conditions tested. Particle-size measurements showed extensive aggregation in ASTM water, whereas PET-NPs remained largely dispersed in both reverse osmosis water and natural freshwater. Natural freshwater also altered particle zeta potential, indicating changes in surface properties. The contrasting toxicity of similarly dispersed particles in reverse osmosis and natural freshwater indicates that aggregation alone cannot explain the biological responses. Together, these findings demonstrate that water type can rapidly transform PET-NP particle state and substantially modify chronic biological effects. They highlight the importance of considering environmentally induced particle transformations when assessing nanoplastic toxicity.

items.title: Headspace-driven metabolic rerouting balances chain elongation and acetogenic pathways for high-efficiency carbon recovery.
items.abstract: In situ assimilation of off-gases (H 2 /CO 2 ) into liquid metabolites during anaerobic fermentation presents a promising approach to maximize waste biomass valorization. However, mechanisms governing the interaction between microbial carbon fixation and chain elongation (CE) through headspace dynamics remain unclear. This study explored gas-liquid metabolic flux and microbial response by varying headspace pressure/composition in batch CE bioreactors. Autogenic pressure reshaped the physicochemical microenvironment, which potentially induced specific biological inhibition and constrained ethanol utilization. Accordingly, caproic acid production decreased by 40.50-51.68%, whereas acetic acid accumulation increased by 70.67-104.44% under both N 2 and H 2 /CO 2 headspace. This alteration reflected metabolic flux redistribution between CE and acetic acid-producing pathways driven mainly by electron donor oxidation with homoacetogenesis as a potential secondary contributor. Meanwhile, an initial H 2 /CO 2 headspace curbed off-gas emissions and induced a final 17.62 kPa (abs) vacuum, enhancing soluble metabolite carbon retention. Consequently, liquid-phase carbon recovery increased to 84.29% under autogenic pressure and peaked at 89.68% following further H 2 /CO 2 headspace replacement. Microbial profiling revealed that self-pressurized conditions suppressed Oscillibacter from 15.14% to 1.93%, whereas H 2 /CO 2 exposure selectively enriched Caproiciproducens to 30.52% as the dominant CE driver. Metatranscriptomics demonstrated that autogenic pressure markedly upregulated the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway genes by up to 28.62-fold, accompanied by induction of stress-responsive genes for physiological adaptation. Additionally, the initial H 2 /CO 2 headspace promoted the expression of gene korA, suggesting a potential partial reductive tricarboxylic acid (rTCA) pathway for carbon fixation. These insights provide a mechanistic framework for optimizing carbon recovery and product selectivity in engineered CE systems, advancing sustainable waste-to-biochemical platforms.

items.title: Manganese-Crosslinked Porous Carbon for Phosphorus Recovery and Soil Remediation: A Sustainable Strategy Featuring Fast Adsorption and Controlled Release.
items.abstract: Developing efficient systems to recover phosphorus (P) from water is critical for mitigating aquatic eutrophication and advancing sustainable P cycling. Herein, a porous carbon skeleton was synthesized via pyrolysis of manganese-crosslinked sodium alginate (Mn/SA-C-S) for efficient P adsorption and subsequent soil remediation. Mn/SA-C-S exhibited rapid P adsorption (14.61 mg/g within 200 min) and controlled release (∼10% desorption over 500 min) via precipitation and surface complexation. The P-rich Mn/SA-C-S (Mn/SA-C-S-P) sustains soil available P (∼109 mg/kg), enhances plant P uptake, and reduces P loss. Crucially, Mn/SA-C-S-P application significantly reshaped the soil microbial community, enriching key functional groups involved in nutrient cycling. Life cycle assessment revealed that Mn/SA-C-S production emits 9.19 kg CO 2 eq, which is 1.9 to 17.62 times lower than values reported in the literature for biochar-based materials. Producing one ton of Mn/SA-C-S-P yields a net benefit of $487.48. This study provides a proof of concept for recovering P from wastewater and reusing it as a resource toward sustainable P management.

items.title: Understanding public preferences for urban wildflower meadows.
items.abstract: Accelerating urbanisation challenges biodiversity and human wellbeing, demanding effective urban nature-based solutions. Urban wildflower meadows are increasingly popular interventions that may offer biodiversity and wellbeing benefits. However, realising their potential depends on public support, which requires robust evidence on which meadow design attributes the public prefers and values most. We conducted a choice experiment with urban greenspace users across three UK cities to quantify willingness-to-pay (WTP) for some of the key characteristics of wildflower meadows in public parks, namely flower colour diversity, native species composition, plant species richness, and pollinator habitat quality. Respondents generally preferred wildflower meadow options over the status quo of mown amenity grass and were willing to pay for improvements to meadow attributes through increased local taxation. Respondents had positive WTP for more colourful, pollinator-friendly meadows with more native species, but not for additional plant species. Preferences were largely consistent across respondents interviewed at different meadow types (annual, perennial, or control sites), suggesting that enhanced attribute salience from direct exposure to existing meadows had minimal influence on stated preferences. Methodologically, this suggests that in situ surveys of preferences for urban greenspace are broadly robust to salience effects and can inform management beyond the surveyed sites. Attributes that offer positive outcomes for biodiversity, such as supporting pollinators and including native species, were aligned with, rather than conflicting with, public preferences. Urban greenspace managers can enhance public support while achieving ecological objectives by designing meadows with moderate colour diversity, high native species content, and demonstrable pollinator benefits.

items.title: Porous geopolymer from cyanobacterial sludge and coal fly ash as shape-stabilizing matrix for thermal energy storage using phase change paraffin.
items.abstract: The consumption of fossil fuels drives both the energy crisis and greenhouse gas emissions, while the accumulation of solid wastes such as coal fly ash (CFA) and cyanobacterial sludge (CS) exerts considerable ecological pressure. This study explores the utilization of CS and CFA as raw materials, employing egg white powder as a surfactant and hydrogen peroxide as a blowing agent to fabricate a highly porous geopolymer (CCG). The organic fibers in CS act as pore templates and reinforcing agents, while their partial degradation in the alkaline environment participates in the gelation process. The optimal formulation comprises a 9 mol/L sodium hydroxide solution, 3 wt% egg white powder, 7 wt% hydrogen peroxide, a CS:CFA mass ratio of 2:8, and a sodium silicate to sodium hydroxide solution ratio of 2.5:1. Following synthesis, CCG underwent vacuum impregnation with phase change paraffin (PCP). The capillary forces within the porous matrix effectively encapsulate the molten PCP, yielding a shape-stabilized phase change composite (CCGP). Relative to CCG the CCGP exhibits a thermal conductivity enhancement of 0.081-0.168 W/(m·K). The solidification and melting enthalpies of the CCGP were 67.58 J/g and 69.23 J/g, respectively, with remarkable thermal stability at temperatures up to 600 °C. This study not only achieves high-value utilization of CS and CFA, but also provides new insights into protein-assisted foaming and fiber pore formation in geopolymer systems, offering guidance for the design of shape-stabilized phase change composites with optimized encapsulation efficiency and long-term thermal stability.

items.title: Microbial diversity in leg ulcer and skin in Sickle Cell disease.
items.abstract: Introduction Leg ulcers are a common, painful, and difficult-to-treat complication of sickle cell disease due to their prolonged healing process. The microbial composition of these wounds remains poorly understood. This study investigated the microbiota diversity in sickle cell disease leg ulcers and associations with laboratory parameters. Methods Samples were collected from leg ulcers, intact skin adjacent to the ulcers, and intact skin from healthy controls. Microbiome profiling was performed by sequencing the V4 region of the 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene. The laboratory results of patients with sickle cell disease leg ulcers were analyzed alongside the identified taxa using correlation-based analyses. Results Microbial diversity was significantly lower in sickle cell disease leg ulcers compared to intact skin. Additionally, leukocytes and mean corpuscular volume were statistically associated with the relative abundance of bacteria of the genera Pseudomonas and Aeromonas. Staphylococcus spp. was the predominant genus identified in leg ulcers and was negatively associated with Pseudomonas spp., reflecting a dysbiotic microbial profile characterized by taxa commonly associated with chronic wounds. Conclusions The observed associations between bacterial taxa and laboratory parameters are exploratory, do not imply causality, and contribute to the characterization of the microbial ecology of sickle cell disease leg ulcers.

items.abstract: Antibiotic residues in waste activated sludge (WAS) may disrupt anaerobic carbon conversion, yet how phenicol antibiotics redistribute carbon between acidogenesis and methanogenesis remains unclear. At 10 mg/g TSS, methane production decreased by 63.2% while VFAs reached 131-fold the control. This functional decoupling was underpinned by microbial fates: hydrolytic-acidogenic bacteria were largely retained or enriched, whereas methanogenic archaea and syntrophic bacteria were severely depleted. Concurrently, bacteria-archaea ecological networks underwent reorganization, with positive correlations partially rebounding at moderate TAP exposure. The network collapsed at high TAP, with substantial loss of connector taxa mediating inter-module metabolite exchange. Metagenomic evidence further revealed a functional asymmetry: genes involved in substrate transport and amino acid metabolism were maintained or showed increased relative abundance, while methanogenic genes and AI-2-associated communication genes exhibited decreased relative abundance. PLS-PM revealed that TAP was positively associated with the acidogenic bacterial community (β = 0.960) but negatively with methanogenic potential (β = -0.998). Accordingly, the methane share dropped from 98.7% to 18.1%, while VFAs increased to 81.9% of the COD-equivalent product pool. This work advances the understanding of antibiotic-driven functional imbalance and carbon flux redirection in sludge anaerobic digestion, providing a mechanistic basis for managing antibiotic-laden sludge prior to energy recovery.

items.title: Weak dispersal and landscape size inevitably promote local biodiversity in heterogeneous metacommunities of competing species.
items.abstract: We provide a general theoretical explanation for a longstanding result in spatial ecology: weak dispersal among habitat patches promotes local species richness. Using analytical approximations of spatial Lotka-Volterra competition models, we show that local species persistence in heterogeneous landscapes can be expressed as the balance between the total density across patches and the local exclusion rate. We further demonstrate that local multispecies coexistence is governed by the feasibility domain, linking spatial coexistence to a structural property of nonspatial competitive systems. Together, these results explain why weak dispersal increases local species richness and why this effect strengthens with the number of available patches, i.e., landscape size. We test these predictions using numerical simulations and find that the theory breaks down only when both dispersal and competitive interactions are very strong, in which case dispersal has a unimodal effect on coexistence. In contrast, landscape size retains a positive effect on coexistence whenever an effect is detectable. We then apply the theory to long-term data from a natural metacommunity of microcrustaceans. We detect strong competition among species and find no detectable effect of dispersal rate on local coexistence, whereas species co-occurrence increases with local landscape size, as predicted by theory. Together, our results identify how dispersal, interaction strength, and landscape size jointly regulate local species richness in competitive systems.

items.title: Global origins of tuna and billfish fisheries reveal the transition from coastal access to oceanic exploitation.
items.abstract: Ocean ecosystems have played a crucial role in people's lives around the world for millennia. However, questions persist about when, why, and how people first began removing biomass from offshore habitats and established fisheries in distant, oceanic environments. We explore the antiquity and evolution of tuna (Thunnini) and billfish (Istiophoridae/Xiphiidae) fisheries, two groups of fishes that occur around the world, are economically significant, and are ecologically important open ocean apex predators. The earliest archaeological evidence of fishing for tuna occurs ~44,000 years ago and billfish at ~10,000 years ago, with early fisheries for some tuna species appearing around the world by 3,000 to 1,000 years ago. Most early fisheries are in areas where tunas and billfishes could be accessed relatively close to shore (e.g., submarine canyons) and/or where these fishes may come inshore seasonally or during warm ocean events. Early tuna and billfish fisheries were often linked to ceremony/ritual, alongside advances in maritime technologies. With few exceptions, sustained and intensive commercial exploitation of pelagic predators in offshore and oceanic habitats is a late development in the human past, occurring primarily during the last 200 y. Our findings document a long-term continuum of human interactions with global marine ecosystems spanning thousands of years, including significant differences between the timing and pathways by which people became dominant ecological drivers in nearshore compared to offshore/oceanic ecosystems.

items.title: Ten simple rules for developing a reporting appraisal tool.
items.abstract: In an ideal world, authors would report clearly and transparently exactly what they conducted. In reality, reporting is often incomplete, and key elements of research conduct are frequently missing from manuscripts. Reporting guidelines were developed to address this problem by helping authors identify what should be reported. These guidelines have been highly valuable for authors, but they are not well suited for appraising reporting during peer review or editorial assessment despite common use. This is because authors and appraisers have different needs: authors require a comprehensive guide for writing, whereas appraisers need a tool that is concise, repeatable, and easy to use. We therefore propose the development of reporting appraisal tools: operationalised tools designed specifically to assess whether a paper has reported the minimum essential elements of a study. To support their development, we present 10 simple rules.

items.title: Physical origins of speed control in swimming fishes.
items.abstract: The linear relationship between tail-beat frequency and swimming speed in fish, first described by Bainbridge in 1958, has since been confirmed in species as disparate as eels and tuna. Dimensional scaling has explained why linearity should emerge at high Reynolds numbers, but the frequency-speed relationship itself has remained empirical, with no physical framework describing its behavior across swimming regimes, and no account of what sets the two quantities that define it: the distance covered per tail beat and the frequency below which forward motion supposedly ceases. Here, we derive a relationship from a balance of fin thrust, generated by a leading-edge vortex, and drag due to the boundary layer on the body. This framework yields an explicit expression for speed in terms of midline kinematics and body morphology. This formulation shows that the maximum stride length is set by the undulatory wavelength and the tail-beat phase offset, rather than by the conventional scaling metric of body length, and that no minimum frequency is required for forward motion. The model reproduces kinematic measurements from freely swimming glass catfish, published simulations, and Bainbridge's original data. Without recalibration, it predicts the results of independent simulations spanning wide variations in wavelength, phase offset, and morphology to within ten percent. Linear scaling is thus one asymptotic limit of a more general propulsive relationship linking morphology and body-wave kinematics to swimming speed in fishes and bioinspired vehicles, where the body waveform, rather than the actuation frequency, emerges as the variable that sets performance.

items.title: Recovering Accuracy From Miscalibrated Item Banks: Scoring Error Is Fixable, Selection Error Is Not.
items.abstract: Computerized adaptive testing (CAT) depends on accurately calibrated item banks, but in practice, the item parameters governing deployment of the item banks are often based on small pilot samples, transported across populations, or assigned placeholder values pending proper calibration. Throughout, miscalibration is modeled in the item difficulty parameters, with discriminations held at their true values. We decompose the impact of miscalibration on subsequent ability estimates into two components: item selection error and scoring error. While selection error is not recoverable, rescoring using better calibrations, and without any additional testing burden, can potentially provide a post hoc fix to scoring errors. In a simulation study, we find that rescoring substantially reduces root mean squared error, with scoring error accounting for 86% to 96% of miscalibration-attributable error. In Study 2, we apply this framework to data from 2,657 children (ages 5-12) assessed across three pilot sites in the LEVANTE project. Using identical scoring methods with old versus new item parameters, we found that rescoring shifted scores substantially and reordered children's relative standing; external validation confirms the rescored estimates are better, not just different. Low-ability and younger children are disproportionately affected by rescoring, underscoring the equity implications. These results highlight the utility of rescoring for any CAT using early-stage, transported, or AI-generated item parameters, and how rescoring can enable rapid deployment of assessments to new populations.

items.title: Comparison of visual tasks for assessing attentional bias in cannabis users and non-users.
items.abstract: Attentional bias toward substance-related cues is a key feature of addiction and may contribute to the continued use of substances, such as cannabis. However, the sensitivity of different paradigms for detecting this bias remains underexplored. This study compared three visual attentional bias paradigms: dot probe (DP), eye movement (EM), and MouseView.js (MV) in detecting cannabis-related attentional biases among cannabis users and non-users. Thirty-one participants (i.e., 16 users and 15 non-users) completed all measures: DP (reaction time to probes replacing cannabis or neutral stimuli), EM (measured via eye-tracking), and MV (cursor-based dwell time). Linear mixed-effects models examined the effects of stimulus type, group, craving, and cannabis use severity. The EM and MV tasks revealed significant stimulus effects, with non-users showing greater attention to neutral images, while cannabis users exhibited more evenly distributed attention across stimuli. In the EM task, a significant stimulus × severity interaction indicated reduced attentional differentiation with increased cannabis use severity. MV results followed a similar, but less precise pattern. In contrast, the DP task showed minimal group or interaction effects and lacked sensitivity to detect attentional differences. These findings suggest that EM-based measures are more sensitive for detecting cannabis-related attentional biases, particularly when accounting for cannabis use severity. MV showed some alignment with EM patterns but demonstrated weaker effects. The DP task, despite its widespread use, may be insufficient for capturing cannabis-related attentional differences. Results highlight the importance of task selection in attentional bias research and the potential influence of individual differences in cannabis use severity.

items.title: No effect of transcranial direct current stimulation on brain age during cognitive behavioral therapy for major depressive disorder: secondary results from a randomized, double-blind, sham-controlled trial.
items.abstract: Major depressive disorder (MDD) has previously been associated with accelerated brain ageing, a feature reported to remain unchanged after antidepressant pharmacotherapy. We conducted a secondary analysis of a randomized trial augmenting cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), a long-established first-line treatment for depression, with active or sham transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS), a newer neuromodulatory approach that has received FDA approval for MDD in at-home device format. We calculated the brain-predicted age difference (brain-PAD = predicted brain age - chronological age) in 38 unmedicated patients with MDD before and after treatment, using a model trained on anatomical MRI scans from N = 3377 healthy controls. Linear mixed-effects models tested change in brain-PAD and predicted brain age, adjusting for age and sex. The randomized comparison showed no evidence that active tDCS produced differential change in brain-PAD relative to sham (β = 0.85 years, 95% CI [-0.83, 2.53], p = .308, BF10 = 0.22). Contrary to our hypothesis, in the combined treated cohort (CBT ± tDCS), average change in brain-PAD was negligible (β = 0.01 years, 95% CI [-0.82, 0.84], p = .985, BF10 = 0.13), despite symptomatic improvement on the HAM-D. Baseline brain-PAD also did not differ among MDD patients, healthy controls, and first-degree relatives after adjustment for age and sex (F(2,93) = 1.31, p = .276, BF10 = 0.04). These findings suggest that short-term depression improvement and adjunctive tDCS were not accompanied by detectable changes in MRI-derived brain age or brain-PAD. However, our relatively young patients, small sample size, wide confidence intervals, limited local calibration, and unmeasured candidate moderators of the brain age constrain definitive conclusions. Larger, longer, and biologically stratified trials are needed to determine whether brain age biomarkers are modifiable and useful tools in clinical practice.

items.title: Assessing Acceptance in Turkish Fathers of Children with Intellectual Disabilities: A Two-Phase Protocol.
items.abstract: Fathers of children with intellectual disabilities remain underrepresented in disability and family research and in parent-support interventions. This article presents a two-phase protocol for developing the Fathers' Acceptance of Children with Special Needs Scale (FACSNS) and evaluating a manualized psychoeducational program for fathers in Türkiye. Phase 1 involved the development and psychometric validation of the FACSNS using data from 220 fathers of children with moderate or severe intellectual disabilities. Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses supported a three-factor structure comprising behavioral, internal, and emotional acceptance. The scale accounted for 71.25% of the total variance and demonstrated high internal consistency (α = 0.917). Phase 2 evaluated the effects of a six-week cognitive-behavioral psychoeducational program on fathers' acceptance of their children with intellectual disabilities. A quasi-experimental pretest, post-test, and follow-up design was used with an experimental group (n = 20) and a control group (n = 20). Repeated-measures analyses showed greater increases in FACSNS scores in the experimental group than in the control group across the three acceptance dimensions, and post-test scores were broadly maintained at follow-up. Because group allocation was not randomized, the findings indicate an association between program participation and improved paternal acceptance, not definitive causal evidence. The protocol may support replication, adaptation, and further validation of father-inclusive family-support programs.

items.title: Impact of a multifaceted intervention programme on antibiotic prescribing in out-of-hours primary care in five European countries: secondary analyses of the HAPPY PATIENT project.
items.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance is a major global health threat, driven mainly by excessive and inappropriate antibiotic use. As most antibiotics are prescribed outside hospitals, primary care measures are crucial for reducing use. The study aimed to investigate diagnostic coding and antibiotic prescribing for respiratory tract (RTI) and urinary tract (UTI) infections treated in out-of-hours clinics before and after a multifaceted intervention. Audit and feedback with analyses of prescription data from five out-of-hours clinics in Europe before and after a multifaceted intervention. The intervention consisted of an audit with reports and feedback to the prescriber, participation in workshops, communication and e-learning courses, and distribution of information materials to patients. A total of 67 physicians recorded 1786 cases in the first period and 1820 in the second. Common cold/influenza was the most frequent diagnosis, increasing from 19.4% (95% CI 18-21) in the first to 28.7% (95% CI 27-31) in the second period. COVID-19 declined by 65.7% (P < 0.001), while pharyngotonsillitis increased by 31.7% (P = 0.001). The intervention did not alter the overall antibiotic prescribing rate for RTIs (49.3% versus 48.7%, P = 0.748), and more than three-quarters of RTI prescriptions were judged unnecessary or inappropriate. For UTIs, the use of first-line antibiotics increased significantly from 70.0% to 79.5% (P = 0.027). The study provided important insights into which RTIs are potentially inappropriately treated with antibiotics, although the intervention did not produce a statistically significant reduction in antibiotic prescribing. Positively, the use of first-line antibiotics for UTIs increased significantly.

items.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
items.abstract: Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children. We developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy-electroencephalography (fNIRS-EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning. Thirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS-EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning. Repeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha-beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning. Combining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.

items.title: Brain-Aligned Multimodal LLMs for Social and Emotional Understanding of Cartoon Movies
items.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) offer scalable annotations of social and affective content, but their temporal agreement with human judgments and neural predictive value require further evaluation. We compared diffusion-based and autoregressive MLLMs with continuous human Theory of Mind (ToM) and affective valence ratings across three short cartoon movies. Behavioral analyses assessed temporally aligned Pearson correlations, rating distributions, and the effects of preceding scene descriptions. Ratings from each source were separately used in subject-specific regression models to predict regional fMRI responses. Model ratings captured aspects of human temporal variation despite systematic distributional differences, with generally stronger alignment for valence than ToM. Preceding context improved alignment in some conditions, depending on the model and movie. In \emph{The Present}, more regions showed significant encoding for MLLM ratings than for human ratings, whereas effects were more limited in the other movies. Spatial overlap across rating sources occurred mainly among MLLMs; overlap between human and model ratings was limited and involved primarily visual, dorsal-attention, and posterior default-mode regions. These findings support MLLMs as scalable tools for generating brain-predictive annotations of social and emotional content, while highlighting systematic rating differences and model- and stimulus-dependent alignment with human judgments.

items.title: Alignment of visual brain encoding models with individual perceptual similarity judgments
items.abstract: Encoding models that predict brain activation responses to images have traditionally been trained to maximize accuracy when predicting observed brain data. However, their internal representations may not reflect individual human perception. In this work, we investigate whether we can fine-tune brain encoding models to better align their representations with individuals' similarity judgments. Using similarity judgments of 100 images from 8 participants in the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we adapt a generic human similarity judgment model (DreamSim) separately for each participant to obtain personalized perceptual similarity models. These models are then used to obtain subject-specific similarity structure across images in their encoding model training sets. We fine-tune each participant's baseline encoder in two conditions, aligning its representations with either generic or personalized similarity judgments, with the same initialization and objective. We find that baseline brain encoders reflect within-subject perceptual similarity more strongly than measured fMRI responses and preserve intersubject correlations present in measured fMRI, but fail to reflect those of human perceptual similarity judgments. Fine-tuning with generic, population-level perceptual similarity information results in better alignment with human judgments than baseline encoders, but these models still fail to capture intersubject correlations of human judgments. However, fine-tuning with personalized perceptual similarity information results in models that are the most aligned with human perceptual similarity judgments and also reflect intersubject correlations of human judgments. Our framework provides an approach for bootstrapping human similarity judgment data into more individualized, human-aligned brain encoding models of vision.

items.title: Upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in spiking neural networks
items.abstract: The input space of single-spike neural networks decomposes into causal pieces, and the number of causal pieces has been shown to provide a lower bound on the approximation error for some spiking neural networks. While this decomposition is applicable to a wide range of spiking neuron models, the limits of how many causal pieces can be realised by spiking neural networks are still unknown. In this work, we derive two complementary upper bounds on the number of causal pieces in feedforward single-spike neural networks. First, we establish a combinatorial bound given by the poly-Bernoulli numbers, which applies to a broad class of spiking neuron models. The bound is of order $e^{2(L-1)N\log N+\mathcal{O}(N)}$, with network depth $L$ and maximum layer width $N$. Second, for a specific set of neuron models, we derive a bound based on hyperplane arrangements. Applying the latter framework, we obtain bounds of order $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{(4L-3)(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with exponential synapses and the ReLU-type spike response model, and $\mathcal{O}\!\left(N^{L(N_0-1)}\right)$ for the leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$δ$ synapses, where $N_0$ is the input dimension. For the non-leaky integrate-and-fire model with Dirac-$δ$ synapses, additional temporal structure allows us to sharpen the general combinatorial bound to one that depends only on $N_0$, independently of the network depth and widths.

items.title: Mutual Information in High-Dimensional Neural Coding
items.abstract: Estimating mutual information in large neural populations is limited by the exponential growth of possible neural response patterns. Here we apply a Monte Carlo framework to make this problem tractable by sampling from a conditionally independent population model fit from single-neuron responses. The estimator accurately recovers analytical ground truth, corrects finite-data bias, and scales to empirical recordings containing 100 to 10,000 neurons from visual cortex, hippocampus, and retina. Across systems, stimulus uncertainty decays exponentially with population size, revealing a simple scaling law for high-dimensional neural codes.

items.title: Transferable conditional brain charts link cortico-subcortical structure to Alzheimer's disease progression
items.abstract: Normative models chart how brain measures vary across the lifespan, expressing each individual as a deviation from a healthy reference. However, most regional models of cortical thickness disregard dependencies between cortical and subcortical anatomy, and transferring them to a new site typically requires retraining or a recalibration of location and scale alone. We condition lifespan norms of cortical thickness on subcortical volume, such that each deviation indicates whether an individual's cortex lies within the healthy range given their subcortical anatomy, and make them transferable. In 21,351 healthy individuals from 216 sites, conditioning on ten subcortical structures improved out-of-sample prediction on average, most for the amygdala and hippocampus. Refitting only the intercepts of all four distributional parameters on about 20 healthy individuals, as implemented in our open-source package NormGAMLSS, calibrated most of six unseen sites without retraining, for base and conditional models. In the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, global deviation and structural dissociation (the reduction in mean absolute deviation under conditioning) predicted conversion to mild cognitive impairment and dementia beyond the Clinical Dementia Rating and dissociation added beyond global deviation for dementia, even at similar clinically recorded impairment. Conditional norms thus provide relevant, individual-level information.

items.title: Neural Computation Runs on Dissipative Structures Under Cyclic Calibration: A Systems Perspective on Sleep
items.abstract: Biological function operates far from thermodynamic equilibrium, sustained by metastable structures that continuously cycle through synthesis, function execution, and degradation--consuming energy and exporting entropy in the process. Neural computation exemplifies this dissipative organization, relying on low-entropy structures engaged in dynamic processes that define key information transfer and processing parameters such as gain, threshold, and integration time. This perspective proposes that sleep serves as a systemic recalibration phase required to reset crucial signaling parameters that drift during dissipative processing. During wakefulness, neural activity progressively consumes and disrupts the organization of the very substrate from which it emerges, leading to parameter drift and reduced computational precision. Sleep maintains computational accuracy across activity cycles by recalibrating function-structure coupling--that is, by counterbalancing entropic drift. Rather than explaining the experimentally observed sleep need through homeostatic regulation of unknown physiological variables, this perspective reframes it as an emergent property of neural computation under thermodynamic constraints.

items.title: Language Models Share a Readout Bottleneck in Working Memory
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) reproduce a human working-memory signature on the N-back task: performance declines as memory load N increases, and errors concentrate on lures, items that repeat the current stimulus at a neighboring but incorrect serial position. We ask whether this shared behavioral signature reflects a shared mechanism. The literature offers two candidate accounts. On a precision account, softmax attention cannot concentrate its weight on the item N positions back, so adjacent items are retrieved instead. On an interference account, attention selects the correct item, but the content of competing items corrupts the decision. We dissociate these accounts in 15 pretrained LLMs from three families (70 million to 14 billion parameters) and in minimal transformers trained from scratch. In all three families, the attention heads that carry the task attend to the target on most missed matches. Linear probes decode near-perfectly whether a matching letter occurred at the target or at a lure position, even on trials where the model false-alarms to the lure, although its own decisions barely distinguish the two. Sharpening attention yields negligible gains, whereas suppressing the letter identity of non-target items improves sensitivity (d') in nearly all model-by-load conditions. In larger models the task is spread over more heads, and removing interference helps more. In minimal transformers, precision limits a single attention layer, but a second layer removes this constraint. The working-memory limit of LLMs therefore lies in reading items out under interference rather than in locating them, consistent with interference accounts of human working memory.

items.title: Alignment of visual brain encoding models with individual perceptual similarity judgments
items.abstract: Encoding models that predict brain activation responses to images have traditionally been trained to maximize accuracy when predicting observed brain data. However, their internal representations may not reflect individual human perception. In this work, we investigate whether we can fine-tune brain encoding models to better align their representations with individuals' similarity judgments. Using similarity judgments of 100 images from 8 participants in the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD), we adapt a generic human similarity judgment model (DreamSim) separately for each participant to obtain personalized perceptual similarity models. These models are then used to obtain subject-specific similarity structure across images in their encoding model training sets. We fine-tune each participant's baseline encoder in two conditions, aligning its representations with either generic or personalized similarity judgments, with the same initialization and objective. We find that baseline brain encoders reflect within-subject perceptual similarity more strongly than measured fMRI responses and preserve intersubject correlations present in measured fMRI, but fail to reflect those of human perceptual similarity judgments. Fine-tuning with generic, population-level perceptual similarity information results in better alignment with human judgments than baseline encoders, but these models still fail to capture intersubject correlations of human judgments. However, fine-tuning with personalized perceptual similarity information results in models that are the most aligned with human perceptual similarity judgments and also reflect intersubject correlations of human judgments. Our framework provides an approach for bootstrapping human similarity judgment data into more individualized, human-aligned brain encoding models of vision.

items.title: Statistical Mechanics of Spike Trains: Self-Consistent Activity Ensembles and Phase Transitions
items.abstract: We introduce a statistical-mechanical framework for spiking neuronal systems in which entire spike trains, defined as spatiotemporal configurations of discrete events, are treated as microstates of the system. Instead of modeling explicit network dynamics, we construct an ensemble over complete spike histories and assign to each configuration an effective energy functional that quantifies its consistency with intrinsic synaptic interactions. This formulation leads to a Boltzmann-like distribution over spike configurations, where an effective temperature captures the influence of external inputs acting as a stochastic drive. Macroscopic states are described in terms of coarse-grained observables, such as population firing-rate densities, and arise from a competition between energetic contributions favoring interaction-consistent spike patterns and entropic contributions favoring spatio-temporal disorder. Within this framework, we primarily characterize the transition between oscillatory and non-oscillatory activity. The non-oscillatory regime contains both broadly distributed, approximately uniform states and temporally localized collapsed states, whereas the oscillatory regime is characterized by repeated activity peaks. These regimes are diagnosed using order parameters derived from the population spike-rate density, including its entropy, temporal localization measures, and autocorrelation-based indicators. To complement the analytical treatment, we perform Monte Carlo simulations that sample the ensemble of admissible spike configurations using a Metropolis-Hastings scheme defined directly on spike trains. The simulations reveal the emergence of the predicted macroscopic regimes and provide a direct sampling-based probe of the free-energy landscape.

items.title: Cross-subject decoding of imagined speech from scalp EEG: a leakage-controlled evaluation on three public corpora
items.abstract: Objective. A decoder of imagined speech that works for a new user without calibration would make a non-invasive speech interface practical. We tested whether imagined-speech content recorded with scalp electroencephalography (EEG) transfers across people, and examined why accuracy within a single person remains low. Approach. We analyzed three public corpora, ds003626, KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion and reports exact binomial thresholds, group tests and bootstrap confidence intervals. We trained decoders on each participant and tested them on every other, compared representational geometry across participants without a classifier, applied subject-level alignment, and tested five explanations for the within-subject ceiling. Main results. Across 482 ordered pairs of participants, no pair survived correction for multiple comparisons; mean pair-transfer accuracy lay within 0.006 of chance on every corpus, while every within-subject reference lay above it. Imagery against pre-stimulus rest generalized at about 0.61 after artifact and elapsed-time controls, but its decoder labelled the interval preceding imagery as imagery as often as imagery itself, so the contrast reflects a post-stimulus state, not imagery. Within subject, only the competition corpus decoded above threshold for every participant (0.3147; chance 0.200); syllable count explained little of this, but its frequency profile failed an artifact audit. Significance. In these corpora, imagined-speech content did not transfer between people through any representation we examined. Trial count per class was the only variable that ordered the corpora, which favors larger single-condition datasets over further model development.

items.title: How large an effect would we have seen? Positive controls, detection floors and dataset pitfalls in scalp-EEG speech decoding
items.abstract: Objective. Studies that decode imagined speech from scalp electroencephalography (EEG) commonly validate their pipelines with a positive control, usually overt speech, and report null results without stating what effect size the pipeline could have detected. Approach. Using ds003626 ("Thinking out loud"), KaraOne and Track 3 of the 2020 International Brain-Computer Interface Competition, we audited decoding of overt speech, articulator preparation and imagined speech with artifact-channel subsets, band-limited decoding and trial selection, under a protocol that enforces split integrity by assertion. We injected class-dependent effects of known amplitude into the real recordings to measure the detection floor of five decoder families, and we checked the ds003626 labels against the dataset's acquisition protocol. Main results. On ds003626, two lip electrodes decoded overt speech at 0.7430 and the eight external channels at 0.7068, against 0.4231 for the 128-channel scalp montage, and no decodable signal survived in the 8-30 Hz band. On the other two corpora, within-subject accuracy rose monotonically with frequency into the range dominated by muscle activity. Band-power logistic regression detected an injected 8-30 Hz desynchronization of 0.54 uV under a criterion fixed in advance, whereas a compact convolutional network (EEGNet) detected nothing within subject up to 4.31 uV. In ds003626, the condition codes are the reverse of the intuitive reading, the class encoding changed between public releases, and condition is a deterministic function of time within each session. Significance. In these corpora the overt-speech positive control is dominated by myogenic signal and cannot validate a decoding pipeline. We recommend that speech-decoding studies report band-limited and artifact-channel accuracy, the direction of accuracy across frequency, and a measured detection floor.

items.title: Awakening as a Trait-Level Transformation of Consciousness
items.abstract: Awakening is reported across contemplative traditions yet remains poorly defined in science, where it is often conflated with transient states induced by meditation or psychedelics, obscuring its significance for theories of consciousness and cognitive architecture. We treat awakening as a functional construct capturing convergence across Hindu and Buddhist sources, phenomenological and psychometric findings, and neuroimaging evidence. Synthesizing these literatures, we find convergent evidence for reorganization across dimensions including self-related processing, affective reactivity, and temporal structure, while exposing limits of paradigms for detecting trait-level change. We argue that awakening is best understood not as a transient state but as a trait-level reorganization of experience, centered on a reduction in identification with mental contents rather than the acquisition of new content. To account for this contentless transformation, we propose the enactive-dereification model (EDM), which treats training and awakening as graded differences along a dereification gradient, from a reified to a relational mode of experience. We offer an operational definition that distinguishes awakening from state-dependent experiences and psychopathology, emphasizing dynamical flexibility and stabilization of a dereified mode. The framework yields falsifiable predictions linking independently assessed trait transformation to large-scale neural dynamics and provides a basis for distinguishing adaptive contemplative change from pathological ego-dissolution.

items.title: Two dissociable axes of brain hierarchical dynamics track universal and population-specific effects of mindfulness
items.abstract: How mental training reshapes the temporal architecture of large-scale brain dynamics and how these mechanisms differ between healthy and clinically vulnerable populations remains poorly understood. Time-averaged neural measures collapse the multi-scale nature of brain activity, obscuring the dynamic processes through which behavioural interventions reorganise hierarchical brain function. Here, applying a sliding-window Temporal Irreversibility Index to source-reconstructed EEG across three complementary cohorts (n = 141), we decompose hierarchical brain trajectories into three orthogonal temporal descriptors and uncover two dissociable, mechanistically interpretable axes of intervention-induced plasticity. Cumulative meditation practice drives a universal, pan-cerebral reduction in the exploratory breadth of hierarchical dynamics, tracking dose-dependently with lifetime hours of practice. Temporal persistence is bidirectionally tuned by 8-week mindfulness-based interventions in a population-specific way: reduced in healthy meditators but increased in trauma-exposed individuals, revealing that comparable MBI protocols engage qualitatively distinct network mechanisms depending on baseline clinical status. A joint Hidden Markov Model further links these dynamical shifts to distinct microstate substrates, and longitudinal changes selectively track improvements in a single facet of mindfulness, attentional presence in daily life. Together, these findings establish a mechanistic framework for how behavioural training reorganises non-equilibrium brain dynamics, with direct implications for tailoring mindfulness-based interventions to individual clinical profiles.

items.title: Automating Observable Closure Analysis for Graph Transformation Models with MolFoundry
items.abstract: Graph transformations model changing systems, with applications in software, biology and chemistry, among others. We introduce MolFoundry, a graph transformation framework, and present a workflow for observable analysis that tracks the dynamics of local patterns through rule composition. Analysing rule compositions avoids the need to enumerate a potentially infinite state space. Building on rule-algebraic stochastic rewriting, MolFoundry's kernel composes rules with nested application conditions, including missing-edge constraints. Given rules, rates and query patterns, the algorithms iteratively identify auxiliary pattern counts and search for closure. Using exact counting identities supplied by graph-family backends, successful searches yield closed ordinary differential equations for average counts or, with justified individual jumps, finite event models describing joint changes and rates. We evaluate conditional composition and automated discovery of auxiliary observables against published calculations and independent rule application. Applications to aldol addition, copolymerization and chlorination show how the framework yields quantitative predictions directly from molecular graph rules.

items.title: Semantic Alignment of EEG and Text: A Contrastive Learning Framework for Decoding Imagined Speech
items.abstract: Imagined speech decoding from EEG offers a promising route toward naturalistic brain-computer interfaces. Traditional closed-set classifiers treat semantic categories as independent labels and do not explicitly exploit relationships among linguistic intents, limiting output flexibility. We adapt a multimodal contrastive learning framework to imagined speech, aligning EEG trials with language representations in the embedding space of a frozen pretrained text encoder. An EEG encoder is trained with a composite objective combining semantically reweighted EEG-sentence alignment and text-prototype-based class discrimination, encouraging semantic structure while preserving separability among 39 intent categories. We evaluate the approach on the Chisco imagined speech dataset across five subjects, reporting Top-k accuracy, macro-F1, and balanced pairwise matching accuracy (2v2). We also investigate maximum EEG-text cosine similarity (MaxCosine) as an intrinsic indicator of decoding reliability and probe semantic structure beyond category labels using five evaluation-time semantic axes and a qualitative Semantic Gallery Probe (SGP) with previously unseen candidate sentences. The contrastive framework achieved decoding performance comparable to a task-optimized closed-set classifier while mapping EEG into a frozen language embedding space. MaxCosine identified subsets of held-out trials with higher Top-1 and Top-5 accuracy across subjects. Evaluation-time semantic axes showed mean agreement above the 50% chance reference across all five dimensions, and the SGP qualitatively illustrated direct comparison with unseen candidate sentences. Together, these findings suggest that EEG-language alignment can retain comparable fixed-intent decoding while supporting similarity-based retrieval, intrinsic reliability ranking, and evaluation of broader semantic structure.

items.title: EEG Correlates of Verbal and Perceptual Reasoning
items.abstract: Identifying the neural underpinnings of intelligence is one of the major goals of modern intelligence research. However, few imaging studies explore the high extremes of intelligence, and most use only a single composite IQ score. This study used quantitative EEG recordings to investigate correlations between the EEG variables of individual alpha peak frequency, relative power, and coherence, and scores on verbal and perceptual reasoning tests in participants with IQs from the low-average to exceptionally gifted ranges. Overall, the results did not reveal any pattern of significant relationships between these EEG measures and the two psychometric tests. Since this study had only a small sample, heavily skewed towards the high-IQ end of the scale, no definitive conclusions about the EEG measures and verbal and perceptual reasoning can be drawn. Nevertheless, it reveals many opportunities for further research, and suggestions are made for progressing this topic in the future.

items.title: Reciprocity coordinates a three-way trade-off in recurrent neural circuits
items.abstract: Biological neural circuits contain both unidirectional and reciprocal connections, but how reciprocity affects circuit computation remains unclear. We varied reciprocity \r{ho} across 21 levels in recurrent-network simulations while holding network size, connection density, and directed-edge count fixed. Low-reciprocity networks produced more diverse stimulus-driven activity and performed better on four continuous-input tasks, whereas higher reciprocity generally improved performance on three delayed-memory tasks. Increasing reciprocity reduced online memory capacity and accelerated recovery from perturbations. A post-cue noise experiment showed that higher reciprocity suppressed internal noise propagation but made cue-evoked states less distinguishable, and component matching separated the contributions of cue separation and within-cue dispersion to readout robustness. Within this ensemble, reciprocity thus mediates a three-way trade-off among representational capacity, local stability, and task-state separability: higher reciprocity lowers capacity, strengthens stability, and compresses separability. Whether it improves behaviour depends on whether the stability gain outweighs the lost separation between task states. Connectome and microcircuit datasets from five species showed intermediate reciprocity, while reciprocity varied substantially across adult Drosophila brain regions, providing compatible structural context and motivating circuit-specific functional tests.

items.title: How Long Is the Coast of a Neuron? Resolution-Dependent Interaction Order and Computational Capacity
items.abstract: Mandlebrot's coastline paradox reframes measurement as a joint property of an object and its ruler. Here we ask how observational resolution shapes the apparent structure of neural computation. We introduce a scale-indexed decomposition that separates the predictive information captured by direct dependencies from the residual outside that model family. Exact constructions show that projection can convert higher-order dependence into pairwise structure. Projection can increase the direct fraction of surviving information even as total predictive information decreases. A schematic branch-to-soma cascade grounds these effects in local coincidence detection, saturating integration and somatic mixing. Resolving organized nonlinear subunits improves approximation and raises effective representational rank. In a nested hierarchy, these gains occur without increasing information about the target. This distinction separates information availability from access by a restricted readout. A point-neuron or direct population model therefore establishes an effective description at a specified scale. It does not uniquely identify the finer computation that generated the observed relation. Which resolution is adequate depends on the observable and perturbation of interest.

items.title: Biodiversity tourism in production-conservation landscapes: stakeholder perspectives on high conservation value areas in oil palm plantations
items.abstract: Purpose Conservation spaces embedded within the production landscapes such as high conservation value (HCV) areas in oil palm plantations have traditionally been managed for biodiversity conservation, yet their potential as sites for biodiversity tourism remains underexplored. They are mostly approached as compliance requirements to meet sustainability certification standards. To address this overlooked opportunity, this study explores stakeholder perceptions of biodiversity tourism opportunities within HCV areas. Design/methodology/approach Employing qualitative interpretive design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with 24 informants (plantation managers, local governments, communities and tourism operators). Data were analysed inductively using the Gioia methodology. Findings Three interrelated dimensions emerged: socio-economic value creation for communities, ecological stewardship and conservation awareness and corporate legitimacy and innovation for plantation companies. The findings demonstrate that biodiversity tourism is interpreted differently by stakeholder groups according to their institutional responsibilities, conservation objectives and livelihood priorities. Challenges persist, including limited infrastructure, lack of governance frameworks and risks of ecological disturbance. Originality/value The study contributes a stakeholder-based conceptual understanding of biodiversity tourism within production-conservation landscapes, extending discussions of multifunctional landscapes beyond conventional protected areas. Through the perspectives of multi-stakeholders, this study highlights how HCV areas are being reinterpreted and negotiated as socio-ecological biodiversity tourism destinations, instead of positioning the areas solely as conservation compliance zones. This study also shows how nature-based tourism can evolve through the intersection of conservation, community interests and corporate sustainability strategies.

items.title: Dhikr and Cognitive Neuroscience
items.abstract: The increasing prevalence of anxiety and psychological distress in the post-pandemic era has intensified interest in spiritual and religious sources of mental tranquility. Although previous studies have discussed the psychological and spiritual benefits of dhikr, the relationship between the Qur’anic concept of tranquility and its cognitive-neuroscientific mechanisms remains insufficiently explored through an integrated interdisciplinary framework. This study examines the relationship between dhikr and ṭuma’nīnah in Q.S. Al-Ra‘d [13]: 28 by integrating Qur’anic linguistic-semantic analysis, spiritual exegesis, and cognitive neuroscience. Using qualitative library research, the study analyzes the linguistic structure of the verse, examines interpretations of selected classical and modern mufassir, and reviews relevant findings from neuroscience and cognitive psychology. The findings show that ṭuma’nīnah is presented as a dynamic and continuous process, linguistically reflected in the verbal structure of taṭma’innu. Exegetically, dhikr involves not merely verbal repetition but the internalization of divine awareness within human consciousness. From a cognitive-neuroscientific perspective, repetitive religious and contemplative practices may support emotional regulation, reduce stress reactivity, and promote physiological relaxation. The novelty of this study lies in proposing an integrative framework connecting the linguistic meaning of ṭuma’nīnah, Qur’anic interpretations of dhikr, and contemporary cognitive-neuroscientific perspectives, contributing to an interdisciplinary understanding of Qur’anic spirituality in addressing contemporary psychological challenges.

items.title: Redirecting Correctional Education Implementation Towards Lowering Recidivism in Nigeria Society
items.abstract: Correctional education programme is purposively for rehabilitation, reformation and reintegration of prison inmates all over the world. This study examined how to redirect correctional education programme implementation towards lowering recidivism in Nigeria Society. Three research questions and objectives guided this study. The study was a qualitative survey carried out in Portharcourt prison. 122 incarcerated inmates in Portharcourt correctional service who have benefited and are benefiting from different Formal and Non-Formal rehabilitation education programmes was the population of the study, all the 122 inmates were sampled based on total enumeration sampling technique. A validated interview schedule was utilized for data collection. Data collected was thematically transcribed. Findings revealed that providers of the correctional education programmes in Portharcourt correctional service do not involve the inmates (beneficiaries) in the selection of choice of programme type; the facilitator utilizes pedagogical approach instead of andragucal approach for facilitation. Also, freed inmates are stigmatized and this contributes to recidivism. Based on the findings, the researchers recommended among others that service provider of correctional programme should always give the inmates the opportunity to choose option of programme to be enrolled into because interest is a motivator for adult enrollment into adult educational programme; facilitators of the programmes should be trained on how to use andragogical approaches to foster learning.

items.title: Effects of cortisol time-scales in a model of emotion regulation
items.abstract: Stress reshapes cortico-limbic dynamics across multiple timescales, with important consequences for healthy and pathological arousal responses. We develop and analyze a Wilson-Cowan model of prefrontal-amygdala circuitry, incorporating excitatory and inhibitory populations involved in emotional regulation. The effects of stress cortisol are represented as history-dependent modulations of two stress-sensitive interactions: recurrent prefrontal excitation and inhibition of basolateral amygdala principal cells. Using numerical simulations and bifurcation analysis, we examine how this self-interacting system organizes transitions between stable activity and infra-slow oscillations, and how this structure changes with cortisol-related temporal memory. To distinguish the effects of memory temporal distribution from those of its timescale, we compare weak and strong Gamma kernels with a discrete-delay limit, representing progressively different ways in which past activity can influence current coupling. Introducing temporal memory reshapes the parameter region supporting oscillations and alters their persistence. Weak and strong Gamma kernels produce remarkably similar global dynamics, whereas the discrete-delay limit generates a substantially richer bifurcation structure, including quasiperiodic activity. Together, these results suggest that the dynamical effects of cortisol depend not only on the characteristic timescale of its action, but also on the shape of the temporal memory through which past neural activity influences the present. Different forms of temporal integration may provide a mechanism by which neural systems implement distinct functional dynamics, while changes in this integration could promote atypical or pathological rhythmic regimes.

items.title: Simulating Alzheimer's amyloid-like pathology on a fly central nervous system connectome
items.abstract: In Alzheimer's disease, the amount of pathology in the brain is an imperfect predictor of how much function is lost. Pathology leads to that loss through neural circuits, but these cannot be observed neuron by neuron in patients. This study therefore simulated the central nervous system of the adult male Drosophila melanogaster: 166,700 integrate-and-fire neurons wired by the MaleCNS connectome. The simulator reproduced a published fly brain model (rate correlation 0.9997). Three kinds of damage reported in amyloid-$β$ flies, a lowered spike threshold, synapse loss and neuron loss, were imposed with assumed magnitudes, and circuit responses were measured in 1,424 simulated flies. The number of neurons lost was a poor guide to the deficit, which depended partly on how many synaptic contacts went with them and whether they included input neurons or one command neuron. With the same 12% of neurons removed, odour-evoked whole-brain activity was 93%, 47% or 31% of the healthy value when damage fell on poorly connected, random or highly connected neurons; these flies lost 20%, 35% and 48% of contacts. When the contacts lost were equalised, the three groups differed less; whether the remaining difference reflects where the damage fell could not be established. In 48 flies, restoring only the contacts that surviving neurons had lost recovered 62% of the whole-brain deficit, and restoring the removed neurons 39%. In flies that had lost neurons delivering the odour, these accounted for about half the deficit due to neuron loss. One neuron could decide an outcome: all 66 flies that lost the giant fibre on the stimulated side, which commands escape, had a giant fibre rate below 100 Hz, against 1 of 254 that kept it. Whole-brain activity revealed damage at milder severity than the learning index, because it changed much relative to its variation between trials.

items.title: Deep learning-based virtual perturbation reveals increasing heterogeneity of gene regulatory responses with aging
items.abstract: A central hypothesis in aging biology proposes that the gradual accumulation of stochastic molecular damage drives transcriptional deregulation (TD), ultimately leading to functional decline. However, existing single-cell analyses largely rely on static expression measurements and provide limited resolution of how regulatory responses change at the level of individual cells. Here, we leverage DKO, a deep learning framework that predicts cell-specific virtual gene perturbation effects from unperturbed transcriptomes, capturing cell-to-cell differences in regulatory context without requiring a reconstructed gene regulatory network or matched perturbation data. Applying DKO to single-cell transcriptomic datasets from humans, mice, Drosophila, and C. elegans revealed that the transcriptional consequences of perturbing the same gene became increasingly heterogeneous across cells with age, indicating that gene regulatory responses become less consistent and more dependent on cellular context. Furthermore, we find that cells with higher somatic mutation burdens have greater knockout-response variability, linking accumulated molecular damage to regulatory inconsistency. Within the same cellular populations, higher impact variability was also associated with higher senescence scores, linking transcriptional dysregulation to senescence-associated states. Our findings identify a progressive loss of regulatory robustness at both the gene and cell levels as a conserved feature of aging, linking stochastic molecular damage to increasing heterogeneity in cellular regulatory responses.

items.title: Two Routes to Interoceptive Prioritisation: Dissociating Likelihood Precision and Preference Reweighting in Active Inference
items.abstract: An embodied agent must prioritise among competing bodily needs. In active inference, it can respond to an urgent need by increasing the precision of information about that need or by increasing its preference for outcomes that relieve it. We compare these two interventions, separately and together, in a foraging gridworld with three lethal needs, and ask how each changes survival, perception and the body model the agent learns. Precision sharpens interoceptive posteriors and improves survival. Preference reweighting keeps bodily states further from their lethal boundaries and changes the states from which the agent learns, so its learned model covers fewer need levels, with lower quality across all levels but slightly higher quality on the levels it visits. An experiment on 72 further layouts does not establish the predicted preference benefit on difficult layouts, but both interventions improve average survival there and their interaction is positive. Survival alone therefore gives an incomplete account of how a model prioritises needs and learns about its body.

items.title: The influence of decay in dynamic models of gene regulatory networks
items.abstract: We investigate the influence of decay rates on the dynamics of three-dimensional gene regulatory networks modeled by nonlinear differential equations with logistic sigmoidal regulatory functions. Particular attention is paid to the existence, location, and stability of equilibrium points in systems involving numerous interacting parameters. An explicit analytical representation of a central equilibrium is obtained under suitable relations between the regulatory weights, thresholds, and decay coefficients, allowing its location to be determined without solving the corresponding nonlinear algebraic system numerically. General formulas for the characteristic polynomial of the linearized system are derived, and spectral conditions for instability are established for several classes of regulatory interactions. We demonstrate how variations in decay rates can change the number and stability of equilibria, transform oscillatory dynamics, and influence the emergence or suppression of complicated attractors. The possibility of chaotic behavior is investigated through eigenvalue configurations, Lyapunov exponents, and the Kaplan-Yorke dimension. Numerical examples illustrate the sensitivity of the dynamics to decay parameters, including the suppression of previously observed chaotic behavior. The results provide an analytical framework for investigating equilibrium configurations, stability transitions, and complex dynamics in parametrized gene regulatory networks.

items.title: Sense-Making phase transition framework for Affect
items.abstract: Contemporary accounts of affect emphasize different perspectives, ranging from the regulation of bodily states in allostatic approaches to the relational and sense-making character stressed by enactive theories. Here, we show that affect can be made explicit within the sense-making phase transition framework previously introduced for the perception of an inner sensation. Within this same formal structure, each stable minimum of the sense-making potential defines an affective state: its position determines valence, while its depth determines arousal. Affect therefore is not introduced as an independent ingredient, but emerges as the associated state in the valence-arousal space, providing a link between allostatic and enactive approaches to affect. This formulation distinguishes valence intensity from arousal, allows for dominant and secondary affective states, and naturally accommodates mixed-valence configurations beyond a strictly bipolar description. Revisiting representative landscapes of the model, we show how neutral, uncertain, polarized, and mixed-valence regimes arise as a function of contextual sensory information, learned historical evaluation, and externally supplied information. We further show that the resulting valence-arousal relation provides a theoretical basis for the upper-open V-shaped organization discussed in the affect literature, while also opening a natural route toward a dynamical description of affect and emotions.
