items.title: Rewiring of adult neural networks - learning from structural plasticity across multiple scales
items.abstract: Synaptic connections are continuously formed and eliminated even in adult neuronal networks. This process - called structural plasticity - allows networks to change their topology to learn and adapt to their environment or compensate for lesions. Yet, in contrast to synaptic plasticity, structural plasticity is less well studied and understood. We here present the current state of knowledge as well as open problems in the field along three guiding questions: (1) What regulates structural plasticity in biological neural networks? (2) What are the functional consequences and advantages of structural plasticity in adult neural networks? (3) How can our understanding of structural plasticity be translated into clinical and technological applications? We argue that understanding structural plasticity is a problem involving multiple temporal and spatial scales. Solving this problem thus requires collaborative efforts of experimentalists, theoreticians as well as computational modelers, and has the potential for comprehensive neuroscientific insights that can guide the development of medical applications, artificial neural networks as well as neuromorphic computing.

items.title: Rethinking World Models for Biosignals
items.abstract: World models promise to learn how systems evolve and respond to actions, enabling simulation, planning and decision-making. Bringing this promise to biosignals requires more than accurate prediction of physiological recordings. We examine existing biosignal world models through two requirements for intervention use: a genuine action and evidence of its causal effect. We identify three fundamental bottlenecks rooted in physiology: Temporal Latency, the variable delay between an action and its observable effect; System Openness, the influence of drivers beyond the modelled intervention; and Endogenous Dynamics, the system's ongoing evolution without that intervention. Drawing on published evidence, we outline corresponding research directions and propose an Intervention-Effect Validation Checklist to guide evaluation. The aim is to help the biosignal community realise the core promise of world models by learning the latent mechanisms that govern physiological evolution and responses to interventions.

items.title: Collective Benefits and Efficiency in Coupled Echo State Networks
items.abstract: Simple aggregation of independent responses ("wisdom of crowds") generally improves collective performance through statistical facilitation, but interaction among members can sometimes hinder group outcomes. However, under certain circumstances, coordination studies show that interacting groups can outperform their individual members and nominal groups, and interaction can also be more efficient than independence. We present a reservoir computing model to investigate how interaction can enhance joint performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency. Echo state networks were trained independently to identify Japanese speakers from vowel recordings and tested jointly with and without coupled feedback. Model pairs reproduced the dyadic advantage reported by Bahrami et al. (2010) with interaction via pooled-feedback, but not when independent responses were aggregated together. Model dynamics revealed that interaction was beneficial whereas aggregated outputs were prone to diverging from runaway feedback over time. In terms of efficiency, larger groups of smaller interacting models outperformed smaller groups of larger models while equating for total amount of group computation. Our results offer a formal framework for explaining when and why interaction enhances collective intelligence.

items.title: The Psychology of False Confessions
items.abstract: False confessions represent one of the most significant challenges to the fairness and reliability of criminal justice systems, often leading to wrongful convictions and undermining public confidence in legal institutions. While confessions are traditionally regarded as compelling evidence of guilt, research has demonstrated that innocent individuals may admit to crimes they did not commit under the influence of various psychological, cognitive, emotional and situational factors. This paper examines the psychological mechanisms underlying false self-incrimination, with particular emphasis on the interaction between cognitive vulnerabilities, emotional distress, and interrogation practices. The analysis explores the principal categories of false confessions—voluntary, coerced-compliant and coerced-internalized—and discusses the individual characteristics that increase susceptibility, including youth, intellectual disabilities, mental disorders, heightened suggestibility, memory distortions and elevated stress levels. Particular attention is given to the impact of psychologically coercive interrogation techniques, prolonged questioning, authority pressure, fatigue and social isolation on decision-making processes. The paper further evaluates empirical findings from forensic psychology and criminology, highlighting the role of cognitive biases, compliance and emotional regulation in shaping confession behavior. From a legal perspective, the study emphasizes the importance of procedural safeguards designed to minimize the risk of false confessions, including mandatory electronic recording of interrogations, access to legal counsel, evidence-based interviewing methods and specialized protections for vulnerable suspects. By integrating psychological and legal perspectives, this paper contributes to a more comprehensive understanding of false confessions and underscores the need for investigative practices that prioritize both the effective administration of justice and the protection of fundamental human rights.

items.title: Beyond Successful Play: Diagnosing Opponent Modeling in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Language-model agents are expected to adapt to others whose behavior changes through interaction. Yet adaptation may rely on learned behavioral patterns rather than theory of mind (ToM): the ability to infer others' mental states, including beliefs and intentions. We introduce a benchmark and diagnostic framework for repeated hide-and-seek against algorithmic opponents with explicitly defined recursive belief updates. Their ground-truth beliefs and action probabilities let us distinguish adaptive play, action prediction, and belief tracking through live interaction, fixed-history evaluation, and controlled information interventions. With structured elicitation and behavioral supervised fine-tuning (SFT), we find improved play in several tested settings, but diagnostics reveal limitations in opponent prediction and belief tracking. We test whether supervising opponent action probabilities can address this predictive deficit in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Predictions improve when the model is told the opponent's type and parameter settings, but become less accurate when it must infer the opponent from history without this information. Training on examples that also omit these details reduces the gap, although improvements vary across opponents. Is this limitation specific to smaller open-weight models, or does it also appear in a frontier model? GPT-5.4 also benefits from correct opponent beliefs: supplying them improves its predictions and choices, whereas deeper explicit belief reports and self-generated memory do not consistently improve forecasting from interaction history. This contrast suggests that using useful belief information is easier than inferring it autonomously, even for a frontier model. Together, our findings distinguish improved play and action prediction from reliable belief tracking, providing a framework for evaluating mentalizing and testing targeted improvements.

items.title: Learning Perceptual Geometry of Natural Odor Mixtures from LLM-Derived Descriptors
items.abstract: The relationship between odor chemistry and perception remains incompletely understood. Many existing studies focus on the perception of single molecules, whereas natural odors contain tens to hundreds of components, adding extra layer of complexity to percept formation. Here, we explore the relationship between molecular composition and perceived similarity in natural odor objects. We study this using a database of more than 1,200 volatile-compound-in-food mixtures containing more than 8,000 molecular components, and use large language models (LLMs) as a scalable surrogate for deriving mixture-level perceptual descriptions. We find that language-derived representations provide useful supervision for predicting held-out mixture similarities from molecular composition. The prediction was consistently strongest when perceptual targets were derived from chemosensory prompts than from other sensory prompts. Further, during the mixture-level training, we learned low-rank molecular embeddings that enabled better prediction of held-out mixture similarities than component-overlap metrics, even for mixture pairs with no shared molecules. Although no single-molecule labels were used during training, the learned molecular geometry showed significant alignment with the independent human odor-descriptor space. Finally, we explored the use of external molecular features in our mixture-similarity prediction task. These features showed modest zero-shot alignment with mixture-level perceptual similarity. They improved prediction under limited supervision but offered little additional predictive benefit with the full training set. Together, these results show that language-derived descriptions can provide scalable supervision for predicting the perceptual organization of complex natural mixtures, contributing to a quantitative understanding of how molecular composition gives rise to odor perception.

items.title: Enforcing Thermodynamic Consistency in Parameter Optimization and Bayesian Inference of Biochemical Reaction Networks
items.abstract: Subcellular signaling pathways regulating, e.g., cell division or synaptic plasticity, are often modeled as dynamical networks of reactions satisfying the law of mass action. To remain physically grounded, these models must satisfy different physical conservation laws, such as conservation of energy. This gives rise to thermodynamic constraints formalized by the Wegscheider conditions, which ensure that the system is in detailed balance at thermodynamic equilibrium. Explicitly imposing Wegscheider conditions requires identifying cycles in the reaction network. This can become computationally cumbersome, especially in large, complex systems. Furthermore, even when these constraints are explicitly available, enforcing them requires choosing a reparameterization of the network, which may introduce asymmetries among the parameters and affect numerical conditioning. Moreover, this approach often causes inverse uncertainty quantification methods like Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) to struggle. Instead of imposing Wegscheider conditions directly in the parameter space, we propose an approach for promoting physical consistency by penalizing parameters that violate detailed balance. We first illustrate the approach on a simple reaction network containing a single cycle. We show that parameter values inferred without thermodynamic constraints can reproduce the experimental data seemingly accurately, while substantially violating the Wegscheider condition. In contrast, the proposed approach preserves the agreement with the observed dynamics while yielding posterior samples that approximately satisfy the thermodynamic constraint. We further apply the approach to a model of PKA-calcineurin signaling in synaptic long-term depression, demonstrating its applicability to a more complex biochemical reaction network.

items.title: Simple model of neurogliovascular unit activity with noradrenaline leading force
items.abstract: In this work we present a model of a neuroglivascular unit associated with a neuronal ensemble. We combine calcium dynamics in the astrocyte, the cascade of synthesis of arachidonic acid and its derivatives, as well as the activity of the network of inhibitory and excitatory neurons with changes in local blood flow. We add equations to the model for extracellular neurotransmitters such as GABA, glutamate, and norepinephrine. We show that the resulting model can exhibit different types of behavior, and also shows a significant connection between the functioning of the neural network and its supporting components.

items.title: Uncertainty-aware integration of deuterium metabolic imaging with genome-scale metabolic modeling reveals diet-associated feasible-space remodeling in mouse skeletal muscle
items.abstract: Deuterium metabolic imaging (DMI) measures glucose-derived labeling in vivo, but noisy time courses complicate network-level interpretation. We developed an uncertainty-aware workflow that integrates dynamic DMI data with genome-scale metabolic modeling (GEM) through soft flux constraints. After injection of [6,6'-2H2]glucose, dynamic spectra were acquired from gastrocnemius, soleus, and tibialis anterior muscles of control and high-fat diet (HFD) mice. A hierarchical four-state kinetic model estimated labeling parameters while accounting for shared plasma input, tissue-specific kinetics, voxel-level fluxes, isotope effects, and measurement uncertainty. Because glucose labeling was more reliable than lactate and glutamate/glutamine signals, only two DMI-derived quantities were used as GEM anchors: glucose processing mapped to hexokinase flux, and glucose-derived oxidative entry mapped to mitochondrial pyruvate dehydrogenase flux. Two-sided soft target intervals with weighted penalties defined DMI-compatible feasible regions for each mouse and muscle. Flux variability analysis and sampling assessed changes across reactions and metabolic subsystems. The constraints were compatible with the muscle network and affected feasible activity in glycolysis, lactate metabolism, pyruvate oxidation, the TCA cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and redox pathways. HFD-associated changes differed by muscle: tibialis anterior and soleus showed reduced glucose-linked feasible activity, whereas gastrocnemius showed mixed changes with preserved or increased TCA and redox activity. This framework connects noninvasive tracer imaging with network-level metabolic inference while avoiding strong claims from poorly identified signals.

items.title: Biodiversity conservation and its associations with economic performance, inequality, and peace
items.abstract: Abstract Biodiversity conservation is increasingly recognized as a product of coupled social–ecological systems shaped not only by ecological processes, but also by economic capacity, social inequality, and geopolitical stability. Here, we examined whether national conservation performance is systematically associated with economic prosperity, income inequality, peace, and the importance of natural resources in the national economy across 142 countries. Conservation performance was represented using the Nature Conservation Index (NCI), a composite metric integrating biodiversity threats, land management, governance capacity, and future environmental trends. We analysed relationships between NCI, Gross National Income per capita, the Gini coefficient, the National Peace Index, and the total nature resources rents using a generalized additive model that accounted for nonlinear relationships and income stratification. Together, these societal variables explained deviance of 52.2% for the NCI model. Economic prosperity was positively associated with NCI, although the relationship was nonlinear across income groups, suggesting that conservation capacity does not increase uniformly with development. Counter to commonly assumed relationships between inequality and biodiversity loss, income inequality showed a positive multivariate association with NCI scores. This result suggests that high national conservation performance can coexist with unequal social conditions, potentially reflecting centralized or exclusionary conservation systems that elevate institutional conservation metrics without necessarily improving equitable biodiversity outcomes. We also found that more peaceful countries consistently exhibited higher conservation performance, supporting the view that geopolitical stability provides enabling conditions for sustained conservation governance and institutional continuity. We further suggest that national conservation indices may partly capture governance capacity, reporting infrastructure, and political commitment rather than ecological condition alone, while telecoupled trade systems may allow wealthier nations to externalize environmental pressures beyond their borders. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, our findings highlight the need to interpret global conservation indicators cautiously and to incorporate social equity and externalized environmental impacts more explicitly into international biodiversity assessment frameworks.

items.title: Leadership, burnout, and organizational mental health: a neuroscience-informed perspective
items.abstract: This article argues that the persistent burden of burnout reflects a fundamental conceptual problem—burnout continues to be framed primarily as an individual condition rather than as an occupational phenomenon shaped by interacting structural, organizational, and leadership conditions. Burnout has emerged as a major occupational health challenge. In a 2024 survey across eight predominantly high and upper-middle-income countries, 48% of respondents reported currently grappling with burnout. Separately, depression and anxiety cost the global economy approximately one trillion dollars annually in lost productivity. Drawing on evidence from neuroimaging, stress biology, cognitive neuroscience, and organizational research, this article examines plausible pathways through which leadership behavior may influence conditions that contribute to or protect against burnout, including social threat–reward processing, cognitive flexibility, emotional intelligence, psychological safety, emotional contagion, and stress-related neurobiological responses. Among physicians, burnout has been associated with depression and anxiety, while evidence regarding substance abuse is less consistent. These proposed mechanisms are proximal and potentially modifiable, but operate within broader structural conditions that constrain or enable their effects. Human-centered work design and neuroleadership-informed leadership practices are proposed as complements to broader structural interventions, with implications for health systems, workforce sustainability, and policy design.

items.title: Christian Education and Child Development in Contemporary Society: Process, Challenges and Prospect
items.abstract: This paper examines Christian education's vital role in fostering children's moral, spiritual, intellectual, and social development within contemporary society. Amid shifting cultural values, rapid technological change, and increasing pluralism, Christian education provides a formative framework that grounds children in biblical principles, cultivates godly character, and equips them with life skills for holistic growth. While acknowledging significant challenges such as secular influences, family instability, limited resources, and the widening gap between faith and practice, the paper argues that the prospects for Christian education remain robust. By exploring its foundational processes, addressing its current challenges, and highlighting emerging opportunities, this study underscores Christian education's enduring potential as a transformative force for nurturing spiritually mature, socially responsible, and intellectually capable children in today's world.

items.title: The neuroscience of transformers
items.abstract: Abstract Neuroscience has long informed the development of artificial neural networks, but the success of modern architectures invites, in turn, the converse: can modern networks teach us lessons about brain function? Here, we examine the structure of the cortical column and propose that the transformer provides a natural computational analogy for multiple elements of cortical microcircuit organization. Rather than claiming a literal implementation of transformer equations in cortex, we develop a hypothetical mapping between transformer operations and laminar cortical features, using the analogy as an orienting framework for analysis and discussion. This mapping allows us to examine in greater depth how contextual selection, content routing, recurrent integration, and interlaminar transformations may be distributed across cortical circuitry. In doing so, we generate a broad set of predictions and experimentally testable hypotheses concerning laminar specialization, contextual modulation, dendritic integration, oscillatory coordination, and the effective connectivity of cortical columns. This proposal is intended as a structured hypothesis rather than a definitive account of cortical computation. Placing transformer operations and cortical architectonics into a common descriptive framework sharpens questions, reveals new functional correspondences, and opens a productive route for reciprocal exchange between systems neuroscience and modern AI. More broadly, this perspective suggests that comparing brains and architectures at the level of computational organization can yield genuine insight into both.

items.title: Physical education teacher education for intercultural citizenship in a traumatized society
items.abstract: In divided and conflict-affected societies, higher education institutions offer opportunities for sustained intergroup encounter. Yet proximity alone does not produce meaningful interaction, trust, or cooperation. This challenge is particularly acute in Israel, where Arab and Jewish students enter higher education after years of segregated schooling, amid tensions and intensified fear, mistrust, and collective trauma following October 7, 2023, and the subsequent war. This perspective article argues that Physical Education Teacher Education (PETE) offers an underexplored space for fostering intercultural citizenship. It synthesizes relevant theoretical perspectives and evidence from studies by the authors and others to develop a framework for PETE in divided and traumatized societies. Integrating intergroup contact theory, intercultural citizenship, Sport for Development and Peace, and trauma-sensitive pedagogy, the framework positions PETE as a space for structured contact, embodied cooperation, civic engagement, and resilience. The framework is illustrated through the “Roaming Course,” an experiential, student-led PETE model combining on-campus learning, encounters in diverse communities, shared physical activity, and guided reflection. Drawing on studies involving Arab and Jewish PETE students in Israel, the article shows how structured, discipline-based contact may narrow the gap between willingness to engage and actual intergroup interaction while strengthening students’ capacity to cope with social tension and collective trauma. It demonstrates the value of embedding intercultural citizenship within core curricula rather than relying on extracurricular interventions. It concludes that PETE can prepare future educators to act as agents of social connection, inclusion, and resilience in divided societies.

items.title: The Extension and Rejection of Self-Cognition in the Saṃdhinirmocana-Sūtra: A Study of Self-Cognition in Pre-Dignāga Yogācāra Under the Scope of the No-Cognition Sentence
items.abstract: While contemporary scholarship has extensively focused on self-cognition in Dignāga and post-Dignāga Yogācāra traditions, early Yogācāra discussions of this theme remain comparatively understudied. Focusing primarily on the Vijñaptimātra Passage of the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra (SNS) and secondarily on the Mahāyānasaṃgraha (MSA), this paper advances three core arguments. First, the vijñaptimātra theory substantially broadens the scope of self-cognition by integrating inner object-directed cognitive activities into its framework, establishing what this paper terms the “broad sense of self-cognition.” In contrast to the Vaibhāṣika’s Outside-Model (OM), which separates object-directed cognition from self-cognition, the vijñaptimātra framework establishes an alternative Inside-Model (IM) of cognitive operation. The IM further accommodates a narrower form of self-cognition alongside its broad counterpart. Accordingly, the vijñaptimātra doctrine fundamentally reorganizes the classical structure of self-cognition theory. Second, the SNS advances a radical “no-cognition sentence” that universally negates all cognitive activities and thereby rejects this expanded mode of self-cognition. Nevertheless, this radical stance generates several textual tensions and theoretical contradictions, which undermine its validity. Third, the MSA rephrases the no-cognition sentence by using the verb “grasp.” By integrating the trisvabhāva (three natures) doctrine with vijñaptimātra, this new expression restricts the scope of negation exclusively to cognitive activities grounded in the parikalpita-svabhāva (mere illusory nature), while validating cognitive operations pertaining to the paratantra-svabhāva (dependent nature). Meanwhile, according to the IM, these cognitive operations precisely constitute broad-sense self-cognition. Accordingly, through a comparative analysis of these two divergent expressions of the no-cognition sentence, this paper elucidates the doctrinal shift between SNS and MSA attitudes toward expanded self-cognition.

items.title: Legal Strategies for Biodiversity Conservation in Southern Nigeria: Lessons from International Laws
items.abstract: Southern Nigeria is currently facing a profound environmental crisis characterized by rapidly rising sea levels, recurrent and intensified flooding, and widespread ecological degradation. These developments pose a growing threat to human settlements, critical infrastructure, and fragile ecosystems. Alarmingly, government projections suggest that over 30 Nigerian states could soon be impacted by severe flood events, amplifying the urgency for a robust and integrated legal response. Biodiversity loss is occurring at an unprecedented rate, with many indigenous plant and animal species either endangered or already extinct due to unsustainable land use practices, deforestation, urban sprawl, and pollution. This paper critically evaluates Nigeria’ s biodiversity conservation framework, with a particular focus on Southern Nigeria, where the ecological stakes are highest. Through a doctrinal and comparative legal approach, it investigates the effectiveness of existing national environmental laws and the institutions responsible for enforcing them, including the National Environmental Standards and Regulations Enforcement Agency (NESREA) and the National Parks Service. It explores Nigeria’ s legal obligations under key international and regional environmental instruments such as the Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD), the Nagoya Protocol, the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands, and the African Convention on the Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources (African Nature Convention). Furthermore, the paper draws on international legal principles and judicial precedents, including those from the International Court of Justice (ICJ), to assess Nigeria’ s compliance with transboundary environmental obligations. Recommendations include harmonizing domestic laws with international norms, improving institutional coordination, and integrating indigenous knowledge into conservation strategies to enhance biodiversity protection in Southern Nigeria.

items.title: Development of Environmental Education Parks for Local Biodiversity Conservation
items.abstract: Community engagement plays a crucial role in promoting environmental awareness and biodiversity conservation. This paper describes a community service program conducted by the Laboratory of Forest Harvesting, Faculty of Forestry, Universitas Gadjah Mada (UGM), in Compartment 32 of HWD Tlogotuwung, Blora Regency. The program, titled “Development of an Environmental Education Park for Local Biodiversity Conservation,” involved 122 participants, including elementary school students from SD Negeri 1 Getas and SD Negeri 1 Tlogotuwung, teachers, lecturers, university volunteers, and representatives of partner organizations. The program included site surveys, collaborative planning, and the collective planting of local species such as Calliandra, Indigofera, jackfruit, avocado, and other fruit trees. The CarbonNature Foundation and the Faculty of Forestry UGM supported the program. Students demonstrated curiosity about the tree species in their surroundings and actively participated during and after the planting activities. Reflection sessions also indicated positive attitudes toward biodiversity conservation. The program further strengthened collaboration among universities, local communities, schools, and environmental organizations. The program directly contributed to Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 4, 13, 15, and 17. In conclusion, the development of the Environmental Education Park can contribute not only to biodiversity conservation but also to enhancing environmental education and fostering environmental awareness among future generations.

items.title: Education, Society and the Idea of the Educated Person: A Philosophical-Sociological Analysis of the Evolution of Education Policies in India
items.abstract: Education policy is closely connected with the society in which it develops. Changes in education are therefore not only changes in curriculum, institutions or teaching methods; they also reflect changing ideas about the individual, citizenship, knowledge and social development. This paper examines the evolution of education policy in India from indigenous intellectual traditions and colonial education to the major post-Independence policy frameworks and the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. The study adopts a qualitative historical-interpretive methodology, combining analysis of major policy documents with perspectives from Indian philosophy and sociology of education. Particular attention is given to the Education Commission (1964–66), National Policy on Education (NPE) 1968, NPE 1986/1992 and NEP 2020, along with the educational thought of Swami Vivekananda, Mahatma Gandhi, Rabindranath Tagore, Sri Aurobindo and B. R. Ambedkar. The paper argues that the purpose of education in India has changed with changing social circumstances: from knowledge and personal formation, to colonial administrative requirements, nation-building, social justice, human-resource development and, more recently, holistic development within a knowledge society. NEP 2020 is examined in this historical context rather than as an isolated reform. The paper argues that the policy represents neither a complete break from earlier educational thinking nor merely a continuation of it. Instead, it brings together several strands of India's educational history, including social justice, national development, Indian knowledge traditions, scientific inquiry, technological change and global engagement. The main contribution of the paper is a philosophical-sociological framework for understanding policy change through six questions: What is education for? What kind of learner does society want to develop? What kind of citizen is required? What knowledge is valued? How is inequality addressed? And what changes in society make educational reform necessary? By bringing these questions together, the study offers a way of reading Indian education policy as a reflection of changing ideas about the society India has been, the society it is, and the society it wishes to become.

items.title: Development of corporate biodiversity conservation management tools
items.abstract: The article examines corporate biodiversity conservation activities as an important area of sustainable development and the ESG agenda. The relevance of the topic is attributable to the fact that biodiversity loss risks are ranked among the ten most significant global risks according to the World Economic Forum Global Risks Report 2026 and are also recognized as one of the ten key areas of the global sustainable development (ESG) agenda. The aim of the study is to analyze the tools employed by Russian companies to conserve biodiversity. Particular attention is paid to the types of non-financial reporting through which corporations disclose their biodiversity-related activities, including GRI, TNFD, and CDP frameworks. The study defines the concept of impact management and systematizes biodiversity conservation tools, which are evolving from a peripheral component of corporate environmental responsibility into an independent area within the ESG agenda. The practices of PJSC Severstal and PJSC Polyus are examined in detail as case studies, as both companies are leaders in the RAEX ESG ranking and in the ranking of Russia’s largest mining companies in biodiversity conservation compiled by the Nature and People Foundation. The article identifies the lack of methodologies for assessing ecosystem services and biodiversity at the corporate level as a key challenge. The findings may be of practical interest to directors responsible for strategy and sustainable development, ESG professionals, and researchers from various fields focusing on sustainable development and the impact of business activities on nature.

items.title: What Humanitarian Work Psychology brings to Occupational Health Psychology
items.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces a newly emerged sub-discipline in work studies – Humanitarian Work Psychology (HWP) – to researchers and practitioners in Occupational Health Psychology (OHP). Focused initially on the eradication of working poverty, under the United Nations (UN) Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), HWP has since its inception contributed to the health and well-being of marginalized workgroups globally. Until today, however, those contributions in HWP have not been integrated with OHP. Key strands in the connecting nexus include how to: (1) set living wages that protect occupational and thus wider public health; (2) tackle infectious diseases as occupational health hazards; (3) bring valuable and skilled in formal work closer into the ambit of OHP; and perhaps the toughest challenge of all, help to (4) combat unfree work . OHP is a cross-cutting theme in all four, and we call for broaden-and-build training initiatives and greater supervisor awareness of links not only between HWP and OHP, but also with the wider social sciences and management disciplines including corporate social responsibility, human resources, and policy and public health.

items.title: University campus green spaces’ potential for biodiversity conservation and ecosystem services
items.abstract: Aravalli landscape is one of the oldest geological formations in India, and has been subjected to various disturbances specifically in the urban areas. University campuses within this landscape represent important urban green spaces that support biodiversity and provide ecosystem services. This study assessed biodiversity and perceptions of ecosystem services on the 57-year-old Jawaharlal Nehru University (JNU) campus, situated within this ecologically sensitive area. Vegetation dynamics were analysed using Landsat derived Fractional Vegetation Index (FVI) data (1992–2025), which showed a consistent increase in vegetation cover, with maximum FVI values increasing from 0.33 in 1992 to 0.60 in 2025. Field-based ecological assessment using systematic transect quadrat sampling recorded 57 woody plant species, including 36 tree and 21 shrub species. Of these, 42 (73.68%) were native, 11 (19.30%) were introduced, and 4 (7.02%) were invasive. Diversity indices revealed spatial variation across the campus, with Shannon diversity values ranging from 1.61–2.41 and Menhinick Richness Index values from 0.52–1.07. However, despite their lower species richness, invasive taxa Neltuma juliflora (syn. Prosopis juliflora ) and Lantana camara exhibited dominance and high IVI scores across multiple study sites. An open-access flora database of the campus was also developed. Public perception showed strong positive correlations with species richness (r = 0.82) and Shannon diversity (r = 0.62), highlighting green space's biodiversity–perception nexus within the urban landscape. In an increasingly urbanized era, such green university campuses play an important role in enhancing health, well-being, and nature connectedness of people.

items.title: Motion, emotion and cognition: The melancholia conundrum
items.abstract: Background The status of melancholia remains controversial. Debate has focused on whether it represents a categorically distinct disorder (binary model) or a severe expression within a unitary construct of major depressive disorder. Its defining core has also been disputed, with competing emphasis on affective symptoms, cognitive distortions, or psychomotor disturbance. Proponents of distinctiveness, notably Gordon Parker, have argued that psychomotor disturbance is central to the syndrome. Objective To critically examine historical and contemporary evidence regarding melancholia’s diagnostic status and to consider whether advances in neurobiology can resolve longstanding conceptual debates. Method This narrative analysis reviews the evolution of the melancholia construct, clinical and treatment-response data, research on psychomotor disturbance including the CORE measure, and recent findings from genetics, molecular psychiatry, and neuroimaging studies of brain networks implicated in depression. Conclusion Phenomenological and biomarker-based approaches have not conclusively established melancholia as a distinct nosological entity. Emerging findings from circuit neuroscience and multiomic research suggest that patterns of large-scale network dysfunction may underlie the clinical syndrome, but have not yet established a reproducible circuit signature specific to melancholia. A biologically grounded, network-based framework could ultimately clarify the relationship between melancholia, psychomotor disturbance and broader depressive syndromes, moving the field beyond the binary-dimensional impasse.

items.title: Popularization of science and education by the Znanie Society in the TASSR (1947–1975)
items.abstract: This article examines the All-Union Znanie Society’s work on communicating scientific knowledge to the general public in the Tatar ASSR. After the Great Patriotic War, the Soviet Union was committed to reviving the destroyed sectors of education and research. Thus, from 1955 onward, the popularization of science and technology rose to a top state-level priority, with the Znanie Society as one of the most ambitious projects to achieve this aim. It played an important role in retaining and raising professional qualifications of researchers, increasing productive capacity, and promoting new technological developments and rationalization proposals. Higher levels of education helped increase labor productivity and encouraged political literacy of the target audience. The Znanie Society reached the public through many ways, but lectures were the most common and accessible option. All lectures were carefully planned according to the instructions on the topics that were covered. Each topic was assigned to a lecturer responsible for it. The analysis, based on materials of the Znanie Society congresses and documents from the State Archive of the Republic of Tatarstan, outlines the main concepts, forms, and methods of knowledge propaganda used by the Znanie Society in its work as part of the broader development of educational organizations in the USSR.

items.title: Rethinking Formal Education through Ivan Illich’s Concept of Deschooling Society
items.abstract: The formalisation of modern education has increasingly contributed to the dehumanisation of the learning process and fostered bureaucratic dependence on formal qualifications and certification. This study critically analyses the implementation of transformative pedagogy at Sanggar Anak Alam (SALAM) in Yogyakarta as a practical manifestation of Ivan Illich’s radical critique of institutionalised education in Deschooling Society. This qualitative study employed a systematic literature review of relevant academic literature retrieved from Google Scholar, ResearchGate, and the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ), followed by qualitative content analysis. The findings indicate that SALAM has deconstructed conventional classroom practices by promoting the principle of “Independent Thinking,” redefining facilitators as learning companions rather than one-way instructors, and developing a community-based learning ecosystem. Its operational curriculum is implemented through a “Learning Cycle” model and independent inquiry into real-world issues, including food, health, environmental, and socio-cultural concerns, while integrating local wisdom (titen) and narrative-based evaluation. Nevertheless, this alternative education model faces several challenges, including scalability, regulatory barriers related to the recognition of qualifications through Packages A/B/C, the sustainability of self-funded operations, and the need to strengthen facilitator capacity. The findings demonstrate how the deconstruction of conventional schooling can be translated into autonomous and community-based “learning webs” that reconnect education with everyday life and learner autonomy.

items.title: From Cognition to Connection
items.abstract: In contemporary times, marked by hyperconnectivity and generative and agentic artificial intelligences that expand the possibilities of co-creating formative environments in ecologically connected contexts, the educational debate has been strained by the need for pedagogical practices that overcome dualisms and centralities, favoring more connective and reflective forms of learning. In this scenario, traditional perspectives on metacognition prove limited in the face of the transformations of our living conditions. In this context, this article aims to understand how ecological-connective pedagogical practices, guided by the OnLIFE Education Paradigm (Schlemmer, 2020) and Ecological Thinking (Morton, 2023), problematize conceptions of metacognition in the teaching of History. Methodologically, this is an intervention-research project based on the Cartographic Method, developed from the ecological-connective pedagogical practice entitled "In the Wine Capital for 150 days! U.V.A. Expedition in Bento Gonçalves Soil," carried out with third-year high school students throughout 2025. The results indicate that reflective processes about learning emerged as ecological-connective phenomena produced in the relationships between students, digital technologies, artificial intelligence, the city, memory, and experience.

items.title: Exposure to Psychology Courses and Misconceptions About Psychology: A Multi-Site Student Survey
items.abstract: In recent years, misconceptions about the value and safety of medical vaccines and many other topics have gone viral on social media, fueling controversies about the wisdom of public health policies, and leading some believers to make suboptimal decisions about their health and other matters. Misconceptions about behavior and mental processes are also widespread and can have significant negative consequences, as when jurors who believe in the infallibility of eyewitness testimony find an innocent defendant guilty. Because introductory psychology courses can reduce students’ endorsement of such misconceptions, especially when instructors explicitly debunk them, we decided to explore the relationship between psychological misconceptions and exposure to advanced psychology courses. Our analysis of responses to an 80-item misconceptions survey taken by 750 undergraduates at eight U.S. colleges and universities found that, compared to students who had taken no psychology courses, those who had taken three or more, as majors or nonmajors, were significantly less likely to endorse psychological misconceptions, especially those typically covered in those courses. Although our research design does not allow causal explanations, the results are consistent with the notion that advanced psychology courses may play a role in combating misconceptions about psychology, thus justifying instructors’ efforts to debunk them. Statement of public significance: Misconceptions about human behavior and mental processes are widespread and potentially harmful. Like other forms of misinformation, they may misguide our actions and decisions as voters, jurors, parents, teachers, consumers, journalists, filmmakers, writers, and in many other social roles. Evidence that taking multiple psychology courses is associated with reduction of such misconceptions supports the value of advanced courses for majors and non-majors alike.

items.title: Research Priorities for Neuroscience Nursing: 2026 Update
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: The American Association of Neuroscience Nurses established a 6-member Research Agenda Task Force in 2025 to update and define neuroscience nursing research priorities to lead the field for the next 5 years. The last research priority setting was completed in 2021. METHODS: A 6-member Research Agenda Task Force selected potential research priorities based on a literature search and review of neuroscience nursing research. Using a 2-round, Delphi methodology, electronic surveys were distributed to neuroscience nursing experts to gain consensus on the research priorities for neuroscience nursing. Survey data included demographics, agreement with selected gaps in neuroscience nursing research, and the impact of selected neuroscience nursing research topics on the field. RESULTS: Thirty-three of 58 experts (57% response rate) participated in round 1, and 32 of 58 experts (55% response rate) participated in round 2. In round 1, 26 topics achieved ≥70% agreement, and 2 new topics were identified by the expert panel: “Technology: Artificial Intelligence in Neuroscience Nursing” and “Nursing Care Outcomes: Value of Neuroscience Nursing.” In round 2, 14 topics were ranked ≥70% impactful and identified as the top neuroscience nursing research priorities. CONCLUSIONS: These priorities span 6 categories: assessment, biomarkers, nursing care outcomes, professional development, quality of life, and technology. The priorities reflect not only the foundation of neuroscience nursing but also raise questions concerning both the nature and volume of scientific evidence being generated by nursing scientists in the field.

items.title: Habitual Sugar Consumption: From Neuroscience to Nursing Clinical Practice. A Tool for Modifying Health-Risk Behaviors
items.abstract: Introduction. Habits and eating behaviour are complex processes influenced by neurobiological, cognitive and environmental factors. Sucrose consumption represents a useful model to investigate the shift from goal-directed actions to automated responses. The aim of this study was to analyse the mechanisms underlying habit formation and their role in eating behaviour, with a specific focus on sugar consumption, in order to highlight implications for nursing practice. Materials and Methods. A literature review was conducted using the PRISMA method and analysis of specialized texts. Studies addressing habit formation mechanisms and neurophysiological responses to sugar consumption were analysed, with particular attention to learning, reinforcement and anticipatory processes. Results. Findings indicate that habit formation is a dynamic process shaped by the interaction between contextual triggers, repetition and reinforcement, in the absence of a unified theoretical framework. In contrast, studies on sucrose show greater methodological consistency and allow a clearer characterisation of neurophysiological responses, although variability related to individual and environmental factors persists. Discussion. The integration of evidence suggests that sugar consumption may evolve from goal-directed behaviour to automated responses. Understanding these mechanisms has relevant implications for nursing practice, particularly in designing interventions targeting environmental triggers and promoting more conscious behaviours.

items.title: The hierarchical levels of information activities in the subject’s psychology and cognition
items.abstract: The subject’s psychological and cognitive activities are important interdisciplinary issues in psychology, cognitive science, and philosophy. The Chinese philosophy of information innovatively provides a philosophical definition of the concepts of subject and object from the dimension of information activity, while also making specific provisions for the cognitive activities of the subject. The subject’s psychology and cognition are an activity of advanced grasping and creation of information. The subject’s information activities have five basic levels. Arranged from lower to higher, they are: the subject’s in-itself information activities, the subject’s intuitive discernment of information, the subject’s memory storage of information, the subject’s subjective creation of information, and the subject’s practice and social realization of information. Higher-level information activities must arise on the basis of lower-level ones. Therefore, the emergence and development of the subject’s psychology and cognition necessarily constitute a highly integrated and complex process of information activities.

items.title: The Role of Biotechnology in Biodiversity Conservation and Ecological Restoration: A Review
items.abstract: More recently, biotechnology is increasingly adopted alongside conventional approaches to biodiversity conservation and ecosystem restoration. In this study, we examined 60 articles published from year 1998-2024 by grouping the literature into six areas: conservation genomics and genetic rescue, environmental DNA (eDNA), biobanking and reproductive biotechnology, synthetic biology and genome editing, microbiome-based restoration and the governance of genetic data, risks and benefit sharing. The studies reviewed show that genomic approaches can provide information on genetic diversity, inbreeding, population structure, adaptation and whether interventions such as translocation or genetic rescue may be appropriate. eDNA has also expanded the options available for biodiversity monitoring because organisms can be detected from water, soil and air samples without necessarily being captured or directly observed. Studies on cryopreservation, assisted reproduction and stem-cell technologies further demonstrate ways of retaining genetic material that may be difficult to conserve through captive breeding alone. However, the evidence was less straightforward for genome editing and gene drives. Although these technologies may allow highly targeted interventions, the examined studies repeatedly raise questions about unintended ecological effects, reversibility, regulation and public acceptance. Microbiome-based approaches are also becoming promising, particularly where microbial communities influence establishment, stress tolerance or recovery, but their outcomes appear to depend strongly on the species and environmental conditions involved. Hence, the studies reviewed suggest that biotechnology should not be treated as a replacement for habitat protection or ecological restoration. Its value lies mainly in extending the range of tools available to conservation practitioners. Effective use will require appropriate sampling, reliable genetic and ecological data, field validation, long-term monitoring and careful consideration of risk, access to genetic information and benefit sharing.

items.title: Transformative peace education in a plural society through the Gus Dur School for Peace
items.abstract: Peace education is a pedagogical effort to realize peace. Peace education in a pluralistic society requires a transformative approach. The Gus Dur Peace School (GDSP), a non-formal youth cadre program under the Wahid Foundation, offers one such model, grounded in the thinking of KH. Abdurrahman Wahid (Gus Dur). Gus Dur's humanist pluralism, this study argues, is not merely a local ethical tradition but a practical instantiation of Galtung's positive peace one that addresses structural and cultural violence through values education rather than conflict resolution alone. This study examines how the GDSP conceptualizes peace, implements its educational stages, and produces observable transformations in participants. Using a qualitative case study approach with interpretive analysis, data were collected through in-depth interviews, participant observation, and document analysis involving senior Wahid Foundation staff, GDSP facilitators, participants, and alumni. Findings indicate that the GDSP operates through nine core values ​​derived from Gus Dur's thinking, including humanity, justice, equality, and liberation, which are realized through a structured series of selection, training, social project implementation, evaluation, and co-living activities. Alumni reported concrete changes: one alumnus described a shift from passive awareness to actively building a tolerant youth community in his hometown; Others noted that the GDSP's gender equality material fundamentally changed their understanding of women's roles in public life. These outcomes align with a three-dimensional typology of peace education cognitive, affective, and active operating as an integrated cycle rather than separate stages. GDSP demonstrates that locally grounded, values-based peace education can function as a vehicle for genuine social transformation a finding that speaks not only to this program but to ongoing debates about whether non-formal, culturally embedded peace education models can offer alternatives to the Western-centric frameworks that dominate the field.

items.title: Problems of Islamic Education in the Reality of Muslim Society
items.abstract: This study investigates the complex structural, philosophical, and operational challenges confronting Islamic education within the contemporary reality of Muslim societies. Utilizing a qualitative research methodology based on literature review and content analysis, this paper systematically categorizes these core problems into three primary dimensions: the epistemological dichotomy between religious and secular knowledge, curricular stagnation lacking technological and critical-thinking integration, and institutional limitations regarding infrastructure, funding, and teacher professionalism. The findings indicate that these challenges stem from historical post-colonial legacies, socio-economic disparities, and rigid traditionalism in pedagogical practices. To overcome these crises, the paper argues for a strategic shift toward integrated education (integrasi-interkoneksi), pedagogical modernization, and policy reforms that harmonize Islamic ethical values with contemporary scientific demands, thereby repositioning Islamic education as an effective engine of societal transformation.

items.title: Does corporate green investment matter? Evidence from biodiversity conservation
items.abstract: Purpose Biodiversity conservation is essential for corporate sustainability, yet empirical evidence on the relationship between firm-level green commitment and biodiversity exposure remains limited. This study aims to examine the relationship between corporate green investment and biodiversity conservation initiatives. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a sample of listed firms from the United States (the USA) covering the period 2002–2023 and uses regression analyses with sector and year fixed effects. To ensure robustness, this study also uses alternative measures and adopts various methods to address potential endogeneity problems. Findings The results of this study show that green investment is positively associated with biodiversity conservation initiatives, and this positive relationship is stronger for firms operating in carbon-intensive sectors. Additional analyses further reveal that the positive association observed in carbon-intensive sectors is more pronounced for firms that have sustainability committees and for firms that have adopted the GRI guidelines. Furthermore, ESG performance positively moderates the relationship between green investment and biodiversity conservation initiatives. Practical implications The findings of this study contribute to the extant literature and provide valuable implications for corporate leaders, national governments and regulators aiming to protect ecosystems and conserve biodiversity. Originality/value To the best of the author’s knowledge, this study is among the first to uncover the association between green investment and biodiversity conservation in the context of US firms. This study extends the existing literature by emphasizing the role of green investments in conserving biodiversity and ecosystems, particularly in carbon-intensive sectors.

items.title: Evaluation of Sustainable Development Goals-Based Projects for Sustainable Education and Society
items.abstract: The Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) aim to create a sustainable future by considering environmental, social, and economic elements from a holistic perspective. Instilling these goals in individuals through education is critically important for increasing awareness of sustainable development and translating this awareness into behavior. This study aims to examine how non-governmental organizations (NGOs) contribute to the implementation of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) through educational projects conducted in collaboration with schools. While the projects involved various educational stakeholders, including students, teachers, school administrators, and parents as project beneficiaries, the qualitative data for this study were collected through semi-structured interviews with representatives of 17 NGOs responsible for planning and implementing these projects. The interview data were analyzed using inductive qualitative content analysis. The findings show that SDG projects significantly contribute to developing environmental awareness, sustainable thinking, and responsible behavior in students. However, the success of the projects varies depending on the level of stakeholder participation in the educational environment, i.e., the active involvement and collaboration of relevant individuals in the process. The research findings indicate that strengthening stakeholder participation and more regular integration of sustainability-themed projects into educational curricula are necessary to promote the dissemination of sustainable development goals through education.

items.title: Systemic approach in sports psychology
items.abstract: The aim of this article is to substantiate the application of the systems approach in sports psychology. The provisions of the system-genetic approach and their implementation in sports practice are examined. For the first time, the hierarchical structure of an athlete's personality traits in ontogenesis and the hierarchical structure of speed of response as a sport‑significant quality are described. The effectiveness of the systems approach for diagnosing and developing the components of speed of response and psychomotor qualities using innovative hardware‑based methods is demonstrated. The necessity of the systems approach for the expert evaluation of diagnostic and correctional tools, as well as in theoretical research, is substantiated. Practical recommendations are accompanied by descriptions of specific methods and equipment for systemic psychological diagnostics and the development (correction) of sport‑significant qualities.

items.title: Rūḥ between Revelation and Psychology: Integrating Scientific Qur’anic Exegesis and Transpersonal Psychology
items.abstract: The Qur’anic concept of rūḥ remains a central yet epistemologically complex issue in Islamic thought because it concerns life, consciousness, morality, and transcendence while exceeding complete human understanding. This study develops an integrative conceptual model of rūḥ by bringing scientific Qur’anic exegesis into dialogue with Robert Frager’s transpersonal psychology. A qualitative library-research design was employed using thematic Qur’anic interpretation, qualitative content analysis, conceptual mapping, and source triangulation. Classical, modern, and scientifically oriented interpretations of Q.S. al-Isrāʾ [17]:85 were examined alongside literature on Sufi psychology, transpersonal psychology, consciousness, and spiritual development. The findings identify three dimensions of rūḥ: ontological, as an immaterial and transcendent principle of life; epistemological, as a reality whose essence remains beyond complete human knowledge; and functional, as a source of consciousness, moral agency, spiritual orientation, and human transformation. Functional correspondences emerged between these dimensions and transpersonal concepts such as self-transcendence, psycho-spiritual integration, meaning-making, emotional regulation, and moral development. Nevertheless, Qur’anic metaphysics and psychological theory remain epistemologically distinct. Transpersonal psychology may explain spiritual experience and development but cannot determine the revealed ontological status of rūḥ, while preserving the epistemic authority of revelation. The proposed non-reductive framework contributes to Qur’anic studies, Islamic psychology, spiritual education, counselling, and mental-health research.

items.title: Algorithmic Intentionality: A Distributed Cognition Framework
items.abstract: Abstract This article reframes human–AI cognition assemblages by situating algorithmic systems within the philosophical and empirical tradition of collective intentionality. Rather than asking whether generative AI augments or erodes individual cognitive skills, the paper proposes that algorithms participate in distributed networks of shared epistemological purposes, norms, and meanings. Drawing on Searle’s social ontology, Tuomela and Gilbert’s accounts of group agency, and Tomasello’s empirical assessments, the paper establishes collective intentionality as foundational to how humans think and act together. It then introduces algorithmic intentionality – the concept that contemporary algorithmic systems function as infrastructures of distributed participation towards the coordination of collective cognition. Rather than neutral tools or autonomous agents, algorithms emerge here as sociotechnical assemblages that mediate and reshape the structures through which shared understanding and distributed cognition emerges.

items.title: Microgenetic Theory meets Spatiotemporal Neuroscience: Situating the Neurodaonamic Psychotherapy Framewdork in Process Neuroscience
items.abstract: The brain can be viewed as a multitiered evolutionary organ. Jason Brown’s microgenetic theory stipulates that the mind unfolds through successive phases from the brain stem, through the limbic system, towards the outer limits of the cortex, recapitulating the brain’s evolutionary and developmental history. While this progression and its phases have been documented throughout the literature, it currently lacks specificity in relation to neural networks such as the default mode network, the salience network, and the central executive network. Given that spatiotemporal neuroscience is process-oriented and already embeds large-scale neural networks within empirically derived spatial topographies and temporal dynamics, it provides a natural integrative framework for linking microgenetic theory with contemporary network-based models of brain function. This article concludes by demonstrating how this synthesis can be applied in practice by using it to ground a novel, process-oriented psychotherapeutic meta-framework, the neurodynamic approach. This article first aims to further develop the microgenetic theory from the work of Jason Brown. In contrast to the reigning paradigmatic neuropsychological approach, which attempts to localize neural and cognitive functioning within specific brain structures and regions, the microgenetic approach is a process-oriented approach that conceptualizes mental contents as evolving through the successive evolutionary layers of neural substrate. In this sense, mental processes are not fixed, static, and localized, but follow a spatiotemporal dynamic sequence as they unfold.

items.title: Textualization and Spatial Cognition
items.abstract: Abstract This article examines how biblical and classical texts textualized experiential spatial knowledge: the cognitive frameworks humans use to navigate and communicate about space through lived experience. Comparative analysis reveals that ancient authors preserved universal cognitive patterns while adapting them for diverse communicative purposes. Comparison with classical sources illuminates what is distinctive in biblical geographical discourse: while both traditions share fundamental spatial cognition, biblical texts predominantly deployed these frameworks to construct communal identity and embed sacred narrative within recognizable landscapes, whereas other ancient traditions adapted the same patterns for purposes ranging from practical navigation to historiographical credibility to epic atmosphere. The study demonstrates how textualization transformed oral spatial knowledge, enabling conscious literary choices that maintained experiential authenticity while serving genre-specific and culturally specific functions. For biblical studies, this comparative approach reveals that biblical geography represents an authorial strategy that is deeply rooted in universal human cognition yet distinctively deployed for theological and commemorative purposes.

items.title: On the meaning of “plasticity” in neuroscience and mental health research and its relation to the action of psychedelic therapy
items.abstract: First-line dictionary definitions of “plasticity” describe it as the ability (of a thing) to be shaped or molded; we call this “plasticity proper” (PP). In neuroscience, however, “neural plasticity” or “neuroplasticity” is defined as an induced change in brain function or structure. These two plasticities are not the same. Several popular biomarkers of neuroplasticity index part of an evoked process, often linked to learning. Paradoxically, these processes often bias phenotypic canalization, the opposite of phenotypic plasticity. Recognizing this paradox puts into question the custom of using “plasticity” as a shorthand for all neuroplastic phenomena. This custom risks an overgeneralization fallacy and the conflation of assays of evoked brain changes with plasticity proper. We also question extrapolating from any biomarker of neuroplasticity to improved mental health, whether it be aligned with plasticity proper or not. The relationship between the two is, logically, context dependent . As a resolution, we propose a new construct, “mediational and recalibrative plasticity” (MR-P) and show how markers of it can describe and predict examples of phenotypic plasticity, where those phenotypes are states and traits relevant to mental health. In contrast to many markers of neuroplasticity, MR-P is aligned with plasticity proper.

items.title: A Sociological Study of Islamic Education: Moral Phenomena and Behavioral Deviance in Society
items.abstract: Moral degradation and behavioral deviance in the era of globalization and digitalization pose serious challenges for Islamic education in shaping the character of the younger generation. This study aims to analyze the phenomenon of moral degradation from the perspective of the sociology of Islamic education and to formulate strategies for the reconstruction of Islamic education that are relevant to the development of contemporary society. The study employs a qualitative approach using a literature review method, analyzing various scientific journals, books, and academic sources related to the sociology of Islamic education, social change, and character education. The results indicate that moral degradation is influenced by various factors, including family dysfunction, the impact of globalization, an unhelpful digital culture, and the weak internalization of religious values. These conditions have led to a weakening of character, a crisis of role models, and an increase in various forms of deviant behavior among the younger generation. Therefore, Islamic education needs to be reconstructed through the strengthening of adab-based digital literacy, the revitalization of the concept of ta’dib, and synergy between families, schools, and the community. These efforts are expected to foster a generation of strong character and integrity, capable of navigating social change without losing Islamic values.

items.title: Islam and Psychology: The Islamization of Modern Psychology
items.abstract: Majoriti sarjana Muslim yang prihatin dengan nasib komuniti Muslim (Ummah) telah terlibat secara mendalam dengan konsep Islamisasi ilmu pengetahuan yang mendapat momentum pada tahun 80-an sebagai hasil kesedaran global terhadap "kebangkitan Islam" pada tahun 70-an. Artikel ini melihat bagaimana kepercayaan, nilai, dan amalan budaya Islam mempengaruhi pemahaman mengenai kesihatan mental dan tingkah laku manusia. Perbincangan ini termasuk penerokaan mengenai impak prinsip-prinsip Islam terhadap kesejahteraan psikologi, seperti konsep Tawhid (keesaan Allah), Akhirah (hidup selepas mati), dan Qadar (takdir ilahi). Artikel ini juga membincangkan aspek praktikal penyatuan ajaran Islam dalam intervensi psikologi, menekankan peranan amalan Islam, termasuk solat, berpuasa, dan penglibatan komuniti, dalam meningkatkan kesejahteraan mental. Kepekaan budaya yang diperlukan dalam bekerja dengan populasi Muslim yang pelbagai ditekankan, kerana variasi wujud berdasarkan perbezaan kawasan, linguistik, dan budaya. Artikel ini membincangkan proses Islamisasi psikologi moden, di mana prinsip-prinsip Islam, nilai, dan konteks budaya berpadu dengan harmoni dengan kerangka psikologi kontemporari. Sebagai institusi pendidikan tertinggi, universiti dapat menyumbang peranan yang signifikan dalam meningkatkan proses Islamisasi psikologi moden yang akan menyokong usaha pembaharuan dan pembangunan ummah. The majority of Muslim scholars concerned with the plight of the Muslim community (Ummah) have been deeply involved with the concept of Islamization of knowledge which gained momentum in the 80s as a result of the global consciousness for the "resurgence of Islam" in the 70s. It examines how Islamic beliefs, values, and cultural practices influence the understanding of mental health and human behavior. The discussion includes an exploration of the impact of Islamic principles on psychological well-being, such as concepts of Tawhid (oneness of God), Akhirah (the afterlife), and Qadar (divine predestination). This article also addresses the practical aspects of integrating Islamic teachings into psychological interventions, highlighting the role of Islamic practices, including prayer, fasting, and community engagement, in promoting mental well-being. The cultural sensitivity required in working with diverse Muslim populations is emphasized, as variations exist based on regional, linguistic, and cultural differences. This article discusses the process of the Islamization of modern psychology, where Islamic principles, values and cultural context harmoniously meld with the framework of contemporary psychology. As the highest educational institution, the universities can contribute a significant role toward enhancing the Islamization of modern psychology projects that would serve Islam and support the reform and development efforts of the ummah.

items.title: Embodied attention shapes temporal cognition
items.abstract: Abstract Humans rely on spatial representations to process both temporal duration and mentally project themselves across time. Yet, it remains unclear whether this spatial–temporal mapping depends on embodied mechanisms or on abstract attentional codes. We investigated whether embodied cues (gaze direction) versus abstract cues optokinetic stimulation (OKS) modulate Mental Time Travel (MTT) and age judgement. Gaze direction induced direction‐specific effects in both tasks: in MTT leftward gaze enhanced the perceived likelihood of past events, while rightward gaze enhanced judgements for future events; in the Age Judgement task leftward cues yielded younger estimates and rightward cues older estimates. Conversely, non‐embodied OKS biased Age Judgements but induced no direction‐specific effects in the MTT task. Overall, these dissociations suggest that embodied cues play a specific role in modulating temporal projection in MTT, whereas non‐embodied attentional cues are sufficient to bias age‐related temporal estimates. These findings suggest that temporal projection during MTT relies more strongly on embodied perceptual mechanisms, whereas judgements of longer temporal durations can be shaped by domain‐general attentional processes.

items.title: Neural Modulation Strategies in Neuroscience
items.abstract: Chemogenetics is a powerful and versatile neuromodulation strategy that enables remote, reversible control of defined cell populations through the use of engineered receptors and pharmacologically inert small-molecule ligands. This review synthesizes the current state of chemogenetic technologies, focusing on Designer Receptors Exclusively Activated by Designer Drugs (DREADDs) and emerging ion-channel-based actuators, and outlines their molecular mechanisms, ligand pharmacology, and recent technical innovations. We examine the broad applications of these tools in disease modeling, behavioral neuroscience, and experimental therapeutics, as well as in biomedical contexts beyond the central nervous system. Particular attention is given to the role of chemogenetics in mapping and causally dissecting neural circuits, where it provides precise and reversible modulation of neuronal activity to elucidate the cellular substrates of behavior. Comparisons with other neuromodulation techniques—such as optogenetics and electrical stimulation—are discussed, together with practical considerations including ligand selection, delivery strategies, and long-term applications. Finally, we highlight the translational trajectory of chemogenetic technologies, emphasizing ongoing advances that are bringing gene therapy-based neuromodulation closer to clinical application in neurology and psychiatry.

items.title: Comparative Study of Education, Society and Culture: United Kingdom and India
items.abstract: International educational immersion provides an opportunity to understand education not merely as a system of schools and examinations but as a social and cultural process shaped by institutions, communities, public spaces and everyday practices. This study presents a qualitative comparative analysis of educational, social and cultural observations made during a 10-day Summer School immersion programme in the United Kingdom in June 2026. The participating group comprised 23 delegates, including 18 students aged 8–15 years and five adult mentors, teachers and caretakers from different parts of India. The group was hosted at Clayesmore School in Dorset and participated in classroom learning, extracurricular activities, boarding-house routines, educational excursions, cultural activities and interactions with UK students and teachers. The study adopted an experiential qualitative approach involving participant observation, informal interviews, discussions, reflective journals, photographs, audio and video records, documentary materials and daily group reflections. The findings indicate notable differences in classroom interaction, experiential learning, reflective writing, student autonomy, assessment practices, practical education, community engagement and learning beyond the classroom. The observations further suggest that educational outcomes are influenced by the wider social environment, including public transport, walkability, civic behaviour, community infrastructure and access to cultural spaces. The findings are interpreted using experiential learning, social learning, ecological systems, cultural capital, systems and urban-community perspectives. Rather than advocating direct transplantation of British educational practices into India, the study argues for contextual adaptation of selected practices, particularly experiential learning, reflective assessment, interdisciplinary activities, student responsibility, community-based learning and structured international immersion.

items.title: Identifying Priority Locations for Sea Cucumber Conservation in Indonesia Using Multimetric Biodiversity
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Sea cucumber fisheries have a boom‐and‐bust history, with most being overexploited and some depleted; thus, biodiversity conservation requires an objective framework to identify high‐priority areas. Sea cucumbers are an important trade commodity in Indonesia and are facing population declines in specific locations for certain species. This study aims to identify priority locations for conserving sea cucumbers in Indonesia based on multimetric biodiversity and to determine environmental predictors of sea cucumber diversity patterns. Surveys were conducted at 23 locations across Indonesia, resulting in the observation of 4109 sea cucumbers (39 species). Nine species are categorized as threatened (endangered or vulnerable by the IUCN Red List), four are listed in the CITES Appendix II, and 10 have high economic value. Nine multimetric biodiversity metrics (i.e., species richness, total abundance, beta diversity, rarity index, number of threatened species, abundance of threatened species, abundance of CITES species, number of high economic value species and abundance of high economic value species) are used to identify priority locations for sea cucumber conservation. The results suggest the top three locations that stand out as Indonesia's foremost sites for sea cucumber conservation: Sekotong, Biak and Kaimana. These locations collectively excel in species richness, beta diversity, threatened species, CITES species and high‐value species, ensuring comprehensive protection of sea cucumber biodiversity, which is essential for ecosystem resilience and sustainable fisheries. Other locations could also be considered areas for sea cucumber conservation, but perhaps only to achieve specific goals. Furthermore, our results demonstrate that a traditional fishing closure (‘sasi’) and marine protected areas (MPAs) benefit conservation. Our findings will address one of the issues related to the government's plans to designate ~30% of Indonesian waters as MPAs by 2045 and will serve as a scientific basis for establishing a national action plan for the conservation and sustainable use of sea cucumbers.
